WILLIAM HOWARD
"MONK"
MONTGOMERY

Interviewer:
Maggie Hawthorn
Las Vegas, Nevada
October 30 - November 2, 1980
It says in the Encyclopedia that you are William Howard Montgomery, but I've never known you as anything but Monk. When did you get that name?
Well, that's a good question, because it was so far back I don't remember.
When you were little?
Yeah, I was named Monk but I don't know who named me. I tried to trace it back, but Monk is all I was ever accustomed to hearing.
Is that what everybody called you, in the family?
Everybody. There were times schoolteachers called me Monk.
But your brothers didn't have nicknames like that, did they?
Not like that, but they had nicknames. Wes's name, his name was...that's not his real name. His name was John Leslie.
Really, I didn't know that. Buddy, I know, is Charles.
Yeah, his name is Charles. So, I guess, years ago...
And you had another brother, too.
I had an older brother, was two years older than I, and he passed in his late teens. He passed, and he was talented...
Did he play?
He played drums, and a very good drummer. I remember very distinctly that, I guess I was about 15, 16 years old, Chick Webb had come to town with his band...
Was this in Indianapolis?

We were in Columbus, Ohio at that time. You see, during that period that we had left Indianapolis to go to Columbus, and I'll tell you a little bit more about that, but...Chick Webb had come to town and there was a contest going on, and he was there to perform this contest...
Was it in a theater?
...in a theater. You know, just youngsters, and he won the contest.
Your brother?

Yeah, right. I remember Chick Webb, being a drummer, that he would sort of praise him for his drumming, for his work as a drummer, but he wasn't what you would call an educated drummer. Just a youngster with natural talent, an expression, not a schooled drummer.
Did he just pick it up?
Oh yeah, he didn't have any background, training; he just picked it up. It was something he wanted to do.
As I understand it, isn't that the way all of you started? Did anybody in your family ever have lessons?

No, not that I knew of, unless Buddy and Wes sneaked out somewhere, there was no formal training whatsoever. As I was explaining, about that period that we were in Columbus, at the age of 9...My folks had separated and at the age of 9 I was left...my mother...let me see. Wes and my older brother -- his real name was Thomas and they called him June. He was a "junior" so they all called him June -- the three of us (June, myself and Wes) had gone to Columbus to spend some time with my dad. We had gone for the Christmas holidays, I remember.
From Indianapolis.

From Indianapolis, where we were actually, my home. We were born there. Because he had moved to Columbus and he was staying with his...he had relatives there, my aunt, his sister, Aunt Maureen. And we went to Columbus and ended up staying there ten years, almost to the day, that I came back. I was 19 when I come back to Indianapolis to live. In the meantime, my older brother June died in that period that we were in Columbus. And Wes and I moved back to Indianapolis ten years later.

And Wes was the first, naturally, to get off into the music. Well, I shouldn't say that. June was, but he passed earlier. He was two years older than I. Because he was two years older than I and Wes was two years younger than I, there was actually four years between Wes's age and his, roughly that is.
But I remember when Wes got involved with the music. I had quit school. I quit school at the age of 14.
That must have been in Depression years, wasn't it?
Oh yes, this was like....
What year?
In the thirties. I can back it up and give you about the year it was. Let me see...'34, '35.
Right in the middle...
Right, hard times, yeah. I remember the Depression very, very clearly. I quit school and went to work, and I was working in an ice and coal yard.
What did you do?

During that time, people used fuel in small quantities, because it was rough times. You bought coal by the bushel baskets and when...the refrigerator wasn't...you know, it was the icebox and they got that by the 25, 50, 75 or a hundred pounds. And I was working at this little shed. That's what I did, was sold ice and coal. I worked for a gentleman that gave me the job, was a very nice man. He was like a father to me, too.
You were 14?

I was 14. I remember that period very clearly, and it was a strange period to me because it was hard for me to understand it. I never got really adjusted, totally adjusted, from the time that I was separated from my mother, that side (of the family), you know. Because it was a whole different life style to adjust to living with my father and having to go for yourself, that type of thing. But, as I look back on it, I treasure that because I think there were some things developed under his roof that wouldn't have been, possibly, developed under the other roof, had it been the other way.
You mean about music, or other things?

No, not music, a way of life. The way of life. Because, you know, it was rough and you had to come through that. You had to. It was quite an experience, and I felt like I was really developed into manhood when I, at the age of 19... there was no question about it.

And at the age of 14, like I said, going to work for this Mr. Cooper, a very nice gentleman, and he taught me how to drive. I learned how to drive in a Model A truck, a little pickup truck that he had. And that's what we used to go to the coal yard to pick up a ton, half a ton, or whatever we bought, to bring it back to the shed and break it down to bushel baskets.

And that's how I made it. In the winter time we sold coal, summer time we sold ice. So it was all year around for me. Of course, we had a little slow season in the spring and fall because they didn't hardly go too much either way. But I was very happy working with Mr. Cooper, because it gave me a chance to have a job and that meant something. You know, even at age 14, jobs were...there just wasn't anything to have. However, my salary didn't speak of anything. I got $6 a week working with him, but $6 a week was a lot of money at the time, because my dad was making $15 a week.
Doing what?
He was working in wholesale fruits and vegetables.

He was working for the owners of this company, wholesale fruits and vegetables, so he was a truck driver. His job was more or less like he would unload the boxcars that would come in, from wherever they shipped stuff in from. Where the fruits and vegetables come in, he'd unload them from the boxcars, bring it back to the wholesale house and break it down, cut bananas and stack them into the boxes. I had a lot of experiences going and working with him, as a child.
Did Wes quit school too?

No, Wes continued going. Wes was like the youngest. However, there was still two younger than Wes but they were Buddy and my sister Lena. But they lived with my mother, you see, so Wes was the youngest there. So you know how it is with the youngest. They get sort of like a special treatment. And he was pretty smart. He learned how to get in and out of things; he was pretty shifty about that.

But very likeable. Far back as I can remember, everybody liked Wes. They loved Wes. He had quite a personality and character even then. I remember when I was working this job, there was...let me get the timing right in my head...at the age...I remember the streets.

When we first moved to Columbus to stay with my dad in Columbus, Ohio, it was at the corner of St. Claire and Star St, upstairs, second floor. And after a few, couple or so, years of living there my dad got another house on Talmadge and Spring. (It's great ) when you think of it, it just comes to you). And while we were living at Talmadge and Spring, which I must have been now about 13 or 14 and Wes was a couple of years younger, I remember during this period living on Talmadge there was a guy living down the street by the name of Preach O'Bannon, a sort of masculine kind of guy.

He was a fairly pleasant man, he's always...he played a tiple, a kind of guitar. You remember a tiple? Five-string guitar? He was the kind of guy, used to walk up and down the street playing his tiple and just singing, just a happy man.
What kind of things did he sing?

He'd sing like blues, he'd sing like things...I don't know that much about music about what was going on. Most of the songs he sang, as I remember, sounded like it was probably something he wrote. Sound like he would just create things as he'd go along, walking up and down the street with his little tee shirt on. He'd be singing things that were... he had to have made those things up. He'd rhyme the trees and birds and things as he'd go along.

And he used to come, like at our house, and because I guess we enjoyed hearing him do that, and the kids dance while he played. We'd be out in the yard or whatever, he'd stop and play for us awhile. We danced in the yard; not dancers dancing, just kids having fun.

And I remember he showed Wes...Wes was interested in the stringed instruments. And the day that he...He said, "The first thing you got to learn how to do is to tune it. And the easiest way to remember how, what your tuning is," and I remember him saying it, "is 'My Dog Has Fleas,'" that little thing, right?
But a tiple has five strings.

Right. So then he showed him how to get to the other string from that, and still had the four. And I remember Preach used to sit on our porch at the steps, and he'd strike at some things, at playing. He didn't know that many changes, all he could do was solo work, but it felt good when he played. It felt like a happy sound, especially when he sang along with it, you see. There's no question about he was just the type of person that picked this up. Just picked it up and started playing, you know. He wasn't...no formal training. Just a natural thing, just finding his way around the changes.
And Wes got hooked from that?
That's my first...that was his first introduction to the stringed instrument, the guitar, the tiple.
What about you?

No, it didn't do anything to me. No more than like the other kids out there that would just laugh with Preach and dance in the yard as he played. Sort of like a little dirt yard; no grass even for the kids. Meanwhile...it just wasn't my time to be affected by whatever happens to this stuff you say that's in your blood. I believe it is. But it just wasn't my period. I wasn't open for it. I didn't have as much going for me in that area as Wes. Because he...it was there, definitely there.
How did he react to that?

It was great, because I remember he had...Preach showed him, let him try and hold it and play. And showed him how to make a couple of chords and whatever, because he was really interested, showed the interest.

And Preach showed him how to tune it and how to make a couple of chords or so, whatever, minor chords. And they would...Preach spent a little time with him. Wes didn't have his own guitar and when Preach was about he'd let him play on his a little bit. I'm not even clear in my mind how much, or what degree, or whatever, but I do know they spent a little time together and Wes was really interested.

I remember that Wes came home and said there was a guy...up at the corner from where we lived there was a theater right on the corner, the Pythian Theater, at the corner of St. Claire and Mt. Vernon, right at that corner. And Wes was saying there was a guy down by the show that had a guitar he wanted to

sell for fifty cents. For fifty cents, he wanted this guitar. And I'm trying to get it in my mind...fifty cents was a lot of money to come by, and the guy just needed fifty cents. I guess he wanted to take his girl to the show or whatever and have plenty of money to do whatever over and above it.

And I remember there was a hustling going on, trying to raise fifty cents for a guitar. Nobody knew that much about a guitar but fifty cents...you can't go wrong. And I remember...this is a long time ago...that it was quite a bit of excitement and hustling trying to come by fifty cents, which we weren't able to do. And, knowing my dad like we did, it was nonsense going to him for any foolishness like that, you know.
So you didn't ask him?

No, he wasn't approached for this fifty cents. But the next thing I remember really deeply about Wes and the guitar, we had moved again from that street to Grove St. That's when I was really working at the ice and coal yard, shed. Wes had saw a guitar in a pawn shop. Thirteen dollars.
That's a lot of money.

That's a lot of money. But it looked like a brand new guitar. I mean, not a little toy thing, a little toy instrument. This was a real, real instrument in his window. He had saw it in his window, and I guess he had gone in and talked to the guy, and the guy had let him see it, or whatever. And it was $13. And he was wild, man, he was just excited about this guitar.

And when I worked at the coal yard, it was like...I was always the sort of person that was really pinchy with my money. It was always important to me to save. Always important to me. I used to hide my money. We had a Victrola, a wind-up Victrola, in our living room. And if you take that front, what do you call it, the facing...lift up and lift that facing out. And where the speaker comes out, reaching in under that speaker, that's where I hid my little stash. I had my little stash.

And the way I accumulated money...it was very honest. There was nothing dishonest about my little money. Say, for an example, when I was selling coal in the winter time, that was my best period, winter time for me. Coal was an item...people had to buy coal. It was 25 cents a bushel, and a bushel weighed 52 pounds. Anyhow, when I weighed up the bushels of coal, when I brought them back, on a scale, you'd get anywhere from 30 to 32 bushels out of a ton.
Well, when I'd go to the coal yard to pick up the coal, I got so that I would weigh the truck. And you'd back the truck in, fill your truck up, that's how you'd figure out you

got a ton of coal, when you'd re-weigh it. And when you got too much, you'd throw a little off, according to weight. So by me going in quite a bit, I got so that I would be...kept seeing the guys, and I'd get away with a few nice big lumps of coal. So that was extra weight, when I would come back to weigh it up and give the people their honest load of coal. But if it was over 32 bushels, that was mine, where the guy threw it on the truck.
That's your profit.

That was my profit. So there were times maybe I sold, in the run of the day, if I had sold a couple tons of coal, made a couple of trips and picked up two or three baskets, the money would add up for me, extra money.
How much did you have in your stash?

In my stash? I've had my stash up as high as, oh, up in the 'teens. Fifteen, sixteen, seventeen dollars. And really, it was a strange feeling. I had to wait until it was absolutely nobody in the house but me, no one within twenty blocks of the house before I'd go in my stash.
Did Wes know you had that?

Nobody knew I had my stash. Well, Wes knew I had a stash but they never knew what it amounted to or anything. I never...that was very personal, what was in my stash. And I had, late hours at night or whatever, when I'd get a chance and it was quiet -- nobody was around, couldn't be seen -- I'd take my stash out and I'd count it, just to be re-counting.

That was a lot of money. That was a lot of money. But I remember, I had taken from the stash and gave him $13 to buy this guitar. And that was a lot of money. But to have a real guitar, that's why he's....
And then he began by himself, from there?
Right there. I'm telling you. I wasn't, like I said, into music or tuned in at that age. I wasn't tuned in...
Not at all? Did you listen to the radio?

But Wes...Oh, yeah, we listened to radio. You know, there was all there was to listen to. We listened to...We had a radio. My dad had one of those floor model radios, the big floor model that...I guess it needed some repair work on it because it would go in and out, the sound would go in and out.
What did you listen to on it?
Well, we'd listen to those bands, the late night things coming from faraway places like Chicago. And there were

...it wasn't that he was a radio listener. He listened and didn't listen; he heard and didn't hear. There was no...you go to the radio to turn to a certain station because there's a certain program. The program had to do with scary stories. There was a lot of that; there was more of that in radio...
So you didn't especially use it to tune in to the bands?

No, there wasn't a whole lot of bands to be tuned. The traffic of music wasn't like it is. There were some to be heard, but Columbus wasn't popular [with the bands], of course. Like I say, I remember that there were stations in Louisville, or in faraway places. But there were times when, on Saturdays I think it was, mainly, you could hear a lot of jazz and bands. And the bands were like...I remember Andy Kirk and I remember } Chick Webb, and I remember, naturally, all the people in that era.
Well, you said you had a Victrola. What kind of records did you listen to?

Well, it was later that I was going to say about, when we got into the playing of records. We found out about a place that was where they take records from juke boxes. After they take them off juke boxes...they take them out to the store, the plant, whatever. And they re-sold those that were on the juke box. You could buy that record for seven cents, you could buy records off of a juke box for seven cents.

So we used to get on our bicycles and ride on the West Side. It was across the street from the mental institution. And they had records that you go in, buy these records off the juke box. And those...that's how we kind of got into it.
What kind?

We'd buy things from, I remember, Cab Calloway. We'd grab Cab Calloway because there's so much humor in his singing, what he was doing...his happy humor, hi-de-hi, hi-de-ho. We got things of...mostly the big band things. It wasn't alot of quintet things. It was mostly big band things, and things of the singers. I remember, I think it was Charley Cooke's band, had Chu Berry, the horn player.

Then my friend, one of my oldest dear friends, who has passed away during the late '70s, he would go out and he would buy whatever, maybe two or three apiece. Ride out and come back with two or three records and that's how we found ourselves exchanging different ones.

What happened was, I remember in the period of the WPA* where the government paid, subsidized...they were subsidizing not only works in terms of manual labor but they were also subsidizing people with professions such as musicians. They would play in the park. And they got enough
*Works Progress Administration.
transcripts,or somehow they just pay them the difference, you know?

Anyhow, I remember going to the park to hear bands playing. Local bands. And there'd be people dancing. A really tight time, tight period. You could look forward to going out on Friday evenings, Friday or Saturday. However, one thing they could go to the park and they just shut out...The band would be playing and the people would be laughing, full of joy over the music.
Is that when you felt you might like to be a musician?

No. I enjoyed just being in the atmosphere. I enjoyed being happy with groups of people that were all suppressed so much. It was a release for all of us, a sort of a thing that we shared. It had nothing to do with the musicians or into the music. It was just that it was a place to go to let it out, you know, to be...Well, the Depression was rough.
I remember going to the YMCA. They had a dance down there, and that's when I remember trying to dance...and no way! I couldn't get into dancing. I just didn't have no rhythm.

And I remember another period where we worked at...on a Saturday at the Empress Theater, we had a thing every Saturday afternoon, was a contest. And that meant that before the movie started -- cowboys and the whole thing, you know, cowboys and cartoons on Saturday -- all the kids would come in and they could line up to be in the contest, to perform on stage, before the movie started. So all the ones that performed got in free. So this was like a free ticket, a free way in to the show.
Now, we'd talk among ourselves and get a little group together to go down and play, see. Wes could play, and my older brother June could play.
But what did you do?
I remember I had a...I can't even remember where this guitar came from, but there was a guitar, and I was strumming it as if I was playing.
But you weren't really?
No! No, you know, I wasn't...
Did that bother Wes?

No, it was a fun thing. It was just a free way to get in the show. Because there were other kids perhaps ten times worse than we were. But to get on the stage and perform, just being on that stage, it was great. And the ones in the audience would...were just enjoying a bunch of clowns on the stage.
Well, at some point did you really decide that you wanted to play something?

It was late for me, it was very late. Because when I left Columbus at the age of 19, and when I moved to Indianapolis -- Wes and I moved there together because my older brother had passed on -- Wes and I came back to Indianapolis. And I went to work in the foundries when I got there.

My folks worked at the Mable(?) in Indianapolis. My mother had been there some years in, they call it the nipple department, where they make the little nipples of the...the little thing they spin around to put like a little sleeve on pipes or something. I don't know what it was, just a little thing that they do. And she had been there for some time. In the meantime, she had remarried, so my stepfather, he also worked there.

So they got me a job just like, right on. And when I went to work at the mill, I was working what they call straight time, something like that. Whatever...40 hours a week, I made $21 dollars a week! I didn't know what to do with myself with that much money, and it was all mine. $21 a week. Because the money I had made prior to that in Columbus, which was nothing in comparison to that, I also had to use that to help provide for the home.

It wasn't like all my money, but when I went back to Indianapolis to stay with my mother, and she had this nice home and everything, was like I'd never experienced it before. And not only that, I had to sort of like, after ten years away from them, I had to almost learn all over again. I had to learn how to say 'Mama' all over again; it sounded funny when I would say 'Mama.' And it was so natural for my sister and brother, Buddy and Lena.

But it was like a whole new way of life, a new concept. Everything was different. It was great! It was really great, especially when I got this job. Because working, to me, was like the most important thing, to have a job to provide for yourself. That's what had been instilled in me for so long. Plus that, I was chinchy and I wanted to have money and see that I could do things for myself. Independent, I guess.

But here I have this job making $21 a week. It just seemed like, wow! I bought myself a car. The car only cost $25 down and $25 a month. I forgot what year it was, but the car was only a year old, you know, the year before that. Imagine me with my own car, my own money. It was just unbelievable, just unbelievable. I'm sorry -- $50 down and $25 a month. Because I had to save $6.25 a week, I think it was, to pay for the car. Yeah, $6.25 a week is what my payments were on the car, $ 25 a month. So I was like going into a whole new life.

In the meantime, my brother Buddy, when I moved to Columbus Buddy now was like 11 years old because...he was a lot younger. So I didn't know him; he was a total stranger...

we were to each other, you see. He was just a baby when I left. And just like a little kid to me, you know. And it was hard for me to adjust to him like I was to Wes, because Wes and I came up. But I remember, Wes was like...he's always been that way, something magical about him. He was...I remember evenings in the summertime, down at the park, you could see a crowd of people and you knew Wes was in the center of the crowd, they were crowded around Wes and his guitar.
You mean he'd take his guitar to the park and play?
Oh, yeah. He was just...he was just...
So he's about 17 at this time?
Yeah, I was 19, he was 17. I was 19 when we first moved back.
What kinds of things would he play when he sat in the park?

Well, there was a guy in Indianapolis by the name of Alec Stevens, and we had heard his name. Alec Stavens, a guitar player. Before we moved to Indianapolis, Alec Stevens was like the musician, the guy, and especially guitar. Left-hand guitar player, you know. When Wes came it was like...heads up, you know?
Somehow in these few years he had become a really accomplished player?
Oh, yeah, he had developed his self completely aside from where...we were in two different worlds. I don't know how he did...
Was he playing with other people at that time? Or was he still just playing by himself?
No, he was just by himself. I'm sure he spent time with other people but not like having a...with another group or, you know, with a big thing going on.
But up until that time, you still hadn't played?

Well, I was making money, you see; I was busy making money...and buying cars. But I was in the prime of my life, at that time, It had opened up another whole new avenue that had nothing to do with playing the music. I enjoyed it, I knew... I appreciated it and all that. But it just hadn't gotten to me. It hadn't really affected me in the same way. I enjoyed music. I like it and I liked being around and hearing it. I liked to listen to it and all that.

But I remember Wes was like always the center of attraction. But very likeable, always happy-go-lucky, just... and that's what his music came out like, it was just that force from the energy inside. I remember he and Alec Stevens got to

be very close and they played a lot together, so I'm sure that he had a lot to do with Wes'...the turning point for him, right there, when he come back to Indianapolis and he got in that kind of company, with the amount of total freedom that we both had, different than what we had lived under the roof of my dad. Because with my mother, it was just like a whole new way of life. Great.

I'm trying to concentrate on Wes because he was the one that was really in the direction of music. I wasn't in the direction of music during that period. As a matter of fact, I was at the age of 21, I had gotten married and had a son and started my family, and I had moved and got my own house and... I worked, I really had gotten to be pretty good at the kind of work I was doing, which was still foundry. And I made a lot of money.

I said a lot of money; I mean for that kind of work. And I managed to, we managed to -- my wife and I -- to save and buy a piece of property and build my own home. That's where my head was, not into music. Really not into music. But I was always wondering or concerned about Wes, what he was doing, because we came up so close, even though he had married and had his...
He married earlier, didn't he?
Oh, yeah. Wes married a little before I did, because I remember we used to talk about it a lot. So he married...I was 21 so he must have been about 19.
But he was playing in clubs and working at the same time.

Yeah, by that time he was working, getting work around. At 19 or 20, he was jobbing around, exactly what I don't know because I wasn't in that traffic at all, I was over on the other path, doing other things, full time.
Well, what was it that finally turned you to music?

It's very strange. I remember a couple of things happened to me. One, the last one, really took the biggest effect. One thing happened, I remember Wes went on the road. It was the first time he'd gone out on the road. And I was sort of like...it struck me a little funny when, even though we'd gone our separate ways, we weren't living under the same roof as brothers...youngsters coming up, we'd turned into our adulthood. And I had my family and he had his family,

And I remember the occasion, it came about that he was gonna go on the road. And I'd come by Mama's house and he was telling us about it, that he had an offer to go with Snookum Russell. Now, Snookum Russell had quite a name, so we knew that was quite a thing.
He was in that band the same time Ray Brown was...

Right, I was gonna say this. As a matter of fact, that's when I first heard Ray Brown's name come up to me. I'm not, still, in the music; I still wasn't into it. But Wes was talking about going on the road with this band and what a great musical venture it was for him.

It was in his blood, it was in there. Not only that, he was a good musician. It wasn't that he was going on a wild goose chase. He went away with that band, and he stayed for a period of time, months I guess, I'm not sure. But when he came back, I remember very distinctly when he came back.

We got a call that Wes was coming home and we met over at Mama's house; it was always like headquarters, or whatever. And when I saw Wes, I said 'Wow!' I was just looking at him with amazement. He had an all-leather bag. He had --and he was a dresser, he always -- but he had really gone into clothes. At this time, he had straightened his hair; he had what you call a conk. His hair was straight. He had a diamond ring on. I don't know if it was a real diamond or not, but you know it was a big flashing ring and...
Impressive, though.

Oh, very impressive. And he had this watch, the chain was gold. Well, that's the kind of guy Wes was. Big cufflinks. Right to the very end, that was Wes. But he was that kind...he liked that kind of dressing, that's what he liked his appearance to be. But he looked different, he looked so different. And I was trying to figure out what it was. Until I...he sat and talked for a while, and finally I saw him do it. He had a little powder pull, a little fine thing, right? And that's what he wiped his face with.
Why?
It powdered you down, like if you're going on TV, how you go to...
Take the shine off your face.

Keep the shine off and keep that look, right. I just loved it for him, because he was genuine and that was Wes. That was him. He had a leather coat. I never saw clothes like that. I guess I saw them and didn't see them, you know. But I never think of seeing Wes with this, and he looked the part. Those clothes fit him to a tee, he belonged in them. My eyes were like...I finally really saw the true Wes. Because that's where his...
He was happy.

He was happy, because he was well dressed and he was gay and he just looked good. He just looked great. And as we sat there and talked, there was a few of us sitting there in the family, and he was telling different stories. You know:
this is where he had been and what they were doing, so-and-so, and I was looking at him like I never saw him before. He was all at once like my older brother, because of his experiences.

I began to feel sort of, such a junior to him, because of his experiences. And I admired him so much because he was successful. He was really successful as a musician. What had happened to him carried him, it was there. He knew that was for him. It was almost like he'd gone and came back and made good and he didn't have to tell you, you see. It was there.

And he was glad, he was happy to be home and he was... everyone was asking questions and I was just sitting there looking at him. And that's when I saw him for the first time in another way. I really, really was happy for him because everything about him just glowed, like... I was really proud of him. I was so proud of him I didn't know what to do.

I think that's one time when I got the feeling of how important, of what it meant to a person to be able to express themselves and do what they want to do. What a joy that was, no matter what the cost.
And did you think that you might want to express yourself in some other way than working in a foundry?

Right. Now, I was sure that... I knew that wasn't what I wanted to do for myself. However, I didn't have any other formal training. I didn't know how to do anything else. And there was always a hidden fear, and I'm sure there's a lot of people the same way. You know, they can look at this and admire that and be attracted to that, but are they capable? Capable of doing that well, without any proper... Some things you can make with training, but the other thing you have to have a natural talent. Now I'm saying...
Is that what gave you the boost to...

I don't think that's what did it, but it sure put it in my mind. Because I was, naturally I had thought... I was exercising thoughts such as, 'I wonder could I be a musician?' But I knew how hard Wes had been at it. You know, I hear this cat saying, 'Well, I think I'll pick up this instrument and I'll play.' It's not that easy. It's not done quite like that.

But when (it puts in on your mind, because everybody wants to be somebody. Everybody wants to have some success. There are certain things that are important, I'm sure, in everyone's life, whether they come to terms with it or not. But I know that there were periods that I came to terms with it with myself, and that was one of the outstanding time that I did, when I was sitting there looking at my brother who had gone off and had some success. And he was a little bit younger...
But you didn't rush right down to the corner store and buy a bass fiddle.

Oh, no. Because I knew even those times when the height of my thing was when I bought the car, the height of that was nothing in comparison to what he had gone through. You see, I was busy doing what I thought was the greatest thing, to work this job and to achieve so-and-so. But none of that meant anything to what he was just sitting there saying and showing. You could see it. And naturally, that said to me I wasn't sure, but I knew that nothing in the world could be any more important than to be able to express yourself.
What did you do, then?

Well, it came later for me, so far as the music. I continued doing what I was doing. What I was doing, I was doing it very well but it didn't have the same meaning...it wasn't what life was about. I had strong thoughts at that time, really really strong thoughts of...Prior to that, to show you how things work, I was very successful at doing what I was doing in terms of a lay person and money. But at that time it was, like, after the war (started), 1941 There was a lot of work.

I wasn't inducted into the army or anything. I was turned down because I had knee problems, no reflex in the knees or something. Anyhow, I remember, I was working, making good money, working Saturdays and Sundays and overtime. Just, if you can call it, making good.

And I saved my money. I bought a piece of property and we started, we built our home. And I started another savings because I was going to go into a business for myself. I had a goal I wanted to achieve. And at the time I thought... I had sort of like chosen that it...something that I think I really wanted to be into...I was gonna buy a dump truck. Go into trucking, that kind of business, construction.

Because there was a guy living across the street from me, and he was a black man and he had a dump truck. And he was sand and gravel-type thing, because of road construction and building going on, quite a bit of it. And he was one of the very few blacks that were able to get contracts here or there, to work independently. And I had some conversation with him. He said, 'Well...' and he was a nice man, and he would say, 'Montgomery, you're a nice fella and you could do so-and-so-and-so, and I'll be happy to introduce you to certain people so maybe you could make it in that.' I could...he was trying to encourage me of getting this dump truck because if you were lucky...it was during that time, too, if a black man could have a decent chance of being an independent business man. And I could have built the business. I could have one truck and bought another truck and bought another truck. So here I'm trying to see myself with a string of trucks, in the trucking business.
Well, that's balanced against something that really wasn't very...
Right, you know, I had to do something. I wanted my

life to mean something besides just working in the foundry. And I remember, I took Wes to a rehearsal. He had a job...he had come home, right? He was working locally. He was working a job at a place called The Keys on Meridian St. Yeah, that was it, a really big street...And he was working out on Meridian St. at a place called The Keys.
It was a private club; class, class, class. In fact, you had to belong to have a key to get in,and this is how they come about the name of The Keys.

I had taken Wes to the rehearsal, and it was with a trio. The guy that was the leader of the trio was a bass player by the name of...I can't think of his name, because everybody called him Stuff. And that was picked up because he calls everybody Stuff. So people just called him Stuff. That was just his name, because everybody was 'Stuff' to Stuff.

And the piano player was a gentleman by the name of Errol Grandy. And Errol Grandy was the, I guess he was the idol of everybody, all musicians in town. Errol Grandy was, like, the daddy of the musicians in town. And he was about 90 % blind. And such a talent. Everybody came to Errol, to get things straightened out, and he was always open to help, teach, do, or whatever.
What kind of music did they play?

Jazz, babe, yeah. Well, by now, we listened to people like...Errol Garner was really in, and Art Tatum and in that era. Back in, oh, what year was this, like the middle forties, I guess. Late forties? A lot of good jazz. Bebop was in then, bebop was straight ahead.

I'm getting turned on to music now, I'm really getting turned on to bebop, Dizzy, Parker and guys like that. I'm really getting turned on. I'm picking up a few records of my own; I'm into buying a few records. There was a lot of it available in the local clubs. Not names, necessarily, but the local guys.
Good local musicians...

Good local musicians. And what a challenge bebop was for them. So I guess that was on a national scale of everybody trying to play like Parker, Bird and Miles, Thelonious Monk, Max Roach and the beboppers.

Anyhow, on this afternoon, Wes had to go to work on his gig at The Keys and I took him to the rehearsal. And we went in the place and the place was just immaculate, fabulous. They played on the second floor. Now, as I said, the guy Stuff was the bass player, the leader.
But you know how that goes. Anybody that get a job and call two more guys, or however many guys, whoever gets the job is the leader. It's always been that way and I guess it always

will be.

Stuff was a good politician. He did a lot of other things beside play music, that was kind of like one of his little hustles. So, being in the right place at the right time, he always come up with the good gigs.
He got the job.

He got that job. That was his gig. So he got the best two players in town, which was Errol Grandy on piano and Wes on guitar. How could you go wrong? And Wes and Errol just loved each other -- madly. And Errol...So naturally, Stuff got it made.
How did they feel about him as a player?

They didn't...it's like...being really professionals, they didn't embarrass him, nowhere. But you could tell during the rehearsal. The rehearsal was between Wes and Errol. They'd discuss the songs and the music and the changes and they would say things to Stuff, 'Well, Stuff, you just play this in this part,' and 'Don't worry about that there; we got that,' and so they were really feeding off each other so great. And I'm sure they were happy to have the job because it was a good job.

And I was sitting there with amazement, watching the rehearsals, how the rehearsal went down, and I couldn't for the life of me...I couldn't get my mind off of Stuff. Because I'm wondering, 'How did this guy get in the company of these two guys?' And I'm saying...it wasn't that he was so bad that he was horrible, but not in their class. He was nowhere near their class at all. As a matter of fact, I remember them playing some things, and they would try to ignore him, but they would have to stop and say, 'Wait, that's not going to work, Stuff. You gotta ...here's what you gotta...' He couldn't hear it. They had to stop him, you know.
But you could.
I heard it. I really, really heard it.
And you could hear what was necessary.

Yeah. While I was sitting there, my concept is what I heard. I had a feeling of what he should be doing, and all the things I thought that I heard, he wasn't doing those things. So it was, for a while, like sitting on the side, playing the bass in my mind.
But you still didn't really know how to play the bass.
No, I never really touched one.
You never tried...

No. And this was upright. It was no such thing as electric bass then, as we know it. And I heard this and it was like, the whole time I was sitting there, in my mind I guess I was playing the bass. Not physically, but just hearing the notes.

And I remember when the rehearsal was over, and Wes and Errol was always laughing and jolly, laughing so much at each other, it was...they had such great rapport and they had such respect for each other. It came out in the music that way, too. They were laughing and talking, and Stuff was putting his bass away. And he came down and I felt like I wanted to ask him a couple of questions.

And I remember asking him, 'What does an instrument like that cost?' So he turned to me, he said, 'Why? Are you interested in playing, Stuff?' And I said, 'No, not particularly. I was just curious.' And so he explained to me how instruments like that are sold, pricewise, what was the going price. Then he wanted to tell me there was a bass in a repair shop down on Ohio St downtown, a guy by the name of...it was Fid's Fiddle Shop. A guy named Fid owned the fiddle shop, and he had it there for sale.

He said he had saw the bass and been looking at it. He really wanted to buy it but he already had two basses and he didn't need another one, but the price was right. He really wanted that bass because it was a good bass. And this went on, and he said, 'Why don't you go and take a look at it because the guy only wants $75 for it.'

Well, I'm thinking $75, wow. I didn't know it cost that much. I don't know what I was thinking because $75 for a bass is like a steal. And he said, 'If you get the bass, call me, because you know I teach.' And oh, hey, the whole thing, a light went off in my head, 'You'll never teach me!'

But I went down to see that bass, to take a look at that bass a couple days after that day. I was really curious, it was really on my mind. So I went down to Fid's Fiddle Shop and I went in and asked him about a bass. He said, 'Oh, yeah, I know what you're talking. Stuff sent you over here, yeah. So I'll show you the bass.' Then he explained to me that the guy had the bass worked at the Allison Air...the plant where they make aircraft parts or whatever. He said this guy was a night watchman out there. He owned a guitar and he owned this bass. And it was something he wanted to do as a hobby; he didn't want to get into a career with either one.

But he told the guy to sell, he wanted to get rid of one. He didn't care which one. Whichever he sold, he'd keep the other one, the guitar or the bass, and he had these instruments. And I saw the bass and I looked at it, not knowing how to appraise it or put a value on it. All I could think, '75 bucks,' which I didn't have to put on a bass. But I remember, I took the bass. It didn't have a cover to it, and I was just plucking it, just sort of plucking it, not knowing how to play it or
finger it or anything, but just plucking it.
Your first...
Sounds all right. I don't know what to expect, what's good, great, you know...
It satisfied you.

It satisfied then, there in the store. So I say, 'Would it be all right if I put some money down on it?' So he said OK and I gave him 20 bucks down. It gave me time to think about it, that's what I needed. Because I'm still the kind of guy that just don't jump into things right away. It takes a little time for me. And it stayed on my mind so much after I gave him the 20 bucks, that I had to come back and get the bass. I had to get the bass.
It was time.
Yeah. I knew it. It was just as if you turn a page in a book. It was just like that. I knew it, just knew it, when I brought that instrument home. I just knew it...
And when you got it home, did you spend a lot of time?

I sure did. When I brought that bass home, I was still working at the foundry, working on the night shift. Work from 4 to 11, right; so I got off and got home about midnight. And I would go into our extra, we had an extra room in the house, and close the doors. And go into that room. I couldn't wait 'til I got home.

When I got off work at night at the foundry, and took a shower, I was always in the car waiting to leave. (You know, you can get a load and ride together for work) And I couldn't wait to get home. Just couldn't wait to get home. And I would go into this room and close this room. And no light or anything, in the dark. Well, you don't need a light to see how to play the bass. And I would just try and learn how to play the scales.

Meantime, there was a guy lived up above me, by the name of Joe Klute (?), who was a left-handed bass player. He wasn't heavy into bass, he wasn't a heavy player, but he had the instrument and he just loved it and he was just a ham, you know. But he knew something about the fingering I didn't know. But it made it awkward because he played left hand. And he was trying to show me how to hold my fingers...
The opposite...
The opposite. And he had a couple of Jimmy Blanton records, whew!
Had you ever heard him before?
I never heard Jimmy Blanton, never heard his music until Joe Klute, this friend up the street, came down and brought these Jimmy Blanton records.
Were they the ones with Duke...
That's right. And he had every little thing that Jimmy did on this record, he had it down.
Oh, and he could show you?

Yeah. But he was left handed, so I couldn't really get it from him, because it just turned around for me. But he did give me some...it was very encouraging for me working with Joe because he wasn't that far advanced, you see what I'm saying, so I wasn't embarrassed being with Joe.

We had fun, because there was a couple of times Joe brought his bass down and we'd just play with a couple of basses trying to get through what was going. But I couldn't watch him, I couldn't look at him and pick up anything. It threw me off because he was really left-handed. I remember when that happened and I was...during that period I was really ...it got me. It was there. I...
How long did you work every night?

I'd see the sun coming up, the sunlight coming through the windows every morning. You know, every morning. I seemed to get so tied up and really tired, and want to go to sleep, but the sound of that bass in that room -- because with the door shut and it's dark -- it was just like that sound went into my body, like sort of molded together. It was almost a feeling like that, playing in the dark, there was no separation. Me and the instrument and the music kind of just...I'm not saying I was great or anything like that. But I could definitely tell when I was...whatever I was doing, whether it was scales or trying out a little passage or whatever, I felt it. I could feel it, I really felt it. It was like doing something, putting your hands on something that...There's a touch to playing an instrument, and I think...
And you just played by yourself, or did you get to the point where you now wanted to play with somebody?
(end of cass. Mast I-A./cy-I
Well, I got to the point before I was ready, because I had a call to work a gig, after...
After how long?

After a very short period of time. And when I say I came home every night, literally every night I was in there practicing. And when I say practice, I mean I had the music out and the whole business. It was just me and the instrument. I hadn't thought about me being a professional or getting on the road or working with anybody in particular.
Did you read music at all?
No, oh no. I was just loving what I was doing, and wasn't able to explain it. I was really loving what I was doing, to hearing the sound of the bass, hearing the notes that I was making.
So what kind of a call did you get?
Now, the word had got out that I had a bass. All right. And there was a guy there by the name of Cy Jones, was a tenor player. And Cy Jones, he wasn't a tenor player's tenor player by no means.
Whose tenor player was he?
Cy Jones was the kind of a guy that, he would get the gigs, you know. He'd get the gigs where... honkin'
The kind where you lie down on your back?

Exactly. I'm very serious about that. And it was like, a good jazz musician wouldn't be caught with Cy Jones. I mean musically, he wouldn't be. Cy Jones wouldn't... He had a big sound, played loud, and he was always happy, laughing and clowning and funnin', but serious music he just... it wasn't exactly C. J.'s thing.

So, I was working at the foundry and I got a call to come to answer the phone, where I was working. And the first thing to think, like that, is an emergency. You know, you think... it worries you until you get to the phone, because you hope there's nothing wrong with your family.

And they called me to the office to answer... there's a phone call for me. And I got to the... and answered the phone and he said, 'This is Cy Jones.' I said, 'Cy Jones?' Said, 'Yeah,' said, 'Hey, man, I hear you got a bass. I need a bass player; I hear you're playing bass.' I say, 'Who told you that? I'm not playing bass. I have a bass, but I don't play. I'm not a bass player. I just had the bass a few weeks.' He said, 'Oh, I need a bass player bad, I gotta have a bass player.'

He had this job on Friday and Saturday night in an after hours joint. And I said, 'I'm sorry, I'm not... I can't imagine you'd call me to take a job.' And I'm saying this to him, and flattered at the same time, I'm sure. But it just... it was just so out of the question to think about going to work. I never thought about going to work with my bass.
You didn't think you were good enough yet?

No. It wasn't time. It's so much like... it just wasn't time. I didn't have those thoughts in my mind. I wasn't spending time with other musicians and getting other kinds of coordination and things down. I wasn't into that.
I was just into listening to bass in my own little room.

Anyhow, he was just insistent. 'Well, that's OK. You can cut it. I know you can handle it. You're a natural.' I was just...He was giving me the kind of razzmatazz that it was just natural for me to play the bass, to play music, that it was in my family.

And I just couldn't hear of it, I couldn't think of it. And I told him that it was completely out of the question, I couldn't think of it. And I went back there to the shop, to work. But it came all these thoughts in my head. Here I am getting a call for a job! Even though it was just Cy Jones. But the point...wow! I couldn't imagine myself performing on the stage. But I knew there was something happening inside of me in regard to the music.

Cy Jones called me back. He was really desperate, begging, literally begging, 'Please, make this gig with me.' And frankly, it seemed like such a challenge for me. But even though it was ridiculous it still seemed like...I was curious to wonder what that would be like, even with Cy Jones. I'd never been on a stage. I mean, I was clowning as a kid, at the Empress Theater, but this was different!
And you'd never played in a group with other people.

No, no. Anything. Now, I'm up in age now. I'm like 26-27 years old, at least 27. And he called me back and he just almost begged me. He say, 'Man, you can just down and fake it. Don't worry about it, because it's not that kind of thing. It's an after-hour gig and it's just where people don't have anywhere else to go, and the guys there are going to cover it, but I gotta have the instrument there, you know.'

And I bit. I bit on it. I said OK. Guess I got my nerve up, or whatever. Anyhow, I accepted. All the way home I was just sweating, thinking about it. The job didn't start until late, I think it was one o'clock in the morning, because the clubs closed and...it was two o'clock, the job started at two because the clubs closed at one. Oh, maybe it was one-thirty, something like that. I forget what the hour was. I'm usually home by twelve on my night gig.

I went home, and knowing I had accepted and saying...By the time I got home, I'm thinking, 'I must have been crazy to tell the man I would be there.' Because I knew the room where he was working. I was familiar with that. It was a place called the Industrial Club. No, I'm sorry...International ...some funny name like that. But it was like an after hour place, everything is closed. And people were, chances are, paying off downtown just to be open selling booze. And they had...one part of the place was, you could buy sandwiches. Fish sandwich and barbecue and all that sort of stuff. It was a great place to go, especially when else is happening, because everybody knew everybody and they just come in and
have a good time, and on Friday-Saturday night they booze up anyhow.
Was there dancing?
No, there wasn't dancing. But the place was so crowded.
They sold liquor?
They sold liquor. It had two floors to it...
Big, hm?

No, but dancing in the other end of it, not in the room where the band was. It was a big place. there was two floors to it. It was not that huge; it was like a house, an old house that had converted into...and the first floor and second floor...

And I got in the car and went over there and just... almost blind with fear. 'Am I crazy for doing this?' I wasn't ready for a job. Cy didn't bother me because I knew musically it wasn't nothing to worry about with Cy. But I really wanted to develop a train and think myself as, I don't know, a musician that's really gonna play some music, not go honking and crawling around on the floor.

And I didn't want to be in that...not what I wanted to get into it for. But, for whatever reason, here I was. I went on the bandstand and I knew the musicians. There was Charlie Hatchett that played piano. I got to apologize; I forgot the drummer's name. Charlie Hatchett and the drummer, myself and Cy Jones.
A quartet.
A quartet. I just can't think of the drummer's name. But he was a woodchopper's drummer, just cha-cha-cha-cha chop wood. And they just played honkytonk music.
Honkytonk...
Yeah, that kind of thing. Because Cy Jones was like... 'Caldonia' and all that kind of stuff.
Rhythm and blues?

Yeah, rhythm and blues, that's exactly what it was, rhythm and blues. You know, honky honky, honk honk. So they had the bandstand was up behind the bar, a high bandstand behind the bar. And the guys were, I can almost see it now, they had the beer lined up across the piano.
And the guy had a little table, I mean a chair, straight chair, next to the drum with his booze lined up there. So they

was just boozers. And it was late at night and everybody was juiced anyhow, so...But Cy was a showman. He'd get the sound started and he'd step up on the bar, off the thing, he'd make the step over to the bar. And he'd walk up and down the bar honking his horn like that, honking his horn...
...with his head going up and down...

Yeah, yeah, and making all these kind of moves and so on, down through his legs. Then he'd get on his knees and crawl across the bar, and then he'd get on the floor and really go through his act, when he'd get out of the danger zone of the bar. And when he'd leap to the floor, you had a show going and the people were just up...
They loved it?...
And the band was just woodchopping away, the drummer just chocka-chocka-chocka-chocka.
And they didn't expect you to dance and do all that stuff, just play?

It had nothing to do with music, it had nothing to do with music. But here I was, up on the stage, trying to play the bass. I was really trying to play it right. And I remember very distinctly, I was trying to block all of that out of my mind, block everything out and still play the changes, play real good, play right, play strong. You know, it was important to me.

Before the night was over, my fingers were just like, if I would just touch them together they would just burst open they were so sore. I hadn't really developed any corns. But I chopped away until I was just...Now, that was another new experience for me. I hadn't realized you had to go through all that business of blistering. But I had tried pulling too hard and squeezing so hard, my fingers were just like, so tender.
Were those metal string?

No, it was gut strings, I think. That was before metal. I remember that just before the set ended, I was playing, I was just playing away, and almost...Just in pain playing, and still trying to play it musically in spite of what they were doing. The piano was playing the right changes, and the drummer was keeping the time, but there was nothing really musical in what they were doing for me to hear. Because when you...for me, hearing it was my thing. Hearing it.
So did you get through it?

Oh, I got through it with no problem, because it was ...nobody paid me no attention. It didn't make any difference, because it wasn't no such thing of, 'Hey, you're out of tune' or...In any case, nobody paid me any attention, nobody but me.
I looked over to my left and, at the end of the bar, can you imagine? My brother Wes and Errol Grandy were sitting there.
Did they know?
Wes was sitting there looking up at me as if to say, 'What are you doing on that stage?'
Didn't he know ahead of time you were going to be there?
Someone had told him. You see, because no matter what you did, everybody knew about it. After-hour place, where else was there to go?
How did you react?

Somebody mentioned to him that I was playing with Cy Jones and he couldn't believe it. He came by. And as I looked over, there he was and Errol Grandy, setting at the end of the bar. And I looked at him, I looked dead at him, and he gave me a smile just like...he wasn't laughing at me. It was -- he understood. I was still embarrassed.
You have to start someplace.
...but I was so embarrassed. Now, he knew that I had the bass. He knew I was practicing it every night. But he didn't expect to be seeing me on the bandstand.

Well, I read somewhere that he had told a number of people that his first job was just playing...all he could do was play Charlie Christian solos. So his first job couldn't have been too delightful, either.
But it wasn't literally that way. He may have said it that way. He was playing more than just Charlie Christian solos, you know.
It just made a good anecdote...

Yeah, right. A great thing to say. If I had to stretch out on anything, I would have been playing, leaning toward what I had...was exposed to, which wasn't very much. It wasn't a whole lot. But, I mean, Jimmy Blanton's the only thing I had heard. Chances are I would have been playing...influenced under what I heard him play. So Wes...
That's not a bad way to start.

That's what I'm saying. So Wes was influenced under Charlie Christian but he went off, he was an extension from that. Anyhow, I remember when I finished that and came down, I was really embarrassed because of Wes and Errol. Boy, the giants that those guys were! But when I came off the stage and we were sitting there talking, I really felt OK. I felt OK when we were just staying there talking. It was
different when they were standing there watching and looking at me playing. Because I knew I didn't have it down, and I knew I wasn't getting it because my fingers were just killing me.
How long did you do that?
That job? Well...
Did you stay on it?

I played the next night, because it was just a weekend thing, Friday and Saturday night. I played the Friday and Saturday night, and the Saturday, I didn't...It was worse than Friday because my fingers were so sore. I remember the following week I went back, because it was a real challenge for me now. Not Cy Jones necessarily, not his music, but it was a challenge for me to play under any conditions...
To get up there and get through an evening...

Yeah, even under those conditions. I remember, I continued practicing that next week, even though they were really, really sore. But that's how you develop corns. It wasn't bad the following week, and the following week after that it was just...And I wasn't there too terribly long but at least I developed my corns, I remember that.
And did you keep on playing and did people start calling you?

I started getting calls then, but that's...there was a terrible shortage for bass. When Cy called me to beg me, he wasn't kidding. It was really a shortage of bass players. There was no bass players in town. So it wasn't that I was that great, you see what I'm saying...
You were just available...
I did. And it wasn't long before I was working with Wes and Errol and the heavies in town.
So your natural ear really did start to help you.

Oh yeah, it did. I was hungry. The hunger to get into something that I...I had no idea that I had any talent that way and when I discovered that Wes...on what degree...it didn't make any difference. And I know there is millions and millions that are living the same way and haven't found that one thing that's really giving them release, and to express themselves.

consideration, there was such a shortage of bass players. You see what I'm saying. They wouldn't have chose me over Ray Brown, if Ray Brown was there. piano. And I was never...There was no piano where I was raised with my dad, or anything like that. And I'd go to the piano. And be kind of saying, 'Maybe if I just take it serious, something will happen here, because it will come back to me.'

Pretty much. I was amazed when he came back from the army playing the piano the way he was. Because he had time to come in. You would ask about getting along on the road?

How to take care of yourself, even about the music, even about setting up on the bandstand, even about how you do your uniform, how you... He had it all. There's a whole thing about that. Now, if you really care, now but some people don't care. And that's OK. But if you, for the ones that really did care, you know, that's important.

I remember when we got to the first town that we got to -- we didn't actually play there. It was a stopover. No, it wasn't. It was outside of town, right outside of town where we were going to perform. Outside of Eugene, Oregon, where there was a motel with them little cabins. I mean cottages around. So we would check in these cottages and the bus would take us in to the thing, to play the engagement that night. And we got there that afternoon.

And I remember when the bus stopped, then everybody just r-r-r-r right off that bus. Guys was rushing out, almost running to the counter, the desk, to register. And the guy opened the big door up so you could get your luggage and stuff out, because he wanted to get the stuff out so he can go park the bus and get his rest, the driver. I had to get my bass off, very carefully getting that upright out through there. And when I got it out, then I had to get my stuff out from beneath, my bag and stuff, When I got up to the thing, and by the time the line had dribbled down, there was no room.
You mean there wasn't any place for you to stay?

Can you imagine? It just turned out that way, that here I was standing out there. And the guy say, 'Well, we're filled up. I don't have anything left.' Well, there's a lot of them double up, but I...everyone was gone.
So what did you do?

I was just...I was standing there for a minute, kind of dumbfounded. I said, 'Well...' I tried not to show it or get alarmed or anything. And Mackel called me. I turned around and he was over there at his cottage. He said, 'Did you get taken care of?' And I said, 'No, they're all gone.' He said, 'I'm in 22' or whatever that was. He said, 'We'll double up; I'm in 22.' (I'm just saying 22 for whatever cottage number it was.) So I went to the counter and the guy said, 'Well?' And I told him I was gonna double up with 22. He said, 'Fine,' so he got the card down and gave it to me.

Simple thing. I just didn't know, I just didn't have anyone to turn to, like. Went over to stay with Mackel and there it was. It had twin beds and was comfortable for two if you wanted to double up. And he started talking to me then about what to expect from the band, what to expect from this, and just kind of give me a little inside and with a lot of humor. Because that's what you have to take to cope with it, is to be, to live with it, is to be able to kind of understand it and deal with it with some humor. You can't get uptight.
How did you cope with playing with that band?

Well, what happened, the very first thing happened, right there that night, Hamp walked up and handed me an electric bass. Just handed it to me. He'd gotten it from the company. Said, 'Gates, this is the sound I want on the band, so...' So I said, 'Hey, man, you called...when I called you,

you told me to bring my bass. You told me you wanted me to play the bass. I don't know nothing about electric bass. I never... This is the second one I've ever saw. I came here to play my bass; you hired me for it.'
So he said, well, there'd be no hard feelings if I didn't want to play it, he understood. He said, 'Then I'll just give you two weeks salary and your fare back home.' No way.
You mean because...

I just left home, right? I didn't come for that. In fact, they had a big farewell party for me before I left. You know, 'I'm going out to California with Hamp.' I couldn't go back home; I couldn't think of going back home. I just left home.

I took it. And when I took it, I was very angry inside. I don't know when I've been that bitter inside. I really was an angry man inside, because I really loved my music, my bass and what I was doing and I'd thought that's what he wanted. You know, I thought that's what I was coming out there for. So embarrassed. I was so embarrassed I didn't know what to do.
But he didn't expect you to play it the first night. You couldn't.

No. Well, the guy...Hampton...to know him...I'm indebted to Hamp for all those years, not just because of that but...When I took it, I remember, I came back to where we were staying, the cottage, and I knew I had to have that job. I knew I had to stay with Hamp. That's what I came for. I knew that.

I had also a real job on my hands, maybe a problem, to be able to play that instrument. Because he had made it very clear that's what... (Inaudible) . Now I'm thinking, I've got to make the choice. It's gotta be, it can't be half way. Because once again, here I am. I can't halfway.

I knew I had to make a decision to play the instrument if I took it, or go home. And I, like, it outweighed it, because I couldn't go home. But I knew if I was gonna take the instrument and play it, I was gonna play it well, the best I could. There was no time for jiving around. I was gonna play it. (end of Master Cassette I/cassette copy II)

We were talking about how Hampton gave you the electric bass and more or less gave you an ultimatum along with it. So, how did you work that out? Did you play the upright for a while, while you were learning to handle the electric bass?
Well, the way it worked out for me was obviously the right way, because it did work out. I had my upright bass, and very naturally, my mind wasn't open to the electric

not
bass. I had/received it in terms of this is what I want to play.
It was just the opposite. But he wanted me, right then, to
concentrate on playing electric bass. He didn't want the upright
bass.

He didn't expect you to start playing it, the electric
bass, right away?

He must have thought of that before I showed up,
because otherwise he could have told me on the phone, 'Don't
bring the upright.'

Well, the Fender was brand new, at that point, wasn't
it?
Yeah.
Had you ever seen one before?

I'd seen one. There was a guy back in Indianapolis,
in my home town, that was working out in a country club, or a
roadside room or joint or something, way a ways out of town.
And I heard the guy was playing electric bass out there. And
he was trying to describe it to me, about the sound and everything.
And I drove out there one night, very closed-minded, and I just
saw it and I thought it was the worst thing that happened to
music, where the electric bass had come into it.

Well, naturally I still had a carry-over of that feeling
when I saw the one Hamp was handing to me. I wasn't, I hadn't
accepted the thought of playing electric bass, by any means.
By any stretch of the imagination I couldn't imagine myself
with an electric bass, with that funny instrument.

So very naturally, I didn't bother to even take mine
out of the cover. This is what he wanted. I also should
mention that when I joined the band, when he called me, at
the time he called me, obviously it was a short, quick decision
for him. Because I was to come before the next bass player
left. You see, when a guy gives his notice, or he gets his
notice, he's got a two week period with the band. So for me...
Who were you replacing?

Roy Johnson, who was working his two weeks out.
That gave me a chance, when we speak about me being qualified
to go in and sight read the music, from the standpoint of how
did I get into it, well, with the two-week period...It wasn't,
I guess it was about a ten day period...I had a chance, the
opportunity to become acquainted with the music. Because by
the time I arrived in San Francisco and we made our way up the
Coast, well, I'm looking, about ten days to learn the music.
So, by being accustomed to...That was, my music was...The
expression was 'playing off of what I heard.' It wasn't...
You weren't much of a reader.

No, But I will have to admit, I had spent some time with musicians that...I'm reading chord symbols. I knew chord symbols well enough to know chord symbols, you know. And fortunately enough, the majority of the music that Hamp had in his book, there were chord symbols over all the four-bar changes. Within every four bars, wherever the changes are, maybe every two bars, whatever. But there were symbols written.
And you could handle that easier than you could handle the actual written-out line.

Right. I couldn't handle the lines and spaces, so it was just symbols. But Hamp's music, there was really nothing tricky about his music. I mean, if you just knew where the breaks were at. You know, enough to hear, and being familiar enough with Hamp's music, a ballad or something like that, with a thing that's an extra edge for a bass player that's not, that don't have the qualifications of reading lines and spaces...If he can read chord signatures, he'll see a chord symbol, and the chord symbol might be a Bb7. Well, you don't have to really be an Einstein to figure out a good note to play out of a Bb7, of that chord. You know, you don't have to play the precise note that some arranger has written out for you. It might have sound...chords that sound better...but for that I had a pretty good ear.

I've often seen cases where a bass player, since we're talking about the instrument, would have a better concept of notes to use in a chord than the guy who might be writing it, because he's just writing basic chord symbols down, you know. We may have a better choice of note to play against the chord.

Anyhow, with that little knowledge I had about chord symbols, plus I could hear what was going on...I remember there were times when the bass player, Roy Johnson, the bass player before me, was playing with the band and I could...I'd have the instrument out, playing along with it, off stage.
You mean electric...
Yeah, because I had to get used to this fellow. I had to get accustomed to it...
Well, I imagine...

...playing horizontal rather than up, you know, the whole strength of it, the whole everything was different. And it felt strange and foreign in my hands. So I spent my days, in the day, practicing. Not really happy with what I was doing, but I had to readjust and part of that practice time was spent readjusting. It wasn't just simply practicing.
Readjusting to the choice you had made.
Yeah.
How long did it take you to come to like it?
Well, I can't put a time period on it because as I think back, it just happened. Things have a way of happening over a period of time, how... I don't know how to answer that.
...Because you have the name of being the person who first, more or less, popularized the electric bass.

Right, right. And I can very well see how that came about. But at the time when I was making the transition itself, I can't figure out. As I think back, I don't know whether it happened over a two-month period, six-month period, that I really got the total feeling of that I was comfortable with the instrument. To be honest with you, I don't know exactly what period of time. Of course, it wasn't like a year or two years, nothing like that. It was a matter of months, but how many months I don't know.

Because what have to happen, what had to happen, I had to work with it mentally as well as physically. See, physically I had to make the transition; but mentally, in my mind, there was a quite... I had to make a major, a master, a huge change in my mind. You know what I'm trying to say? I would take... I was playing that instrument, or any instrument... you could play the basic thing that was right but music requires a little bit more than that. Especially, then, I felt like where I required more of myself than that. I had to play it with good feeling, good time.
Well, particularly in that band, there were so many good people in that band.
Not only that, see, I was like a... I was playing a bastard instrument. I was a freak.
And you were conscious of that.
Yeah, I was conscious of that.
How did the other guys look on it?
But that's what, that's the other thing of great effect to it, was the musicians in the band.
Did they have problems with it, or not?

Because when I was beginning... Yeah, right, when I began to play. But I was very serious about it. Number one, I had to be in tune, the thing had to... I wanted to be in tune. I didn't want to be critical because of that. I didn't want to be critical because it was too loud, because it was an electronic instrument.
You could take a dial, that dial tone, and turn it up

so the volume would distort or disturb. It had nothing to do with music. And I was conscious of having a good sound, you know. I was conscious of not having too much treble, or all those things that make a sound as close to that instrument, my instrument, the bass, upright bass, as possible. That was my main concern.

And in doing that I also had to think about really playing a good feeling, good lines, good notes, because those things are important too, you see. It was most important to me. And I think that's one of the things that caused it to be accepted by the guys in the band, so much. But I wasn't trying to impress them. I had to fall in love with it some way, I had to learn to like it and really dig it.
But they weren't...were they not happy with the idea either at first?
Oh, yeah, they had no objection to it because, like I said when I...In playing the instrument, I guess I have to say I played it good. I played it good.
So that it overcame any...
It overrides whatever, you know...
...negative feelings they might have had.

Right, right. Still, I got a lot of...there was a lot of cracks and jokes and like that, it had to be. You know what I'm trying to say. I remember a few occasions that people would walk up to the band, it's be a dance or something, and I could see people standing offside of the stage, because Hamp had an electric guitar player and I'm playing the fender bass.

Why, they'd never been introduced to the electric guitar, so that they could hear the bass. They could hear the bass but they didn't know where it was coming from. And I could see them looking across the stage, around the stage, trying to find out where the bass was coming from. Because, traditionally, a guy look at me and thought I was playing a guitar. He thought he had two guitar players. He couldn't imagine this thing laying this way in my hand being a bass.
At that time, wasn't that the only company that made it, too?

Yes, Fender was it. That was, Fender bass was the electric bass at that time. There was not a competitor, to my knowledge. And if they searched through the bandstand trying to find a bass, and sometime you see somebody just discover, 'Hey, there he is, that's where the bass is,' and they'd be pointing at me. People would be pointing to the others, 'that's the bass.'
See, because Hamp, when we were traveling with Hamp, Hamp liked that sound because he could hear the bass. Really hear the bass. Now, you had to realize, then, when there was

an upright bass in a band, you always have to have it there, and you didn't really hear it as much as you felt it. You didn't really hear it as much as you could really feel it. In other words, you could...A band, if you took the bass out of it, it would be something empty. But you didn't really concentrate on the bass player, you know, because it was...the instrument blended into the music. It wasn't dominant. It never dominated the music in any way.

Hamp used to come back to the amp, because there was a control on the amplifier and there's a control on the bass, the instrument itself. There's a volume control, treble and that, on the bass itself. He would come to the amp and turn it up. He'd be, whatever the tone was, as the tone built up he'd be... You know how Hamp would sort of prance or parade in front of the band. That happy sound, and he'd be sweating and the music getting to him, and he had a...(imitates Hamp's monotone singing and his clapping). And he'd clap his way over to the amp and turn it up because he wanted more bass, I guess. He liked that sound. But I didn't want it up...
So then did you turn it down?

...So I turned it down on my control back here. I always made sure when I went on the stand that I had my gain up high, because I knew that Hamp was going to turn his up and I'd turn mine back. As soon as he'd kind of walk out of my range, I'd turn it back down to what I thought was a good balance for the band, you see.

But back to what the musicians in the band...and he had quite a few good, top people in the band during the period I was there. Just to name some of the personnel: in the trumpet section it was Art Farmer, there was Quincy Jones, there was Al Williams, there was The Whistler. There were changes come along a little later, like Clifford Brown, Benny Bailey. And also Emory -- gosh, I can't think of Emory's -- big, fat trumpet player. I can't think of his name, but we used to call him the Fat Boy because he was huge, maybe 300 pounds in weight. Then another guy by the name of Davenport, I believe, were some of turnover people in the trumpet section.

The trombone section was Jimmy Cleveland, Buster Cooper and Al -- oh, I'm sorry, I can't think of that trombone player's name (Hayes). And the rhythm section -- the reed section was Bobby Plater, he was beautiful, Bobby Plater; Morris Lane, Clifford Solomon, Oscar Estelle, the baritone, and...who else am I missing? It's been a lot of years and I keep...I've got up to the date in my mind.
