Anyhow, the rhythm section was Elmer Gill, piano player, and I later worked with him for a spell, and after Elmer, me playing bass and William Mackell playing guitar. And after Elmer, Hamp went without piano. The band...
He just played vibes...
...working without a piano, he used to play the vibes. But that's what the band consisted of. Benny Golson played with us for a while. Pardon?
He didn't have an organ player during that period?

No, there was no organ. But we had periods where... there was a short period Benny Golson worked, and a short period Philly Joe Jones played drums. Who else came in and out of the band, just short periods where they did a segment of the thing? Papa Jo Jones played some, a couple of gigs.

But it kept me in company like I'd never dreamed of being in before, plus the opportunities when, say, we'd go to New York. We went to New York and we were working at the Band Box, right next door to Birdland, and guys would come in and play the first set, because the first set was just an instrumental thing. Hamp would have the thing set up that the band would go out and play a few tunes and he wouldn't come out on the first hour. Then we'd have a break and come back and Hamp would be there, when he'd bring on the singer, like a show-type thing.
Who were the singers that you...

Oh, Ernestine Anderson worked. Jimmy Scott, and I had a short period...Sonny Parker, before he passed, he was with it for a lot of years. And also, I got there just in the tail end of Winnie Brown, I think her name was. Her name was Winnie Brown. She made the "Midnight Sun" thing kind of popular.

Anyhow, as I was saying about the time we worked the Band Box, there'd be occasions on our first set we'd played, before Hamp came out, if somebody was in the audience, a player. would come and set in with us. Like Bud Powell came up, oh yeah. Like Charlie Parker came up and played some with us.
What kinds of things would you play when...

Straight ahead jazz things, guys were doing fours. It was just really...that's when the players would play. They'd pick tunes, I can't think of the titles now, that were tunes that you play on. And these guys would...they'd play. And they'd play fours back and forth, just be a fun thing for the band. And once Hamp come out, then you'd look for the hits.
Back to the show.

Back to the "flying Home" closer, every time, the marching through the aisles and all that. But it was show biz when Hamp came out. Which was OK. Hamp stretched out on some good playing things, too. But that's what that was like.
And that experience of being in the company of...that type thing was great for me. It also made me be more conscious of the instrument, I think, during that period. Because it was
a freak instrument as it was, I had to be more conscious as a player than they are today.
Because everybody was looking at you, you mean?

Because it's a common thing now, and it was a... there wasn't that many players (then). For example, I didn't have anyone else, there was no one else out there that I could communicate with that was playing it.
Nobody to compare notes with how you do what you're doing?

That's right, how to do it. 'Listen here, this cat's doing something different. Hey, hoe do you like this chord, this cat doing something different...' There wasn't a whole lot of other people doing things different, because as I remember, the next person I heard had started playing it was Jimmy Garrett. Then I heard later somebody else was playing it, then somebody else was playing it. But I never got a chance for us to cross our paths and sit and talk about it.
Did you ever talk to anybody from the Fender people about using the instrument?

Yes, I was very close with them because once I started playing the instrument, when I was in California I would always go out, because we kept a close relationship for promotional purposes. They furnished the amplifier and the bass so they would constantly be on top of it. And with a person like Hamp giving it the exposure, that was great.

Because I really truly feel like that I was one of the first, anyhow, that exposed the instrument throughout the United States, in our travels, which we went all over the United States. And also in Europe, I was the first to expose it in Europe. In fact, when I went there with Hamp, for the first time when he went to Europe, I actually got more write-ups in the newspaper than Hamp, because it was this new thing happening with the band. And we didn't have a piano...
I don't suppose he was terribly thrilled about that, was he?

Well, it was all done in good taste because it wasn't that they were talking about me and not talking about Hamp. But Hamp had to, he had to feel good about the fact that he, Hamp...it was Hamp's doing. It was something, a creation; it was still Hamp's creation. It wasn't mine, it was really Hamp's creation.

Like I said, when I got into it, I was very concerned about sounding even better because I...you know what I'm trying to say. I had to make it sound, come off great. But there were very often reputable players would come to me and make all kind of weird criticism.
Well, a lot of people, including bass players, put it down.

Mainly bass players, because it was a threat to a bass player. It wouldn't be a threat to another person. And I can understand it. I really...that's the way I felt about it when I first saw it. I was very closed-minded about it. And didn't want to open my mind to accept it because...
Did they criticize it mainly because of its sound, or...

Yeah, because...I'll be the first to say that an electronic instrument is an artificial sound, you see. I'll be the first to say that. However, my feelings about it now, and it has been for some time, is we're talking about two different instruments. So you don't have to confuse it. I don't have to compare with upright bass. It's not an upright bass. It is what it is, and upright bass is what it is. It's not going to take the place of an upright bass. I don't think it was meant to be.
Well, the final answer to that is hearing you play duets with an upright bass.
Yeah, and I think that's the way I want to sort of continue to pursue my instrument as I see it and the way I feel, my concept about...
Did you ever go back to upright any more?

Yeah, I did. I had some periods where I was threatening to go back to the upright, because I didn't make the move by choice. It wasn't my...It wasn't by choice that transition, you see. And I always felt like the upright bass was still my instrument.

In the meantime, I had just made a total commitment to play the instrument and I tried to play it well. But my love was still for the upright bass. I know there were times when I have gone out where there was a jam session, there was nobody playing an electric bass. And the upright sounds so great, especially if the guy was a good player. I would just drool, because I really missed it.

You know, when I got into the electric bass, and got all I thought I was getting out of it, and got a certain amount of satisfaction, and I'd go back and I'd hear somebody play the upright bass, I almost got sick again. Because I'm saying, oh, you know...
That you missed it?
Yeah, I really missed it, and it lingered on in my life years after that.
You stayed with Hamp for how long? Almost two years?
I stayed with Hamp for like two and a half years, it was. Then, when I left Hamp's band...
Which was when, about '52?
Yeah, about '52, I don't have dates but it was in the period...I went to Los Angeles to live. I didn't want to go back to my home town, Indianapolis, to live.
What made you decide to leave? Were you just tired of being on the road, or...?

Well, not exactly. When I was with Hamp, it's like an experience. The whole idea was going. And that's customary. Everybody do that for a period of time. You outgrow a certain thing. There's no room for advancement. I mean, that's it! I couldn't spend my life playing "Flying Home." You know, I loved him and it was a great experience and everything, but after a couple of years, it wasn't a thing where I was in a position where I could make enough money to retire. I wasn't making anything like that.

And the routine of traveling, making one-nighters and going through all the aches and pains that go with a big band, especially during the time you were traveling by bus, sleeping on the bus, sleeping on the bus, playing one-nighters and going on like this...
What was the pay like?
The pay when I joined the band...I got $20 a night, when I worked. But the nights you didn't work, you don't get paid, you see. And there were...
Doesn't leave you much margin, does it?

Right, it really don't. Because you have to live dirt cheap if you intend to send some money home, you know. So it's...he can only do that so long. But the experience you get from it is priceless, believe me.

The experience of living with, say, a personnel of 20 or 21 people, including the stage manager and...It's like a family. You learn how to live and adjust to it. It's really like a family. It's always something going on. It's either a lot of laughter, a lot of tears, a lot of just everything. A mixture of things when you're all practically living together, from one stop to the next stop to the next stop to the next stop. But it's such an experience. It's one of the highlights of my whole life, especially when we went to Europe and all the whole thing.
But after that period I had spent with Hamp, and I knew that I had served my term, I knew I had served my term...
It was time to go on to something...
It was time to go on...or even time to settle down. Time to not lead only that type of pace, because...
Did you live in Los Angeles by design; I mean did you pick Los Angeles?

Yes, I picked Los Angeles because, it's got to do with my private life. I had met a young lady that was living in that part of the country, and I wanted very much to live in that part of the country. I was ready for a change in my life then, to elevate. I couldn't think of going back to Indianapolis and making my home. Indianapolis and Columbus were the extent of my life, and when I got an opportunity to experience other areas, such as California, New York and so on, I said, 'I can't go back to Indianapolis.' I just couldn't do that.
Were Wes and Buddy there?

Yeah, Bud...Wes and...Wes was there but Buddy was in the service. Just about running his period out of the service and coming home. But in the meantime, my mind was made up to move to California because California was...the opportunities were there.

There was less prejudice. You know, in Indianapolis at that time we had...The blacks couldn't go into certain clubs. It was still that dark shadow over that whole scene. We couldn't go out to this club, or somebody couldn't go in that club because...But the whites could come into any of the clubs. And they come down to the Avenue and catch all the jazz scenes. And they had to come and hang with us but we couldn't ever go back out to where they was at. So I couldn't go. I just couldn't bring myself to go back with that kind of...readjust back to that kind of attitude.

And I wanted to...it was no question in my mind that my future was going to be involved with music. I was going to be a professional musician. There's no question about, 'Well, I've tried it and now I'm going back to the foundry.' There was no such thing. From that point on, I was going to be a musician. So I needed to get in an environment that's going to be better for what I was going to do, for my head and everything else. So...
Did you quit Hamp with another job in mind, particularly, or did...?

As a matter of fact, I had put my notice in with Hamp before we went to Europe because, like, you know when the time comes that you...it's time to move on. You know that. It's nothing personal against Hamp, no hating Hamp, and like that. I love Hamp very much, throughout the whole thing. However, there come high and low periods where things didn't go right and it happened. It's just human nature with everybody.
So it was nothing personal about Lionel Hampton that I had to leave the band. I felt very indebted to him; but it was time to make a change.
OK. So you left...

I had planned to leave before the European trip and I remember I went to...spoke to him in his room and he said, 'Monk, I understand,' he said. 'But if you stay on with me now until we...because I don't want to break in another rhythm section before we go into New York.' And we went into New York because he had a month in doing the Apollo Theater.

I think it was a month in New York; two weeks at the Apollo Theater and two weeks somewhere else, I forgot. But, and then that's when I found out we were going to Europe. I said, 'Wait a minute,' to myself. 'I can't quit; I've never been to Europe.' I'm thinking, I'm getting confused now, because the European tour...I think it was to go out to some six weeks in Europe. We were going all through the Scandinavian countries. It was just...when I saw the list, it was just going to the moon.
So you decided to wait a little while longer...

Yeah, I had to. If I stayed that long, hey, another month or so and we'd go over to Europe. And when...but I still tried to be firm about the fact that I'm going to leave him. And sometimes that becomes a hard thing to do, to walk up and tell a guy, 'I'm giving my notice because I just want to leave.' Because I knew he was happy with the rhythm section and he didn't want...He'd go through this all the time, changing sections, changing things and changing things. But he don't have to be happy about it, you know.

Anyhow, I remember when it came time to negotiate the European things, we...they reported back to us to what we were getting paid. And there come up some discrepancy because there was some people were going to quit. They weren't going to go for that; they didn't agree with the arrangements and the money wasn't right and whatever. And there was a big hassle about that.

Now this was Hamp's first trip to Europe too. It was his first trip to Europe because he's always been afraid to fly, see. So he had taken through this religious thing that he was in study with. Obviously it got him, controlled him enough that he would get on a plane and fly to Europe. And it just so happened that it happened while I was in the band, that it was the first trip he made to Europe.
I'm surprised that that was his first trip to Europe.

It was his first trip to Europe. Anyhow, that thing worked itself out because I remember there was a big board meeting at the union, Local 802 in New York, working out this agreement. The guys, it ended up about four of them quit

because they didn't agree on whatever conditions and the money. Ernestine Anderson quit, Elmer Gill quit, and Moon Mullins quit, the trumpet player quit, and somebody else. I can't think of who the other people were.
So when we went to Europe, Lionel Hampton had to get a replacement for the piano and the singer. So he got George Wallington on piano and Annie Ross as a singer, as a replacement for Ernestine...
Oh, my! Annie Ross?

Annie Ross made the trip over. But it didn't last long because people in Europe...she got horrible write-ups, so badly that she had to cancel out. We never, I never understood it but the write-ups were so bad for Annie Ross. And George Wallington and Annie came together, so George quit too. They just left, and both came back to the States.

But I think what happened about Annie Ross, originally something had happened in the past and they wasn't ready to accept Annie Ross. And they didn't want...couldn't accept Annie in the context of Lionel Hampton, some kind of way. They just wanted Hamp, or something.
Anyhow, it worked out and we went the rest of the tour without a piano and without a singer. They both left and came back; I think they left from Brussels and came back to the States.

The trip extended itself. We went through, all around and up to Africa, North Africa. And he got...he did so great that when we came back into Europe out of North Africa, he did some repeat performances. He went back to Paris, back to the Scandinavian countries, some Scandinavian countries. And we stretched the tour out much longer than we were anticipating.
So the reception was very good...

Fantastic, just absolutely fantastic. But by that time there were...the whole band had sort of decided to leave. And I remember when we were in Paris, getting ready to come home, there was a sort of mutual agreement of who all was leaving the band. And it left Hamp with such a few members in the band, he almost had to re-create his whole band when he got home. Because having to give a two weeks' notice from the time we left our last engagement in Europe, the next working period was almost automatically two weeks, because we had to have some time off. And we took advantage of that time off to extend out our two weeks' notice. Not everybody, but just about everybody put their notice in. The majority of the guys left the band then and there.
Because there had built over a while all kinds of ill feelings, and I think that happens automatically, be it Hamp or who it is. Those things have to build up. I remember when

we were in Europe and some of the guys wanted to go out and record. Hamp resented it, and it obviously come from the office, or Gladys Hampton, his wife, who took care of the business, that they didn't want guys out recording on their own. Which I didn't agree with it. I thought it was very poorly to have that kind of...
Did some of them do it anyhow?
But some of them did it anyhow. And had made...
Did you?

...some kind of arrangements that they would be released after we were gone, or anything. But Quincy and Art Farmer and Gigi Gryce, who were very talented and had a possibility of exposing their things in their little jazz world, where Hamp wasn't in it...And I just felt it was only fair that he should allow them the opportunity to do that, because we were working with Hamp at the lowest prices and the worst conditions. Give a guy a chance to get something going somewhere else...
Did you do some of those?
I only did one.
What was it?
I got called in on one, it was...Actually, Hamp was on that one. Hamp set it up. I forgot what it was.
Small group?
Small group, yeah.
Don't worry, it'll turn up somewhere. So you went back to Los Angeles and...

I left the band when we came back from Europe, back to the States. Automatically, like the rest of us did, we put our notices in in Paris; by the time we got here, we were free. Because the next working date was long after two weeks and we were all glad to be finished.

And I went straight to California. And I stopped in Indianapolis to see my folks, and went out to California. And ironically enough, when I got out to California, I had built up enough reputation that people knew about this electric bass player. And we had made some engagements in Los Angeles while traveling with Hamp. And guys wanted me to play the electric bass. Even though it was very new, it was something about it that was unique, I guess. A gimmick...
It was a novelty.
Yeah, just a novelty.
But your name was associated with it by now.

It was associated with it, right. I went to a jam session on...It was Christmas, during the holiday, New Year's. Anthony Ortega, he was also in the band. I forgot about him. We called him "Batman." Batman was in the band, and he lived in Los Angeles. And when I got there, well naturally, he was kind of showing...He and Clifford Solomon lived in California, Los Angeles.

And we had talked about forming a group out of Hamp's band, within the band, after we left. And there was a jam session going on, and Batman said, 'I want you to come over to...' what was it, I forgot the little town they was having the jam session at. 'And there's a New Year's Eve party, and we can play, man, we can play.' And I'm anxious to do that because I need to meet the local musicians, find out what's happening, try to get in on it, in the clique or whatever.

And so I joined Batman for that New Year's Eve party. And I had my bass and my amp in the trunk of the car when we rode, in Batman's trunk. When we got there the house...it was in a house...was filled with people. A good time, like a party. And the music was just great, because guys was just playing. I mean the music was so powerful!

And I remember that Carl Perkins was playing piano. Carl's from my home town. And I felt comfortable about Carl being there because Carl was like, sort of a key figure. A great player, and knew all the tunes and everything.

And there was about three bass players. Myself, one bass in the corner, another bass playing, another guy playing upright...about three basses. And...but I wanted to play; I really wanted to play. I was hungry to play, really hungry to play.

Now, you got to realize, now I really got that instrument down. Because we did a lot of playing with the jazz cats in the band, that had nothing to do with Lionel Hampton's working. We would have jam sessions; we'd have all kinds of things where we would be constantly playing, and my chops were really up. My chops were really up in terms of speed and control over...I was...They were up from constant working and playing. I was ready to play and I was hungry to play.

And I asked one of the guys could I sit in. He said, 'Oh, yeah, man, come on it, yeah. Have the place. You can use my bass or there's so-and-so's bass over there.' I said, 'I got my own bass in the car.' He said, 'OK, fine. Bring it on in.'

In the meantime, I'm feeling comfortable with Carl Perkins there and meeting the other guys. I went out to the car and got my bass and when I come back in, it was understood that I was going to play the next set, after the break.

And as I came back in, guys were kind of tuning up and getting ready for the next set, the next bunch was gonna play. And they saw me come in with this bass, and it got quiet. The room had really got very quiet inside. I knew what was happening. Now here, that group of guys didn't expect me to come in with this and perhaps over 75% of them wasn't aware of who I was. But I wanted to play. I knew I had to break this ice somewhere and...
This was a test...
This was a test. Some of the horn players...I remember a couple guys put their horns down and they walked out. They didn't want to play with electric bass. They really put me down.
Somebody you knew?

No, I met most of those guys for the first time, all but Carl, and I can't remember any of the other players. But they were local, the better players around. And Bateman came up, because he knew, he was standing tall and strong because he was ready to play. He wasn't afraid of me. Carl Perkins, he wasn't.

That was enough to start the thing off, and we had this drummer and...oh, I'm sorry. Carl wasn't the piano player on that set. Because what they did to me -- and I knew they did it deliberately, which was all dumb -- the guy started out with "Cherokee," real fast. I mean, "Cherokee" was so fast the drummer couldn't hardly keep time.
...killer song, killer tune...

Right. So now I said, 'Oh, now they're trying to put me in trouble.' They gonna get rid of me, right? Well, it so happens that I was really ready for "Cherokee," it was to me like playing a ballad. My chops was just so ready for it, and in order for me to get even -- let's see if I can say that -- I just got just as nonchalant and looked around the room, not even looking at the instrument like I was playing, as if to say, 'Is that as fast as you can play it?' I just whaled away through that thing. I never turned the volume loud; it was down, like, the right mellow sound for that room.

And at that time, the Fender Company's first amplifiers were the best ones. I wish I could find one today. They really made a quality sound in an amplifier then, and I had one. It was a great amp. I put that amp in the corner, something about the room, the way I would always set it, and I lean it back a little way so the sound could kind of be tilted up. But I would always keep it down at a low level. I wouldn't put the gain up because the gain was there. It would always have to be in balance with what was going on, and the rest of the control down in my hand.
When I started to play, it sounded good. Not because

I'm saying I was great, but it really sounded good. And it was a different sound than what the upright got. It's what I always say; it's got its own sound, Maggie, it's got its own thing. And I knew I played with good feeling. It was just there.

And after they went past a point to prove what they were trying to prove, I was OK. Guys were shaking my hand, and patting me on the back, 'Yeah, yeah.' Because at one point, when the tune was up like that, after the horn players took... whatever...they left it open for me to solo. And I knew right then I had to outshine anything I'd ever done. Because here somebody's putting me through a test. I didn't.

But it came out great. I succeeded and I was accepted. And that's the way...Al Bartee came up to me and said, 'Man, I'm working at a place in North...up in Hollywood, called the Tailspin, with Georgie Auld. We need a bass player. Can you make the gig?' And I said I was looking for a gig, yeah. And he said, 'Oh, this is great, man,' he said. So he got ahold of George and the next day George called me to work this job.
So you didn't have any trouble getting a job.

I went to work right away. And the funny thing about it, though, is when I got out to the job at the Tailspin with Georgie Auld, he had a quartet. He had a piano, bass, drums and he played the tenor, in a place that people danced. There were professional dancers and a lot...out of Hollywood, right there. And it was packed.

It was a place you had to really swing, so...Georgie Auld's a real swinger. When I came in on the gig, George looked; they were standing laughing, talking, he and Bruce, the piano player, laughing and talking with some more people. And they looked and saw me coming with the electric bass. He didn't think I was playing electric bass. He didn't know. And his whole thing just fell when he saw me.

And he spoke in an off way, trying to be friendly, but he looked like he was just sick when he saw the electric bass. He expected Bartee...Bartee didn't tell him I was playing electric bass. So I was embarrassed, and I always had...it was enough for me when a stranger or the public would see me and pass judgment. It was bad enough. But when a fellow musician had to show his feelings like that, it made me feel bad.

Because what happened with me was the guy judged me before he heard me. That's what I used to hate about it. I used to judge the instrument but I wouldn't judge the player. When a guy showed me some sort of expression like, 'Oh, well, I don't like it,' and that's the way it was, before they even heard me...
How did he feel about it after...
I swear to God, when I played that first tune, he turned around and said, 'Yeah!' and went straight ahead from then on. He begged me not to leave the group when I finally left.
How long did you stay?

I stayed with Georgie Auld about three months. And then, I was going through some changes then, I guess that was just a period in my life where I couldn't get really adjusted, somehow. But the job with Georgie Auld swung every night. And I'm not saying, once again, not because I was great but that sound, it really made it.

I went to...I was gonna...I had planned to go back to New York. Because, in answer to the original plan, we had talked it over a few times in Hamp's band with...you had the little in crowd with...you always had your little circle group within a big...
The people you hung out with.

Right. So, like, Quincy and Gigi and Art Farmer and Jimmy Cleveland and, you know. It was all these things like, Quincy would go and get into his writing thing. He was talking about getting a small group together, and I thought I was going to be working with that group. Because these were the people I was very comfortable with on a personal level as well as a musical level. And we had...there was some conversation about our starting this group, within.

So when I decided to leave Los Angeles, I was gonna move back to New York. And I wanted to go back and get into the kind of traffic that was there. Maybe it was because I missed traveling so bad, every day the changes and all, or it's hard to just readjust that fast.

Anyhow, I stopped in Indianapolis on my way to New York to visit my folks. And while I was there, there was a guy came up by the name of...Gee, I forget the name, disregard that...wanted to start...There was a club in Indianapolis called The Turf Bar and this guy owned the Cotton Club up on the Avenue there. He was good friends with these people that had the club out on 16th Street not far from Speedway Races, which was a nice little place for the traffic.

It was called the Turf Bar, and these people were going bankrupt. Nice people, but they were going bankrupt. They had a duet, working the club, where the lady played organ and her husband played drums, and that's what the entertainment was like. And the place was dying; they were going bankrupt.

He talked to this lady, Mildred Thompson was the proprietor there, said, 'What you should do, Mildred, is bring in a black group, would turn the whole thing around.' Well, you know, they ain't gonna...She was thinking, like, well, see...
We were back in that period in time when she was afraid to bring in a black group because she thought it might attract some black trade, or something, and you can't do that.
They didn't want black customers.

Yeah, you couldn't mix. How you gonna...She just couldn't figure out how it was gonna work. Anyhow, this guy talked her into it, and they had discussed it. But they were going broke, so she was ready to try anything.
She didn't have anything to lose?

Right, she had nothing to lose. Now, this guy knew Wes was there, Wes had some drawing power. 'You get the group together,' he said, 'and I'll...' I guess they had talked some with Wes and Sonny Johnson, who was a drummer, to bring in a group in this place. And...Buddy was just coming home from the Army and I was just passing through there, so the three of us was home. So they felt, 'This is it, put those guys together and make a band.'
Now, I guess in terms of exposure, I was hot because I just come off the road with Hamp's band. After Los Angeles, I...
Was this just going to be for a couple of weeks?

Well, I didn't want to do it. I was on my way to New York. So they came up, they came and was talking to us about it. And the guys were saying, 'Yeah, hey, let's go and do the thing at the Turf Bar. It's a great gig, steady gig.' And I said to them, 'Listen, I'm on my way to New York. I didn't come home to stay, now. I'm not here to look for a gig.'

And I mean, that was one of the main reasons why I could adjust myself to come home, was because of the prejudice scene. I had gotten away from it and I didn't want no part of it, no more than I could...I wouldn't want to volunteer to come back any more to what I just left. There's a certain amount of it everywhere, but you don't just go where it was thick and heavy, like it was there.

Before I went with Hamp, I remember working at a place out on the Avenue on 16th Street, at a place called the Tropicana, and we had to come through the back door. There was no blacks in the club, and on our intermission we had to sit in the back room where they had the beer and stuff stored. It was like a storeroom; they had a...
You couldn't talk to the customers?

No. The customers could come back and talk to us, but we couldn't go out there and set with them. We wasn't allowed to sit in the room. That was just a way of life. I didn't pay it too much attention 'til I had gone and come back, and I said, 'Wait, I can't come through there. What am I doing

coming through the back door?' I wasn't voluntarily coming back there, looking for more of the same. I was passing through. So they said, 'With this thing happening, you will be...' They had blown it up, which was good for Indianapolis, and they wanted the Montgomery Brothers out there. It so happens that to make the quintet up, there was a tenor player by the name of Pookie Johnson and a drummer by the name of Sonny Johnson.
Were they related?

No, they weren't related, but their last names were the same. So we decided that the best way to title the group was the Montgomery-Johnsons. Not "Brothers," but the Montgomery-Johnson Quintet. The tenor player, Pookie, was just a great player. He and Wes, the front line, played so well together, because they dug each other and they (unintelligible) the music. So all the things worked out with tenor and guitar.

And what a sound it was, because when those guys played ensembles and heads of tunes, they sounded like one instrument, the phrasing and everything was so close together, it sounded like a different sound, but one instrument. It was just that close, and they both played so good together.

We consented...I said OK. I agreed that I would start the job until they found a bass player, because I was going to New York. It so happened, we went out and worked. The guys started and there was a big full page in the paper, and what-ever. In no time flat, that place was jam-packed. People were lined up, just bursting open with the place. It got to be the place. It was very very successful for a couple years. I mean very successful; you couldn't get near the place in those days.

They had a policy, on every Saturday was a jam session, on Saturday afternoon, and that way the black musicians could come over and play, jam. Because the jam sessions were where all the musicians could come and jam.
But they still couldn't sit in the club.
No, no blacks as patrons, the listeners coming for the music. The doors weren't open to the black trade.
But you stayed...
I'm talking about '56, '57.
That's late...

Yeah, that's late to be making up your mind, living with that kind of thing. But it was very, very successful. I remember...Freddie Hubbard's also from my home town, that's where he was. He used to come out to play.
He was younger...
He was much younger; he was just getting started, at a very early age. I remember Roland Kirk, used to come down from Cleveland, Ohio. Jack Wilson came through.

After we were there, and got so we were established, the group had got so established that when there was a concert in town, after the concert, all the musicians from the concert would head there, because that's where the happening was at, as far as jazz.

Now, we had to close the place. The liquor law was to close it depending on what time zone you were in, what slot you were in, we had to close at 12, or daylight saving or whatever, it would be one o'clock. But whatever time it was that was the closing period, when there was a concert in town, the musicians would come where we were for a jam session afterwards. So they locked the door and pulled the shade down, and we'd play all night long. I mean, all night long. There were times Count Basie's whole band was in there. Al Hibblar, Gerry Mulligan, Stan Getz and all. Whoever was there, it was where they came to look forward to playing afterwards.
To the Turf Bar.

To the Turf Bar. Now, our group was so tough, that group had gotten so tight and tough, and guys would come in, they'd come and sit awhile before they'd set in. Because we had it together. And then, when the session started, then everybody would mix up and play, and that place was just... Whoever was there got locked in.

So people began to know that, be aware of that. So the night of a concert, people were standing around the doors, just like the concert was there. Because they knew the guys were coming over after. So in spite of the circumstances, during that period, there were also come beautiful moments musically.
And so you didn't go on to New York for a while?
I ended up there; I never got to New York. I left there...When I finally left after a few years and a few very ugly scenes, I left and went to Seattle.
Why did you choose...or, when did you do that?
I went there in '58.
And why did you choose Seattle?
Elmer Gill called me.
He was living there then?
Elmer was living in Seattle, and he was working at

the downtown Washington Hotel. He had the job there in a little lounge, it was a good paying job. And Elmer called me and said, 'What you doing?' And this time, I said...I was very depressed and ready to leave.
Ready to get out of Indianapolis.
I was ready to get out of there, I had had it by then.
How did your brothers feel about that situation? Were they...?

They adjusted to it like everybody in town, same as the other. We adjusted to it, we didn't like it, wasn't happy about it. And we knew it was gonna be eventually some changes made, but they happen in their own time, like anything else. Things happen...
But they had both been out of Indianapolis and seen that it didn't have to be that way.

Bud was in the service; he spent his time in the Army. It wasn't like he was exposed to the same traditional ways that Wes and I were. But maybe Wes was better about adjusting to it than I was. I wasn't too good at it, I really wasn't too good at adjusting to it. However, I never picked a fight or anything like that. But I never did adjust to it. I didn't, I couldn't handle it maybe as good as somebody else.

But when Elmer called me, it sounded like music to my ears. And Elmer called and said, 'What are you doing?' So I said, 'Well, I'm working gigs.' So he said, 'Hey, man, I got a gig out here if you...I sure would like for you to come out and do it; I got a good thing happening.' And he started telling me about it.

Now, I'm listening to him, and he made me an offer. And the offer was so good, I said, 'Are you kidding?' And he thought it wasn't enough. He upped the offer. It wasn't just dollars and cents; he even said, 'Well, I'll tell you what. Maybe I can make up to it by...I'll let you have the studio apartment I got downtown and a car to drive.'

And I'm saying, well, how could I resist? Because it wasn't that I was putting the squeeze on him. It was, the timing was right. I needed it. And I was...That appealed to me more than New York, for some reason. It appealed to me more than going to New York. Maybe it's because I was going to an altogether different place with a steady job, with a friend, somebody I knew and was fond of. And the opportunity was just there.
And I took it. I went to Seattle. That was in '58. When I got to Seattle, here I go again. The same thing it was when I came to Indianapolis, they wanted electric bass. The

electric bass was a sound that...I should have said that about the Montgomery-Johnson. Still playing electric bass, because it really got a unique sound. The sound was so unique that it would have been all wrong to change to upright bass just because I wanted to please myself.
So you really hadn't been playing upright for a long time, by this time.
No...
But you still had one?

Yeah, I still had my one back home. Now, when Elmer called me and I went to Seattle, he wanted me to bring the electric bass. He wanted electric bass. I didn't ask him which instrument do you want me to play; he said he wanted the electric bass. Because the electric bass now, it just beginning to get a little kind of like, a little more awareness in the gimmick.

It was still a gimmick, but kind of like the awareness of it was happening. There was country-western players and different guys was...not just in jazz. The electric bass was a sound that people were getting just a little more accustomed to, turned on about.

And when I went to Seattle to work, to play with Elmer, it worked out fine. Elmer had a trio, which was piano, guitar and electric bass. So just because mine was more a -- well, I just keep using the word gimmick -- novelty, I got a lot of attention. Elmer gave me a lot of solos; I got a lot of playing in. I got a lot of playing in.

In the meantime, by the consistency of playing, the length of time in Indianapolis and before, I still had good chops. After I worked with Elmer, and it wasn't a long period, I was a little bit unhappy because that wasn't the way I wanted to play.
Musically it wasn't right?

Musically, I wasn't satisfied with working in the New Washington Hotel, playing 'Tea for Two' and all that. And we had to play dressed in tuxedos and bow ties and play 'Tea for Two.' I wasn't too thrilled about that. That wasn't playing, to me. We were answering requests and all. The tunes were OK, some of the tunes were OK, but it just wasn't hardcore jazz playing.

I wanted to hear the drums and some horns and all that. So it didn't take much for the newness to wear off of that. I felt very bad because I thought that's what I was going to do. And I felt bad because, well, I made another stupid move, I'm thinking in my mind, and I need to get out of here. And that was...Meantime, I'd gone to Dave's Fifth Avenue...
A tavern...
It's a tavern, right?
I remember that place.

And he was having groups there like Billy Tolles, and the local guys were playing. And it had more...it had some fire to it. It wasn't necessarily that there were any...that those guys were so far out with their jazz things, but they had more fire and I wanted to...
They had a pretty strong rhythm and blues feeling, didn't they?
Oh, yeah. They had that; they really had that. And it was just straight ahead. And on the weekends, they had the union, out on...what street was it? We used to go to the union on weekends.
East Cherry Street?
I think it was Cherry Street...
It was the Blue Note.
The Blue Note, exactly! And that was the hangout on the weekends, because...
That was an after hours place.

After hours. It opened late and it would go all night, sometimes we'd come out; it would be daylight. You'd come out and it would be Saturday morning, Sunday morning. Fridays and Saturdays it was open all night. And the musicians had a key, all the musicians, a guest. If you were paid up as a musician, you had a key to get in and
There was a strong after hours scene there because the liquor laws were so repressive.
Uh-huh. So now, the guys would come there and play, like Chauncey Locke and -- what's the guy's name, the drummer, Brown? Something like that...
Vernon Brown.

Vernon Brown. I used to love Vernon Brown. Floyd Standifer. The players that were reaching for notes, reaching for some bebop, reaching for...You know, Miles Davis and Dizzy Gillespie and all that music.
Gerald Brashear was active then...
Gerald Brashear, oh gosh, all those guys were there.
And that's what I looked forward to on the weekends, because playing that other music with Elmer was making me nervous. And to the weekends, that's all I had to look forward to.
(end of Master Cassette II-A)

And I remember, I was going to Dave's Fifth Avenue on Saturday afternoon, because we worked at night and they had jam sessions on Saturday afternoons. (This remark cut off by tape.) Cal Tjader was working that day and on Saturday, that afternoon, I had gone over there and people were just lined up to get in. I got inside the room and I was standing, because the place was just jammed.
And Cal sounded...great artist and has sound. And it did something to me, like, wow, I just got to play different than what I'm playing. I got to play something. I got to play.

It was close to the holidays, the Christmas holidays. And I was going to go home for Christmas and I was afraid I wasn't going to come back. I was really afraid of that, that I wasn't going to come back. I wouldn't want to come back.

Meantime, I had spoken to my brother Buddy. At this time, Buddy had it so far as Indianapolis was concerned. He was ready to make his move. Anywhere. He was ready to get out. When I came home, I was telling Buddy about...and I talked to Dave before I left, at Dave's Fifth Avenue.

And I said, 'Dave, I know I can get a group out here,' and I was telling him about my brother and so-and-so. He said, 'Well, we'll see. Bring me back a tape of what it sounds like. I don't have no kind of money to be bringing, to be importing somebody in, and so-and-so.' And I said, 'OK. We'll talk about it when I come back, but I know I can bring in something that would really make it happen here.'

Because I had seen some jam sessions going down there at times when a band...I remember Count Basie was playing an engagement in Seattle and they came by there and started like a jamming thing. The thing was, people were ready to hear some real music. There was really a big market for it, but there wasn't any groups around there producing it...strong players, a whole group thing...producing it.

There were one or two players here and there, but they were scattered and had their own jobs. And Dave said, 'Well, bring it back and he'd listen to tape or see, whatever. And I went home and I was talking to my brother about it. He just wanted to make some changes. Benny Barth lived, was home, and we were talking about it and said, hey. Buddy was playing vibes now, and I was talking about us...it would be a great sound for a quartet. And Benny said, 'Let's go. I'm ready, man,' because he was...had reached that stage and he had outgrown Indianapolis, too.
That's when you cooked up the Mastersounds.

That's when we put the Mastersounds together. So we all threw some names in a hat and drew out the right name, and we drew out the name Mastersounds. Richie Crabtree had come through Indianapolis with some group traveling, and every chance he got, he was at the Turf Bar sitting in, playing with us. And he was a good player and we remembered him.
Richie lived in Sidney, Montana. And we called Sidney, Montana and Richie happened to be home. And we were talking about getting this group together and he said, 'Yeah, get me out of here.'

So we sort of decided we would meet in Seattle. The guys were ready to go. Just the weekend, and they were ready to go, to get out of Indianapolis. Benny and Buddy drove from Indianapolis to Seattle, and on the way through they picked up Richie.

When we got to town, I was so excited, because I knew we could play. We could get together and get a place to play. Meantime, I explained all this to Elmer, what was happening. And Dave let us come in. He was, by that time, Dave was convinced, because I did bring back a tape. He was convinced. And he got the group so cheap! The guys...it was just like single guys getting together driving around and playing their instruments. It's good to get out, make that trip.
We went in there on a Sunday. They got there kind of late as to what was planned, according to plan. We were supposed to open on a Monday -- Sundays is off in Seattle -- it was dark.
It was closed?

Right. So the guys got there Sunday, and we went in there Sunday evening, afternoon, to set the instruments up. And when we set the instruments up, we played some. And it was just like that group was, just like we'd been together for years.
Right from the start.
Right from rehearsal. We'd call the tunes off and the tunes were halfway rehearsed and planned. We just fell right in the thing. Even Dave was just so impressed to know...
He was there for that?

Yeah, he let us in; we had to come in at night and set up, and have the heat on and the whole thing. And we started rehearsing...We stayed in there so late, because we were just exploding to get...Here we were, with a place to play. And from day one, that group made it.
How long did you stay there?
The Mastersounds stayed there for about a year. We started doing a few little things in Tacoma and the Air Force Base, playing out like that. We got popular so quick in Seattle.
And many people started hearing about you up and down the Coast.
What brought that about, we made our first recording. This guy, Joe Boles, brought his equipment in, in Seattle. He brought his equipment in and recorded us live.
I didn't realize that.

That's where our first record date came from. Then after we were there for a spell, we felt that we were ready now, had outgrown Seattle. And I was the business person in the group. I got in my car and drove to California, to represent the Mastersounds. I came down to Los Angeles and went to Pacific Jazz Records. Dick Bock. Dick heard the tapes, and he was so impressed with the tapes that we didn't have to re-record, no studio time or anything. He just bought that master and pressed it. The first album came out.

On my way back to Los Angeles (means Seattle), I'm bursting open inside. Stopped in San Francisco, and I spent time there scouting. I met this guy there, Ray Gorham, who was associated with a new club opening called The Showcase. And Ray was doing the booking for the new room.

And how we met up was, this whole thing was kiind of strange, but he bought the group to open his room. Brand new, opening, right? On Market Street, downtown Market Street in San Francisco. It turned out to be the first club that had... a teenager could get in because they didn't serve any booze. But it was a nightclub.

So he said, what they would do because the Mastersounds ...we didn't have much of a name but the group was so tight, he got us so reasonable, he was going to make us the house group. Because he brought in the names and we'd alternate, with the house group. The house group had to really heavy because we... our thing had developed, like, it just happened for us. It just made it; the timing was right. And we were so tight, we'd burn the house group out.
Did that coincide with the release of the record?
Yeah. That worked great. That's one of the main things that brought it about, because of that new release.
You had two records right close together there, though.
Yeah, but that was later, after we got into San
Francisco, moved down there. We moved down and started recording with Dick Bock. In fact, we had to hold him back; he was going to make them too often.

So the group moved down to San Francisco because we had this job there. We went over great and after...The guy that... There were two partners that owned the Showcase and they were both attorneys Auerbach and the other guy was named David Something. And Arthur Auerbach ended up buying a place up there on the Strip (Broadway) in San Francisco. I t was called the Jazz Workshop. So he invested in that place, but all he wanted that for was just to have a door open on Broadway. He was using local people, like the Freddie Gamborel (?) trio, which was a local trio. They did OK, good players and all that, but he wasn't bringing names in.

So after the Mastersounds had worked the Showcase, the Showcase was sort of like...the life of the Showcase was sort of ending because I guess it wasn't too much of a success without selling booze to bring in the names.
The tourists wouldn't come in without it?

It just didn't happen. I guess they couldn't make it off of selling coffee and soft drinks, without the booze. And Arthur Auerback was the owner of the Workshop, and he was just satisfied with just using a little local trio. So then I saw the thing coming to an end at the Showcase and I started talking to Art about the Showcase. He said, 'Why should I bring in a group like that?...'
You mean to the Workshop?

The Workshop, I'm sorry. 'Why should I think about bringing the Mastersounds over there? We're doing OK.' And I was telling him, 'That's not the point,' because the Mastersounds were beginning to pick the momentum up on a national thing. 'We're making records. We're going to be traveling, and when we're out, then you can bring in the locals, then you bring in what you want. But while we're there, we'll add prestige to the club.' Well, it was very true. But by the same token, we needed a home base, I'm feeling. And finally I talked him into it.

And just so it would take all the risk out of it, he gave us a very lean budget to work with. We wasn't making any money to speak of. As a matter of fact, we felt like if we were home, and had something as a home base, it would be great for us. And, if I'm not mistaken, we were getting like $150 a man.
Was that under scale at the time?
No, there was nowhere near under scale, but it wasn't a good shake for the money, because he really made it. It would have been different if he wasn't doing it. The Master-
sounds started in that place, and our records began to really kind of make it, and that got to be the place. The Jazz Workshop with the Mastersounds really opened it up.
That was a pretty good time in San Francisco.
Oh yes...
There were a lot of clubs then.

We're going back now to 1959 and 1960. The Mastersounds were recording and working with... a lot of good playing, nationally and internationally as well. So San Francisco, we were like a home group there. We became local people, and we just could do no wrong.

When we went into the Workshop for four weeks or five weeks or six weeks or whatever, it was successful, cleared out, no question. We'd go out and do a tour and come back, and we'd have a home base to come into. And I remember we had talked about, with Art Auerbach who owned the place, I think we were doing like $150. I'm going to talk about a percentage. And finally, he dropped the percentage 'cause it was really making it.
He thought you made too much money?
Right, we began to make too much money that way.
At that point, it's still you and Buddy and Richie and Benny Barth.
Yeah. But our sound was unique. And one of the strong things about it, we had the same instrumentation as the Modern Jazz Quartet, who was really hot at that time.
But the sound was entirely different.

The sound was, because of the electric bass, we had ...the whole concept was different. So we really had a strong thing going. And I remember after we had got settled into the Workshop and was going out, I came back and said to Art, 'Art, you really ought to make this a leading jazz club.' We had the Blackhawk going, naturally.

He said, 'I don't want to get into that, Monk. I'm doing all right, why should I go through so-and-so.' And I kept talking to him, and I said, 'Now, while we're out of town, you ought to bring some of the names in, to keep the prestige of the place up.' We were the only thing coming in there. While we were out, he used to use locals. Finally I said to him, 'Let me try it, let's try it out. I'll get...I'll talk to the artists and see what kind of a price we can get, and let's give it a try.'
The first person I talked to about working at the
Workshop was Horace Silver. And Horace accepted, so he was the first one to come in at the Workshop.
And it was very successful, wasn't it?

Very successful. Then we brought in -- I was doing the booking, I was lining the artists up while I was gone, I would talk to them and book the room. After going out and coming back a couple of trips, Art...He didn't need me any more. And he began to talk real hip. He had all the slang down, 'Hey, my man,' and so-and-so. Great, he turned into a real jazz person. He knew the language, he knew the guys' names, he knew about prices, conditions and everything.
He probably thought it was his idea, by then.
He turned the Workshop into a very, very successful room for a long time. He finally passed away and his wife taken over, and it went some way...
But during the time that we were working with the Mastersounds, and as we had put some time in, I remember we were trying to bring Wes into the fold, Buddy and I were.
It was hard to get him out of Indianapolis, wasn't it?
Yeah. For one thing, it was hard to get him out and one of the reasons being so is because he had seven kids to provide for, so he couldn't just go out haphazard, trying to look around.
But eventually he did...
Oh, yeah.
What was it that finally got him out of Indianapolis?

What finally got him out of Indianapolis, he came to California. Buddy and I were very stable in San Francisco by then. He came out and...let me get my things right...I think he brought his trio at one point and we set up a thing, a couple of gigs for him.

And we'd been going to Ralph Gleason, was talking to Ralph about it, and I was telling Ralph I had this brother back home and he was so-and-so. And Ralph ended up putting all of this in an article, which I was very pleased about because he finally heard Wes. Like everybody else he was flabbergasted.
Was this about the same time that Cannonball Adderley told Orrin Keepnews...?

No, that was earlier. And Wes somehow wasn't able to attract any attention. He just didn't have any luck. In fact, he came to San Francisco and he had his trio, and he worked some around town. It was an organ trio, with Melvin
Rhyne and Paul Parker.
They did make a record together, though.

Yeah. They recorded back home together. And when they came to California to try to make it, they did all right but never really made it. They did some things, they did a few concerts with us and made a couple of albums with us. And we were trying to get Wes introduced into the thing through our pipeline. But it didn't really jell out too well.
Was Wes happy being out here?

He like it, being in California, but he didn't like it being away from his family. He came out by himself. One of the things, I think, was taking its toll...Well, it had to be ...something gets a little deep, deeper-seated, like can happen in a family, with brothers. And we were all very close. We were very close.

At one point, Wes tried by bringing his whole family out to San Francisco. His wife just couldn't handle it...
She didn't like it on the West Coast?

...just didn't like it. She just couldn't get adjusted to it. It just wasn't right. She just couldn't get into the...All her friends were back...She was just really set in her...You know, people out of that one type of mold or school, and when you change them or something, it's not an easy thing to do. She did try but she just couldn't adjust to the San Francisco...I mean this California life. They ended up going back to Indianapolis, moving the whole family back.

After the run with the Mastersounds, and the Master-sounds broke up, it was about...that was about '62 - '63. We decided to go back as the Montgomery Brothers, the three of us, to try. Because music was our lives, and we always managed to spend time -- either one or both of my brothers would end up playing together.
Can I take a break?
So, you were going to get the Montgomery Brothers together; how were you going to do this?
Now I'm getting to the...
How were you going to compromise Wes's family wanting to live in Indianapolis...

Yeah. In the meantime, they were living in San Francisco, they had moved back. They had moved out to San Francisco after living in Oakland. But they had made their decision. And about that period, when the Mastersounds had

broke up, and we had said, 'Well, hey, we're all there in the Bay Area. So we just said why don't we get together and now's the time we can go back to the Montgomery Brothers. Because that's what was kind of like in the blood anyhow.

The idea sounded great. I remember, we got some consideration from one of the...from a recording company. We had gone to Fantasy. Fantasy provided us with a station wagon, and then we were prepared for traveling. This was great, because Buddy wouldn't fly anyhow.

So we had a brand new station wagon and we were ready to go out as the Montgomery Brothers. Now, this is the interesting period because, I'm saying, finally, 'Well, I'm going back to the upright bass.'
What made you decide that?

It was just a natural thing that came. Because I wasn't...I had to find out for myself. I had to know for myself where I stood. I'm playing the electric bass in the beginning because of Hamp, and each period after that it was because of somebody else. It was never because of me.
Somebody else always wanted it.

Right, and rightfully so in some periods and points. Like with the Mastersounds, it was very natural for that sound. You see, it wasn't just a selfish thing by another person; it was a very natural sound. But I wanted it for myself. I had to go back and find for myself where I stood with the upright bass. Because I still had strong feelings for it, so I had to find out.

Now, because of me being who I am, I can't tear myself between two, whether it's instruments or people or whatever it is. I had to make a commitment to one. In other words, I couldn't pick the upright bass up and be true to it and still playing the electric bass. I had to go with one or the other. I have to make a total commitment to whatever I'm involved with.
I was ready for it mentally, and I thought I was ready for it physically. So I bought me an upright. I don't know; the old upright I had from some time back at home got stolen, or something...
So you hadn't had one for quite a while; you hadn't played one for a while?
Hadn't played it, or anything.
For how long?
We're going, now, since when I first started, when I left with Hamp...

Yeah. I hadn't played it since then; it's a long time. But the feeling was there and I had to find out what that is, find out where I stand, find out my own self. Is that a choice I want to make. And by '62 or '63, electric bass is beginning to come in a little bit more in its own.
...because of rock and roll...

I was by no means the only electric bass player around, fight? But I thought also, it would be a contrast of sound with Wes playing the guitar. I just had...it just made it more, my feeling more solid about I had to get back in the upright, into the other contrast, away from the string sound, the electric string sound, to the upright string sound.
I bought me an upright bass, a good bass. Our first job, as I recall, was back East at the Five Spot.
And who else was with you? Because it wasn't just the three of you.

No, it was a quartet at all times. We always picked up a drummer, an extra drummer. I just can't think of who the first drummer was. In fact, we went back East without a drummer, that's what it was. For a quartet, we made a contact to have Jimmy Lovelace, I'm pretty sure it was Jimmy Lovelace who was the first drummer. But we were going back as the Montgomery Brothers, and we would just pick up a drummer.
You've seen a lot of cases like that; the drummer wasn't part of the contract or anything. And we knew we could get some good drummers in New York; there was probably somebody there that could play.

So we were going back to make the Five Spot gig, which we considered a very good gig. And we were picking up things as we go, but we had this opportunity to go out and make that so we go ahead and make it.

Wes had some tunes worked out, Wes and Buddy's tunes were great for my....., working out songs for the Brothers. We had a two-week engagement at the Five Spot and we end up eleven weeks. We ended up working the Five Spot for eleven weeks. We changed drummers about five times; we had five different drummers. Bobby Thomas.....
Why was it so difficult to settle on somebody?

One of the reasons being so is like, for example, we had a period where Mickey Roker played with us. But he only played because he was off during that period, and that pretty much was the case. Bobby Thomas worked with us, because he had that period away from school or whatever it was. Who else worked with...Pete LaRoca played with us. They were all great drummers. But the group was so well together it didn't...it wasn't like an intricate thing for the drums. The drummer just
listened, and played.
Had Buddy stuck to piano for this?

At that time, Buddy had gone back to piano. He was playing piano, Wes was playing guitar and I was playing upright bass. We played the Half Note, downtown. And I remember that very, very clearly, when we went into the Half Note. Now, I'm going through a very, very depressed period because I wasn't able to make the transition yet. It wasn't coming. The transition wasn't coming around.
You didn't feel comfortable with the upright any more?

I was still fighting it. I wasn't loose; it was stiff. I just didn't have the thing that I had when I was playing (it before). Oh, I played the right notes and the time was...I could keep...My fingers got accustomed enough to keep the time, but it was stiff. It didn't swing at all. And it was really getting to me, really getting to me.

And I remember I picked up a bad habit of sort of stomping my feet to try to make...to get the feeling. I just couldn't find it, I couldn't find that split second.

As we well know, music is a mathematical thing anyhow, and you center on two and four. It got to center on two and four, is right the split second...

H: ...right in the center...

...right, to make that thing swing. And I couldn't hit it, I just couldn't. Wes and Buddy was playing so good, and I really wanted to give them that feeling, to make it swing and feel right. And then I began to get paranoid. There was something wrong with the instrument. Every day I was going to the fiddle shop: the guy had to re-set the bridge, another set of strings, maybe you better file it down, the soundboard. It was just...nothing was right. Even the peg re-adjusted. I did everything.

I couldn't get it right. I just couldn't get into the instrument. And I had it...One night, I remember, we were at the Half Note and late that night Wilbur Ware came in. And Wilbur Ware said, he was...He had just come in and we were on intermission and we were talking. I said, 'Wilbur, do you feel like playing one?' He said, 'Yeah, I'd love to play one.' And so I started apologizing for the bass.

Wilbur didn't pay it any mind when we was talking. And he went on the stage and picked that bass up just like he made it. Just played so beautiful. And I'm sitting there looking at Wilbur and...it wasn't the bass. You see, it was me.

H: And is that the point where you realized that maybe
you should go back to electric?

It was coming around, but I still didn't want to give in to it. I'm thinking, well, maybe I'll... In a little time. Because it's not the instrument, it's me. And there was another period that... Charlie Mingus came in one night. He was there when we got there, the early part of the night, and he was eating dinner. And we played a set, and when I came down, we was talking and he said, 'Hey, you really sound good, man,' and the group, oh, he thought the group sounded good.

And I was blushing and apologizing. I felt so bad when I was on the stage. It really wasn't sounding right, but you can't kid yourself. And I said 'Charlie, why don't you play a tune?' And he said, 'Yeah, I'll play.' You know, just, whoop, without thinking. Because guys liked to play with Wes, anyhow. Or Buddy as well.

And the group was popping. I think Pete LaRoca was playing with us then. And those kinds of jobs are very loose. You could walk in the Five Spot and anybody be sitting in. Anybody could take your place. It was just loose. Mingus went up to play, and Mingus played that bass and I said, 'There's no problem with that bass, no problem with it.' Scotty LaFazo came in one night, he played it. Nobody had a problem with it.

And I'll pick it up, it felt like everything was wrong, the wrong size strings. And I just... But it wasn't the bass, it was me. I just couldn't make that transition. It was beginning to bother me psychologically; I began to get paranoid. But I was still saying, 'I have to be patient, because it's coming around; it's going to come around.' It went on and on and on and on and on.
And it wasn't coming around. But I was determined not to give it up. I was just delighted that I was going to stick with it and play that upright bass.
How did Wes feel about it, or did he say anything?

Nobody said... There was nothing really said. I remember one night when I spoke out, I had to speak out. We were working in another place, called the Village Gate. No, not the Village Gate, something else, not the Village Gate. The Village...
Vanguard?

No... the Village something else. Because I remember right during that year, Ornette Coleman had moved back East and he was like a new... He was getting attention, really getting a lot of recognition. And he was working there the week before we came. We came in, Art Farmer was there. But that was like a hang-up. All the musicians came in.
I wish I could think of the name of this place. Anyway, we were there for two weeks. The first week, we worked opposite
of Dave Brubeck. The second week we worked opposite Stan Getz. The second week, on that weekend when Stan Getz was there, Gene Ammons was in town for 72 hours.

He had come to town. You can be there in New York for 72 hours, but you can't work because you have to have a police card. But Gene, by him having a record, he couldn't get a police card. So without a police card, you were only allowed 72 hours; you couldn't work any beyond that.

That was a dumb law they had then. But they had an opportunity to use Gene Ammons just for that weekend, and they took it. Jug, wow. When just the word got out that Jug was going to be there, that was it! People just...They brought Jug in, and he played with the Montgomery Brothers, used our group as a rhythm section, just running by ourself as a special added attraction.

So it was like Stan Getz, the Montgomery Brothers featuring Gene Ammons. Now Gene...There wasn't no way in the world you'd swing with Gene. I'm really looking forward -- we all were -- to work this, it turned out to be 72 hours, or two days and a few hours, or whatever it is, two nights working with Gene.

And when Gene came in Friday night, I remember, we were just all lit up because the place was just packed. That was quite a package with Stan Getz and the Montgomery Brothers featuring Gene Ammons. Gene came in, and when he came in that night, people were just all over him juke like he was king. And he came up on the bandstand, tuned up and everything, said ...We said, 'What are you gonna do?' He said, 'OK, let's do some blues, down here,' and he counted it off.

And it looked like I just started stiff. I'm playing while he was...And there was Wes and Gene, they were laying it in there, after they got into the tunes. And I'm here playing, and people were just, 'Gene, Gene!' And he had this big, fat sound. And it looked like I even got stiffer, because I was trying even harder. I was trying too hard to really make it lay in there and swing and flow and everything.

It didn't happen for me, and that hurt me worse than anything you can imagine. My eyes was filled with water while I was playing; I was almost crying. Because this really meant that much to me. And it really meant that much to me that I couldn't play the instrument. The right notes and things, but I couldn't get a better feeling...I knew I played better than that.

I really knew I played better than that; not that I was no Ray Brown or Charlie Mingus, but I played better than that. And I couldn't get to my potential, to the height of my playing. And as I was playing, my eyes was filling up with water because I'm wanting to play so badly and I just couldn't
make it happen.
Did you decide consciously at that point that you were going to go back to electric?

No, I still hadn't, but I remember on that break I said to Wes...I told them on the intermission, I said to my brothers, I said, 'I think I'm going home.' And they said, 'What are you talking about, what's wrong, are you sick?' And I said, 'No, I can't play.' I had a quiver in my voice when I said it. I was almost at the point of crying again. I said, 'I'm going home because I can't play.' And they said, 'What are you talking about?' I was talking about the thing.

My brothers are very...had always been really understating and very cool and all this sort of thing. They realized I wasn't where I wanted to be, but I was the only one to make an issue out of it. They weren't. And they said, 'Oh,' they would say to me, 'Oh, man, cut that out. Man, you know, if you go home, we're going home. You know, there's nothing to feel...Your're doing all right. Just...we're not ...if you're going home, we're going home.'

That almost made me feel worse. I didn't want to feel like a kid, but something that close to you is that important to you. Anyhow, I stayed. I came back, and we did a little tour around and the guys...I was still trying to push all these things out of my mind and just play. It was kind of encouraging, the things they were saying, because they weren't angry, they weren't making little insinuations or anything. They were just saying, 'We're in this thing together and we're going to play. And whatever it is, that thing have to have an extra edge, don't worry about it. It'll come. Let's just keep playing,' you know.

And I felt a little bit better about it. I really so badly wanted to play the upright. I stayed with them and we came back after the tour and we made maybe another round or so. Wes came to us and said, 'Well, I'm going to have to take my family back. We're not making it. We make a trip, we make a whole tour, and every time we come home we really haven't made any money. And we got to start making arrangements to go back out on one of those circuits again.'
Our name wasn't big enough. Our record thing wasn't in it enough. We wasn't trying to capitalize off the Mastersounds; we wanted to make it as the Montgomery Brothers.
And it just wasn't well enough known?
It just wasn't happening, or well enough known 'til Wes, or mainly Wes, could make...Well, neither one of us were making that much but Buddy and I could get by a lot easier than Wes.
This was before Wes really took off, right?

Yeah. And he was saying, because...Plus that his wife and even the kids weren't happy about that part of the country. Everybody wanted to go home. And when we were out on the road, we stayed so long trying to make some money, that it kept him away from home. It kept us all away, but a guy with a bigger family gets affected more. And he was no two ways about it; nothing to do with the music, nothing to do with us personally. He had to go.

Because his family was unhappy and he was too, because he wasn't making anything. So there was no question about that. He did what he had to do. So he went home. And that sortof brought the Montgomery Brothers to a dead end.

So Buddy and I still had to make a living, so we started jobbing. And then we got kind of scattered, jobbing and scattered. I moved to Los Angeles, because I wasn't happy with jobbing here and jobbing there. I wasn't really making it. There wasn't that much to be had. I could have taken some of the dumber jobs, to make ends meet, but it just wasn't happening.

Plus that I was kind of depressed because after we had some directions with the Mastersounds, some directions with the Montgomery Brothers and all at once there was...Not all at once...but then there was nothing. And I felt like, oh, well, about time for a drastic change, maybe. There was no use trying to bleed San Francisco for this, Buddy and I...

I took a day job. It was a very short period of time, but that frightened me because I'm saying...I had this friend that was a contractor; he built swimming pools and things. And he liked me, and he offered me a deal that I couldn't refuse. It was working in construction and it was kind of like full time. Maybe I'd have to, if I was going to make a commitment to that, I'd just have to play part time.

Then it kind of frightened me because I was saying, 'I don't want to get hung up in building swimming pools with this guy, or anybody.' I still wanted to play, but if I was going to make my music...put the priority or make it second, I could get in a lot of trouble, I'm thinking.

This paid good money and it was steady and consistent. But I wasn't ready to give up playing. Anyhow, I was working a job out in Sausalito. Howard Roberts, Jack Sheldon and a couple of more guys, I think. Maybe it was Jimmy Rowles. Some guys came up from studio work, that came up to work this thing. And I was playing bass for them. And they were telling me things were good in Los Angeles and how the studio work was and recording. And 'Man, you ought to come down to Los Angeles.'

I went to Los Angeles. Howard Roberts had a record date, and I went to make the record date and while I was there, I went over that Sunday night to a...I can't think of the name of this club, down on Adams...and a tenor player was working there by the name of...Gee whiz, will you look at that, I can't

think of his name — anyway, he had a steady job. I'll get his name; I got a record by him in there. And I went by and sat in. And he said, 'Man, are you in town? Are you...?' He had some kid playing bass. He was telling me on the break, 'Man, I could sure use a bass player. This kid don't know all the tunes and ...' blah blah blah blah. And I said, well, I had moved down but I'm trying to think about it. 'Oh, man, I'll get it straight with the union and we could take care of business, because if I don't have anybody...' and so-and-so. Curtis Amy! He had a little quintet. He said, 'We're steady, man, it's a group. Why don't you come on down, man? It would be great.'

So I thought about it, because you know, for me, a six night a week gig, that's better than digging swimming pools. Anyhow, I came down for the job with Curtis Amy. After I was down for a couple of weeks, I brought my family down to Los Angeles. That was her home anyhow, and it was very easy to get comfortable right there.

After I was in Los Angeles a short while, I got a call from Cal Tjader. He wanted me to, he needed a bass player and wanted to know would I join the band. And we talked about it, and I said, 'Man, all these years I been in California up in San Francisco, and as soon as I move to Los Angeles you want me to come back to San Francisco and join your band.' You know it worked out.

At the same time I got a call from Lou Rawls. And I had to make the thing, would I go with Cal Tjader or Lou Rawls. But Lou hadn't yet... I think he'd made 'Tobacco Road' or something, he made his first thing, but hadn't really hit that hot traffic. And Lou had called me first and I said, 'Well, I'll get back to you, I have a little something that's pending.' No, Cal called me first and I hadn't confirmed it when Lou called. I said, 'It depends on something' and then I spoke to Cal.

He said, 'Man, well, I'm getting hot and we're traveling here and we're doing this...' and I said, 'Well, you better let me get back to you.' Because I wanted to be more in an instrumental than backing a singer. A singer doesn't give you much time to play, much room.
Were you back to electric by this time?
Still playing upright...
Still playing upright.

...I hadn't given it up, and it looked like it was getting just a little bit more looser and I was still sticking with it. Diehard. And I wasn't happy because of what happened with the group breaking up, and all, and I was stuck with it.
And I went back to play with Cal, and I was playing
upright. And I began to get a little bit more loose with it, a little bit more loose with it. And I played with Cal for a long time, maybe a year.

Meantime, while I was working with Cal Tjader, was when Cannonball did this thing with Riverside Records, introduced Orrin Keepnews to Wes, being in Indianapolis. When we were with the Mastersounds, our last recording with Dick Bock, we did a thing with Three Brothers and Five Others. It was Freddie Hubbard and Pookie and Punchy, Joe something on piano and Paul Parker on drums, and the three brothers. They were the five others.
