And when we made the album, there was some time left in the studio, so we said, 'Well, let's just play some kind of straight ahead thing.' And Wes stretched out on it, and it turned out to be a tune called "Finger Pickin'." It got more play than the other thing.

Wes wasn't really a total stranger to them when he talked about it, but he did have a little something going there. And "Finger Pickin'" was getting some play when they introduced Wes to Riverside Records. Riverside brought him in and they did an album. The first album was with Jimmy Jones. I remember the album vaguely. I wish I could get my hands on it now, because I remember it was different. It was a good album.

But then someone heard the sound, I think it was Creed Taylor. And the next thing they did with Wes was with Oliver Nelson, and they came out with "Going Out of My Head." I don't have to tell you what that did for him.
Now I'm working with Cal Tjader. I knew that he had...
Well, he (Wes) had quite a few albums for Riverside before he went to Creed Taylor and became popular...
Oh, yeah, that is right. I'm backing my thing up. It wasn't...The next one he came out with Oliver Nelson, that didn't have anything to do with Creed Taylor, did it? I think it did...
Creed Taylor was then with Verve as a producer.

Well, Verve...The deal went some way that Verve or whoever it was brought Wes and Creed Taylor together. Anyhow, whatever that was, the difference there was...OK...But I remember when I was working with Cal, Wes was telling me about it. You know, we always kept close, all of us, the brother did.

I'd be a phone call away. He was saying, 'Man, I went to make this thing at Riverside Records and, man, they really want to make me a solo guitarist.' I said, 'Oh, great, man. Jump and get it.' He said, 'Whah...' He was working for Polk's Milk Company, cleaning the place up with them high boots and that slop and stuff, and that one job,and then he had a ...
In Indianapolis?

Indianapolis, yeah. He had another job he was going to at RCA, and then he worked an after hour joint on the weekends. See, the day work...There was just a little playing time, doing it just on the weekends in this after hours joint. He had his own little trio in there. And they called him back ...He wasn't really hungry to make a living otherwise, he was hungry to play his guitar. He just needed to play.

And they set him up just right. They got the sound. When I first heard that record on the radio, I heard it...and he used to tell me about it. He told me he had the recording thing and, 'It sounds like it might be a hit, man, because it don't sound like my playing.' Like, he's...
Are you talking now about "Going Out of My Head?" *

Yeah. It don't sound like his usual thing, boy, they've sweetened his stuff on...He was telling me all these things, how they...I heard the record, I heard the music on the radio. It looked like every time you turned around it was "Going Out of My Head." I never...People begin to come up and say, 'Is this your brother?' And all at once it began, it was like everybody was talking about Wes Montgomery, and that's what I like to hear. It was just like a little thing, when you hear his name, when somebody mention Wes's name, it just a little tingle come up inside. A little tingle.

Because he was getting popular. I said, 'Wow!' When we were out here in California he couldn't buy a job, when he was there, he couldn't make a living, he couldn't exist. And that's all you could hear. Club owners was talking about, 'Hey, what do you think are the chances of getting your brother out to do a thing...' and there was a little tingle would go up inside of me, because Wes is really making it.

So Buddy and I, when we would talk, we would just laugh and say, 'Man, this cat is doing it.' Then when we'd talk to Wes, Wes would say, 'Yeah, man, they say it look like we got a hit. You know, it's gonna be a hit!'
And he made several more after that.

He sure did. Those hits were coming up, and then he went on, he came out on tour, out to California. And he had Wynton Kelly and Paul Chambers and Jimmy Cobb. Miles's rhythm section was working with him. But they first sent him out on tour as The Wynton Kelly Trio featuring Wes Montgomery. So the trio would come out and play, and then Wes came out like a singer would. He didn't come out to open the set up, and it made him very uncomfortable, because he just couldn't adjust to being a star.
Having that kind of attention?

Yeah, he couldn't adjust to that, to sit there while the group played four or five songs and he'd come in and play just a couple of things. He had to be a part of what was happening, like. Well, I remember working with Cal was just great for me. It was one of the best jobs I ever had in terms of being musical, relationships, good feeling with the guys in the band. The work was not overly...Cal spent most of the time on the West Coast, as you remember.

I wasn't doing a whole lot of heavy traveling. When we went to New York it was always first class. I just enjoyed working for Cal. And Carl Burnett was the drummer at the time. Armando Peraza. It was an education for me to play in the group...

And then we got extra monies, like...He had the van. We would drive the van, we would keep the van between Carl and I, when we was traveling. Because Carl had most of the instruments, which was drums...By the time he broke the drums down... And there was the vibes, which went in cases, and that was it.

We got paid extra for driving the van, plus doing the loading. Well, that was perfect for Carl, and I could use the extra dough, use the van, where you would go you kept the van, credit cards for the gas, and everything. Anyhow, it was good working for Cal.

When Wes came out and made a...and I could really see the impact of what was happening. And it was so strong, it was so definite. There was no question about it, he was on his way. They worked at Jazz Workshop. The night he worked at Jazz Workshop, I was playing a concert with Cal over at -- what's the name of that place, the Music Hall or something like that. We played a concert and we got out and rushed over to the Workshop, and couldn't get near it. Couldn't get near.

And I wiggled my way trying to get...finally got up to the door and I knew the guy working the door, and they made room for me. Just an exception because...Wes was there and everything. And I came in and saw him, and I was watching him perform on the stage, and you knew he was on his way, that people was looking for that sound.

Anyhow, it wasn't long after he'd left San Francisco, is when I got a call from him. Because he was very unhappy with the trio because...Well, God rest their souls, Paul Chambers and Wynton were...you know...
...not behaving themselves.

...not behaving themselves up to Wes's expectations, not the image that Wes wanted. Jimmy Cobb was great, he didn't think that was Jimmy's fault. He was complaining too with the trio. And Wes was saying, 'Man, you know, these guys are great players and all that, but...' He had missed me and Buddy, too. Now that he was back in it again, and he said...'Man, it looks
like it's all right now. I can afford it. The money's right and I can offer you guys a decent salary, and we'll be a unit, be back together again.'
But it was Wes Montgomery this time. Not the Montgomery Brothers, not the Mastersounds.
You were now his sidemen.

...sidemen. He had a hard time trying to explain to us we was just sidemen. But he wanted us to be like a family thing with Cal. And we wanted to. I mean, I wanted to. Not to the point where I would shake the boat for him or anything...
What year are we in now?

We're now up to about '66. He passed in '68. And I went to tell Cal, because it was hard for me to leave Cal. Cal was just great, it almost got to be like a family thing with Cal. I was really enjoying it; it was just great for me. I was really happy working with Cal and I enjoyed playing his music. I had a lot of respect for him and his wife Perci (?), and he had a lot of respect for me, and that's what —

When I went to tell Cal, I said, 'Cal, I need to talk to you about something.' I wasn't sure about the best choice of words, about Wes had asked Buddy and I to join him, and Buddy had consented to it, Buddy and I talked. And Cal said, 'Well, man, you know I can't...what can I say? I hate to see you leave because of selfish reasons, for myself,' he said, 'but if it was me, I'd do the same thing, or anybody else that was...' He said by all means to go with his good wishes, to join Wes.

And I joined Wes's thing. Wes, now, was using a conga player and the four of us, and it was good. Now Buddy's playing piano, I'm still playing the upright bass. I had really amplified it, I had to get an amplifier because the congas...I couldn't cut through with the bass sound. I'm playing bass and I just couldn't cut through. The congas just drowned it out. I had a great bass and...
Was Wes...On the job at this point was he playing his hit tunes?

Oh yeah. That was, he had to. His...The songs were so strong, he was putting one after another. But what happened was, we were still doing night clubs, type of thing. We would play...He would play all the things he wanted to play to satisfy himself, but before the set was out, you got to go into "Bumpin'," "Going Out of My Head" and "California Dreaming," "Tequila." He sneaked them in, but they were just short versions. He didn't even stretch them way out, and that kept the people screaming. It's like, he did it with a science.
When we got the set up, we played "Jordu" and all the tunes we wanted to play, the first portion of the set. And as we got into it, he'd play one of his hits. And then he'd sneak

another one in for us to play, maybe something we really liked. It could be "Tenderly" or some kind of ballad thing. "Rainy Day" or something, and then he'd sneak some of these other things in. But he got them in in the course of the night, he kept the people really satisfied.

I was still fighting this image of trying to play the upright bass. I wasn't that unhappy with it at this point, but I just couldn't get...Here I am complaining again. Because the sound was so strong. When you think about how firm and heavy Wes played, with the congas...and Buddy was a strong player, he still is. It was like there was no way in the world I could... With the congas, and the drums. Billy Hart is such a strong drummer. You had to be that to give Wes what he was calling for. I just got drowned in it.

So now I got me a big amplifier and a big bass, and I'm carrying these two, just so I can cut through with this thing, right? One day I was saying, I was just tired of lugging them and I had to be...The hassle of traveling that way was really hard on me. And I said to Wes once, we were in Pittsburgh, 'Hey, man, it's not the same thing. Every time I change rhythm the sound changes, the least little thing, if I got a crack in my bass of something, or the amplifier, or there's not room on the stage, or there's always some kind of problem. I can't get comfortable. You know, I better give some thought about going back to the electric bass.'

He turned to me. He said, 'I thought you never would find out for yourself.' He said, 'I never thought you would. Look, why would you want to go back to the upright, now that everybody's playing the Fender?' He said, 'You made the Fender; you put the Fender there. The proven ground you did with it, a lot of guys are trying to play like you were playing, trying to come into the thing, the pace that you set with it.'
And he was---held from saying that, all that time?

All that time, until I made up my mind. He said, 'I thought you'd never change. What took you so long?' And he said, 'Now...' And I'm asking him, like, 'I don't know what your feelings are, but I think I'm going to...' He told me his feelings aren't important. He knew how I was feeling all along, but why was I fighting it? But he knew I had to fight it out until I was satisfied with it. And when I came back to him, like I was reporting to him, he was saying, 'Whew, what took you so long?'

He said things to me I never thought of, but sometime we'll get bogged down in our minds about things. He said, 'Your name comes up more than anybody with the electric bass.' He said, 'Who is going to be talking about Monk in relation to the upright bass? It's not going to come up.' He say, 'You know why? Because they're going to be talking about Ray Brown. They're going to be talking about Ron Carter. They're
going to be talking about some...' He say, 'You're way down the line on upright bass; you're way down the line...'
But he never said that to you all the time you were agonizing about it.

Never one word. When I came back there with tears in my eyes, he didn't say one word. Those were the kind of brothers I had. He allowed me all the time in the world for thinking, for myself. And when I came back, they didn't either one say this to me. Maybe in my mind it would have helped me more if they had said it a long time ago.
So you finally did change back.

When they said that, I was just like...happy inside. Inside me was just like, 'Wow!' That had to have been a problem that I had lived with so long, and never got around to really being comfortable, totally comfortable. And I went back to the electric bass, it was in Pittsburgh. It felt so good. Even though I wasn't sharp as I was, and had to make some transition, it felt so good, so right.
And I had times I could be playing, and I'd look at one of my brothers, they'd look at me, and give me a little smile, as if to say they knew I was OK. They knew I was comfortable now.
That you made your own choice.

In my own way. That it was my doing, you know. They knew that I was satisfied with the choice I made because I looked comfortable. It was...the shock was all gone. Not the image of the upright, not the image of this, it didn't mean anything. I know when he looked at me as if to say 'you look good,' it...
How long did this group last?
Until Wes passed.
It did?
Yeah, and was about maybe a year after.
(end of Master cassette II)

You were talking about the three of you working together, and Wes was at that time very popular. But in your club dates you didn't play all...I mean you played some of those but you didn't stick to that.

Very naturally, we would lean heavily toward the hit things, because that's what was drawing, and that's what was making Wes, was the hits. There were times that we would go in and...Wes was so hot that we would go into a club, even the larger clubs -- and when I say the larger clubs, I mean so

far as seating capacity, a club would seat as many as 250 or something like that, was considered a large nightclub -- and when we got to work, the place would be full and people would be lined up outside.

I remember occasionally we worked at the Concerts by The...no, the Lighthouse, in Los Angeles. And it was during a period when there was a heavy fog-rain mixed together. It was just a nasty night, very nasty, cold night. And when we got to work that day, even out at the beach, Hermosa Beach, it could be even worse with the dampness and the fog.

The line was at least, it seemed like it was a block long. I couldn't imagine that many people standing in line, knowing the place was filled. We hadn't started to work, we hadn't even started, so how they would be content to stand in that line...

Wes to go on, took care of the set, they'd clear the house up or whatever, so they'd have the opportunity to get in. It's just the way he was drawing; the people were content standing in line under those conditions.
So you were traveling pretty constantly?
Well, he wasn't exactly...When you say constantly, he wasn't working as hard as he was when he was because he could afford to space his jobs better...
He was making better money and had the power...
...and not work as hard. There were times when he could, when we were working like maybe two nights in a place... out of the week, or maybe the week off, or traveling times were distributed better.
How long did this period last, where you were working together as a unit?

The last time, we were working as the Wes Montgomery Quintet. That was when he was traveling with the hit things. That period lasted less than two years. And then, the thing that happened was that he come to the unexpected end.

And I remember very distinctly we were working a concert; and we weren't working, we were beginning to lean on...Well, as a matter of fact, John Levy, his personal manager, had come out to California, I believe it was. His manager and the publicity man, they had a meeting saying 'Wes had outgrown the nightclubs.' And in fact, they felt that nightclubs wasn't conducive because of the type of crowds that we were drawing. But at concerts, people were the same way, and huge, more than thousands now...
In other words, he was ready to make more money.
Yeah, that's what he mean, John. Plus that, they

saw Wes, the thing where he was going to have to also take off more time, because his money had developed to the point that he...They have a system where if you make too much money on a certain period, a quarter...
And his asking price was up pretty high by now...
Right. His asking price was so high that unless you balance it out some way, the more you make the more tax, what-ever. You don't get the benefit of it.
You were all living an easier life by this time?

Especially Wes. It wasn't that Buddy and I were taken care of like Wes was. That's not business, you know. We were still sidemen; that's all they regarded us in terms of the administrative thing. It was strictly business. Wes Montgomery. Buddy and I, we were just side people. It had nothing to do with The Montgomery Brothers any more.

And this kind of affected Wes, and Buddy and I knew it, but it sort of affected us a little bit, but that was business. We accepted it for what it was. If it had been the other way around, had been me, or had been Buddy, they would have treated it the same way, because that's the way...that's business.
But you were still close.

Oh, yes, we were close. And that sort of took its toll a little bit, because it caused some separation for us that wouldn't naturally...normally happen under normal conditions. But these are forced to happen, so you allow it to happen, to continue some kind of relationship. That's how frictions come about. But just for us to rise above that, we had to accept the other, and whatever it meant

And no matter what the situation was, we would maintain our relationship as brothers, and no love lost... ...We always let the business go, let the business people take advantage of the business, for Wes. Because he had earned it, in every sense of the word. His whole life had been spent doing that, plus the talent was there. He had a chance to express himself, and he most certainly earned it. So there was no malice there as far as Bud and I were concerned, because of his success.
But there might have been some tension, that contributed to his illness?

Well, I don't know if I can speak in medical terms of how that taken effect, but he did have a...What he died, because of a heart condition. His heart was really, really gone. Even then, we weren't aware of it. His heart had had it. And he detected the fact that he did have a heart problem.

But back to what I was saying. John Levy and his

business person came and met with him, at a meeting to discuss with him the fact that now he had grown to another bracket, so they were going to look more now at concerts and performances such as Las Vegas appearances and that type of thing. And there was mention of a movie background, what do you call it...
Soundtrack.

...mention of soundtrack and that type of thing. Because he had reached another plateau now. He was ready to, like, any time he would go to a nightclub it would be for his own personal satisfaction, of getting a chance to play... He was ready for big business now.

I remember we played a concert somewhere in the East, I just can't remember the town, I think it was somewhere in New Jersey or something. Big sort of concert. It wasn't a festival. It was similar, I just wouldn't call it a festival. And it was like the tour ended there.

No, I'm sorry. That's when the meeting was. Actually, the engagement we came for, we had a week off. And everyone went to their own direction, in terms of going home during that week off. I was living in Los Angeles, Buddy was living in San Francisco and Wes was still in Indianapolis.

In the meantime, Wes was complaining about...there was a...Prior to that, I remember just a few weeks of whatever, he was saying to us that he had a couple of scares. Like, because he'd wake up in the night short of breath. They were warnings, I'm sure. And it was in San Francisco and it was in Chicago, he way saying that he had gone to the Emergency, at the hospital, because of these symptoms he was having.
It frightened him enough to go...

It frightened him, and he went to get some kind of medication. Now, he had gone...he was visiting his doctor at home but...Well, long after, we figured that Wes wasn't telling us all of it at the time.
You think so?

...And I don't think he knew all of it himself. But, you know, sometimes you can, speaking about how much knowledge you can have, you can have enough knowledge to be dangerous and I think that's what the doctor was keeping from him. But then, he was keeping a portion of what the doctor told him, from us.

But he would still tell us about...I mean, he mentioned to us about he was having these attacks. And I remember saying to him, 'Man, that's just...' I was making some kind of excuses, I can't think of for it. Anything I could make up. I was making them up because the farthest thing from my mind was he had any kind of problem that he should be that alarmed with, especially if he had gone to see the doctor.
Well, after all, at that age, you wouldn't...
He was the picture of health.
In his early forties...

Oh, yes, he was the absolute picture of health. It looked like every time he turned around he was saying he needed to lose a little of that weight. He was just healthy, skin clear, eyes clear, just strong attitude; he was just a picture of health. I couldn't imagine anything was happening to Wes at the time that would cause him to be that alarmed to wake up in the night with fears like he was dying. I couldn't imagine a person...
But he did have them.
And he was...His sense of humor...He was a very, very ...His sense of humor was just incredible.
Did you stop playing after he died? I read that somewhere.
Yeah, I did, for a period.
For how long?
It went into months, I don't know how many. Four or five, maybe. Just wild guesses, but it was just a few months.
And then how did you start again?

It was kind of strange. Let me just wind up this one part about Wes because our last and final engagement as it would happen. During that week that we were off, we went to start back to work...Our last date working was in Phoenix, Arizona. We played three nights down there at a place called Caesar's something; the guy was called Caesar. That was our last engagement. We were off for one week and we were to start back on these concerts. We had just ended the nightclubs and...
...and into the next phase...

...going into the next phase. We had a week off. I came home, went to Los Angeles; Buddy went to San Francisco. And it was a thing like, even when we were off, we'd talk to each other every day or so. We were very close.

And he called me on a Tuesday, and we were just talking, just talking. And I was looking forward to going back. And we had a whole week off. I hear from Wes all the time; you know, we'd call back and forth, like that, but I thought it was unusual to keep talking so long. We had just finished that Saturday night and it was like Tuesday. Maybe there was something to talk about in between, but not that long. We were
talking a long time.

And then he was saying things like, 'Is everything all right?' And I would say, 'Yeah, everything is great.' That was his way of asking, do you need anything. And he would speak to my wife, and it was sort of like hanging on to the phone. I didn't pay it too much attention, but then he called me Thursday. Two days later he called me again. And we talked for a long time, so he was telling me about that he had gone to the doctor and they had him in...He was a chain smoker, and he was smoking these cigarettes was made out of lettuce. Just couldn't give up the cigarette thing, right? And he had to give up meat. And he had to give up salt and he was taking some pills and so-and-so. I knew he was nervous about his condition, I knew that.

And we talked so long on Thursday. And Saturday morning, early Saturday morning, I got a call from my sister. And when I answered the phone she said, 'Monk, Wes is dead.' And that about...I never experienced a shock that I had that morning. Just simple and to the point, she said it. Then I began to put all those other pieces together. And then, naturally, all of that was explained to us by his doctor, afterwards, his real condition. They kept it from us but they told his wife more than they told us, and she kept it from us.

The doctor knew, the last time Wes had visited him, that he couldn't go back to playing. He knew he wasn't strong. He knew it was over but he couldn't tell Wes. So he told Wes to take off three weeks, and then we'd talk about it. And most of the things he was telling me, that the doctor wanted him to stay off for three weeks. He said, 'Man, I can't do it. We got these things coming up and so-and-so...' I said, 'Just take it easy, man, I'll carry your guitars to the airports and things.'

You know, his wind was short and he couldn't do this. 'No problem, man, you're living like a king now, you're flying everywhere and the best hotels. You just play a little bit at night, you cut that back. We'll...Let the band play more. We don't have to rehearse. We'll do a whole lot of things, right?'

But he was living in that fear to the point of not knowing the extent of how bad it was. But the doctor told us afterwards it was over. His heart was just, the condition of it...His playing days was over then.
Was that something he had had all his life and nobody knew? Rheumatoid arthritis or one of those things that you don't...

Don't know, didn't any of us to my knowledge. I know I didn't. I didn't dig it up, or stir it up, or try to do a 'roots' thing on his health. That was it. Wes was gone. He was gone and that was it. And that's when...
It stopped you dead in your tracks, didn't it?

Adjusting to that was, very naturally, one of the hardest adjustments I've ever had to make. Because when I started thinking, it really began to dawn on me how close we were. See, we had never been separated. Even from the early stages, when I was separated from the other parts of my family, Wes and my older brother and I went off to my dad. When I lost my older brother, Wes and I came closer.

Wes and I were just like, he was...when it dawned on me, I didn't only lose my brother, I lost my best friend. Because we were never separated, and there was never throughout our whole lives, we didn't have a fight or a serious argument of any kind. I just didn't realize that I had lost my best friend, not just my brother.
So it took you a while to settle that...

It affected me like I couldn't imagine. You take things even like that, life, for granted. Love for granted. Closeness...and that brotherly...protective thing. That's what life is about. But it was somewhat of a lesson for me, and I experienced out of that, too.
From loss,,,Maybe it's not a good thing to say, but it is a fact. But, anyhow, I had experienced other losses, my mother and my father and my older brother...
Those were more natural things?

Yeah, but I didn't have the same life with them that I had with Wes, and that made the different. Anyhow, after that happened, I went back to Los Angeles and Buddy went back to San Francisco. And both of us, very naturally, were very down about this, because Buddy was experiencing the same things I was. Not to the degree, maybe. I don't know. Maybe even more, you see, when you stop and think about it, but I had no way of judging to what degree and it wasn't even important to what degree. But I did know that we were experiencing the same...
So that you just didn't feel like playing.

No. Music was like...well, to me, Wes was music. And right at that period in my life, it was like...and it kind of unfolded. And I couldn't relate to music. I couldn't imagine myself performing. So we went—

I was trying to collect myself. Because it wasn't the point where it was the only way to make a living, or life ended there, I knew that. I hadn't gotten into the idea that (my) life ended, but it was...I was having problems picking up the pieces, gathering the pieces. And I wanted to stay away from Bud. I think Bud wanted to stay away from me.
And that was right, I guess. After that, a while
after that...I never attempted to go back to the instrument, or even go out and hang out and hear music and all that.

Bud and I were talking, talking and not saying anything, You know what I'm saying? Just talking. We didn't get on every subject and we wouldn't dig up the past. We didn't see much of each other during that period; I really didn't want to see him.

He called me, after a spell had passed, and he said, 'Well, we're going to have to go back to playing, we're going to have to go back to work,' is what he said. 'And that's the way it is. So we're going to have to pick up the pieces and go back to work.'

And I remember a thing that happened, and that's when I was telling Buddy about it, because when it happened, it struck me kind of funny. Not funny; it just struck me. I got a call from a...I received a letter. First I received a letter of condolence from -- what's his name, from Columbia Records? --
John Hammond?

John Hammond. And then John Hammond called me. And they were very fond of Wes. Oh, everybody was. Even though that wasn't his label he was recording with, or anything. He was very fond of Wes. So he was saying, while he understood where everything was at musically, with us and Wes, and blah-blah-blah, but he was wondering was it possible if Buddy and I could hook up with George Benson and sort of continue...George was so close, was closer to Wes's thing. Because what Wes had created was like a factory, going...Like, the factory continued on. Because there was such a demand for his music. It left such a gap.
And he thought George was the logical inheritor?

Right, especially if Buddy and I were with him, to give the Montgomery relationship. Plus, Wes was really George's idol. There wasn't no razzmatazz behind it. And George will say it even today, that was his idol. I know for a fact the relationship between the two of them was deep. Respect; Wes had the greatest respect for George. He loved George.
Did you pick up on that? I don't...
Pick up on what?
With Columbia" I don't recall ever seeing...

Oh, no. I couldn't imagine that! Are you kidding? At the time he called me, I thought there was a...I knew the man perhaps meant well, but it was in such bad taste, I felt that I couldn't be part of something like that. If George took it upon himself to...in respect out of Wes...I had to honor the man for it. But I couldn't see going into that. I'd
rather Wes just fades out as Wes.
Did you go on and do something that was...

Right. He was Wes Montgomery. Everybody do their own thing. He thought Buddy might be saying, 'Look, I'm going to join if you don't.' So-and-so, it put me in the mind of saying even worse to me. Because Wes was gone. Are we doing it for Wes? He did his thing. That was the feeling he left, mentally, and when I spoke to Buddy about it, Buddy felt...His feeling was the same as mine.

He didn't make a big thing out of it. I think what we sort of...When we talked about it together, which it was quite a thing to look at...not as 'are we making a mistake?', not that way. But we understood, we really understood the whole thing and sort of approved the way that our feelings ran parallel, alike...that we could talk about it lightly and pass right on.
Then you felt better going on and playing just as a sideman with other people, at that point?

No. That was a turning point for me. That was really a turning point, not only in my life but in my music. A major turning point. And I think I was using that period of off time, thinking it out. Thrashing it out, rather. It wasn't no thinking it out. It was a turning point, so I wasn't thinking, I had to thrash it out.
At that point, thoughts was just running through my mind that I had to deal with. We're all, like, reborn. I couldn't go back and settle into the other, my pattern of things...
You had to take another path?

Completely. That path was completely closed up. Now, I recall, as I was thinking, as far back as my music went, I was with one of my brothers or the other, or both. I wasn't into any other particular place for any length of time, that I joined in with my brothers. It just automatically branched in there. And I guess one of the biggest gaps is when I, that two year period I spent with Hamp.
And that kept me, it always would emerge that when I was with my brothers, I felt secure...
Didn't you feel secure when you were with Cal?

Not the same kind of secureness, you know what I'm saying? Musically, even, because it was a thing like, I didn't realize how...what an insecure person I was until that point, musically. I was a very insecure man, musically. As far back as I...In my mind, is when I started into music, even to when the time I began, I didn't begin...when I picked the instrument up, it was like my brothers were there. And I knew that the

attention I was getting wasn't all mine. It was because I came from a strong family musically. But the strength came from Buddy and Wes. So I was leaning on them. Which is right, you know, what's wrong with that? What are brothers for? It's like Iwasn't heavy, you know.

But that was true. Because I was...right at that...I could see it all. I could really see it, to relive it, to go back and say, 'That's why, that was it.' I was comfortable because I was leaning on my brothers' music. I never wrote a tune, I never arranged anything, I never really ventured. I knew when it was...They always had it prepared for me. It was always prepared for me, but it was prepared with love. I was their man.
Well, you sort of changed your direction, but you didn't stop playing. I mean, you did for a while, but you did come back.

No, but I had to regroup. Believe me. Because then, what happened, was I was saying, even though Wes wasn't there, for the first time in my years of playing, it wasn't that the upright and electric bass, or this kind of thing, disturbing me, making a choice about that. For the first time, I wanted to be on my own. I didn't want to lean on Bud. I didn't want to go that way.

I love Bud dearly, and it was almost like...But he had to understand where I was coming from. He really had to understand where I was coming from. I didn't know exactly which way I was going, but I knew I wasn't going that way no more. At least for now.

I remember, Buddy called me and said, 'Well, we're gonna have to go to work. Things take time, but we're gonna have to do it. There's nothing you and I can do, but give it time. We have to continue on, and we may as well get started.' And that's what he was saying. Buddy's the kind of person, he's a very matter of fact person, and he still is, and I love him to death. But he was saying, 'We have to get on with it.'

And I remember I started mumbling, and I realized that what he was saying was right. I just didn't know how to handle what I was going through and explain it to him. Because Buddy always depended on me, too. Not depended on me in music, but depended on me being there. I mean, really depended on me. Because he had his shortcomings. It wasn't that I was the only one with a shortcoming because I was insecure, musically...
But you're still his big brother...

Yeah, I sure was. You know, I took care of things where...I had a job to do. We always had an assignment within our...to make a group. One guy could be...Wes was a...Playing, he did that to death. But you hand him a microphone and it was over. He couldn't do it. Or if he had the business to take care of, it was over. But that was kind of like in my department.

I've always had my...thing.... But it worked, that's what had become important. Buddy's quiet and withdrawn. He's the most withdrawn person, a hard person to communicate with, on a one-to-one. So, they didn't have to worry about it, because I...Big mouth was there.
This is the talking Montgomery brother...

Right. I was the one that could get it on, I could get it on. I could walk in a group and be the life of the party. But what was happening, that was I was covering up for the insecurities, making up for the insecurities I had over there. So it balances itself out. But right then, something happened. Something ended. And something else had to come in.
How long did that period last?

When Buddy called me about going back, I said to Buddy right then, I said, 'Bud...' He said, 'I had talked to Miss Thompson,' that's the lady that owned the club, the Turf Bar where the Montgomery-Johnsons started.
In Indianapolis.

In Indianapolis, that was so successful during '55 - '56, whatever. He talked to the lady there. He always kept a good relationship, because once we sort of made it, we were like...When we went to Indianapolis, home, were were the heroes. We were known, even that day, in Indianapolis we were the heroes of the jazz music to come out of that...
He had spoke to Miss Thompson, and she said, about coming to work. And she was delighted. She still had the place and at the time, the thing had quieted down again and she would welcome anything.

She was delighted and was happy to do it for us. She knew what we were going through. That Buddy and I would come back as The Montgomery Brothers, just the two of us, and we would build a group around that. Buddy was ready to put a group together and still is , and I knew he would have a good thing happening. There was no question about that.

So he said he wanted to continue playing vibes and he was going to get a quartet together. So I understood what he was asking and I knew how important it was to him, for him to be able to go back now. And the same for me. To play, to be able to be as comfortable as possible. With me there, it would, at least he'd be halfway there.
I didn't have the same feeling, and I felt bad, because it wasn't that I had anything personal against Bud, but I had to do for myself.
And you didn't want to move back...
Yes. I didn't want to go back. I really didn't

want to say that to him, because I knew now, of all times, how I would be needed.. He had it in his thinking but it wasn't that way. He had it that we were the Montgomery Brothers and there were two of us.

That was harder to tell Bud. But I had to, I couldn't live with it. So I said to him, I said, 'Bud, I know you're right and we're going to have to go back to work.' And I guess I'm just about ready. I've been thinking things out, and I guess I'm just about ready. I'm just about strong enough; I don't mean physically but I mean mentally. And Bud, there's only one problem, is that I don't see things the same way right now and I have to deal with that. I'll go back with you to Indianapolis to get the job started, and work with you as long as it takes for you to find somebody else that you can...'
But you didn't want to stay.

I said, 'I'm going to have to do my own thing.' We went back and he thought about it, but he accepted it because he knew he had to push on. We went back to Indianapolis and we worked that job, with Buddy and I and Eddie Moore and George Cables, the quartet. And it was out of sight.
George Cables is a good player...

But I broke it off. After the job, the engagement, ended, I came back home to Indianapolis (he means L.A.) and I began practicing, with just locking myself in the room. And I had a tape recorder, a very good tape recorded with four tracks and I would tape and overdub and do all those things. And I heard something different.

But the main thing is that everything was strictly... I was playing what I heard, felt. And it was just like, that's when I think I uncovered something there. I'm pretty sure it happens in the average musician over a period of time, if they're playing well enough and they're seeking, something happens, or something causes something to happen. It's too bad it happened the way it did in my life, but that don't mean everyone has the same kind of experience.

Something happened, and it was like a whole new thing for me. But it took all those years to develop into being able to be better and predict a time, ready, prepared to make that next step. And that step, for me, had been there for years but it was just right then when it developed.
How did you take advantage of it? What did you do about it when you realized...

When I realized it, like I said, I locked myself in and started playing and I hear the things, and I knew that I ...didn't...all the time, I began having that security began to happen. Just strength, that can happen inside.. I was ready to get my own band, because I hear in the things, expressing
myself. Not limiting...
You came back out to the West Coast about that time?
Yeah, I was still there. I was living on the West Coast. I only went to Indianapolis and worked about a month with Bud.
Only a month.
Yeah, it lasted about a month.
How did you meet Bill Cosby; wasn't it about that time?

Bill Cosby I met, I actually met him during the time I was working with Wes, and he was...this is the early Bill Cosby and he was working in San Francisco. The first time I heard about Bill Cosby, it was from the drummer, Benny Barth's wife. She had heard this guy; he was working down at the club called the Hungry Eye in San Francisco.

And I was in San Francisco, and we began to hear "Bill Cosby..." and he was really breaking it up. And I had gone to the Hungry Eey to hear him, because people were remembering his jokes, and they were telling his one-liners about kids and things. And I went to see this guy, and I couldn't get in. It was packed, all up the stairway; I couldn't even get down the stairway. And I went away, and I came back again before he had closed, because I knew some of the people downstairs. So I presented I was working there.

Got downstairs, and the guy at the door was saying, naturally...he was telling me they were completely sold out. And I was just kind of talking to him, and told him I wanted to catch Bill Cosby. So he kind of made it possible that I got inside the thing and stand to hear him. He really broke me up. But I'm just saying, the first time I met him was when he was like then, when he came off, I just introduced myself and shook hands. The name registered in him, but we didn't have no conversation. About a while later, we played a concert, with Wes, out by the...in South Los Angeles, what was that, International something, out by the airport.

It was a huge concert-dance like, the holidays, it was. Bill Cosby came in, into the room , and he just stole the crowd. But he came down to see us, he came there to see us, and we were all just absolutely knocked out. And so was he. You ever see that thing happen? He had been familiar with the music, and he's really dedicated to the music.
Well, did you work with him?

Yes, after that I had an opportunity to...I'm trying to think where did the first one come off at. Oh, I remember. At that time, I had formed my own band, my group, and I was doing little things on my own. And Bill Cosby, he was...I'm

not sure whether he was making a movie or doing a show, but he spends a lot of time in Los Angeles, and he had his own place there, his home and everything. He would come out and make engagements because he just dug performing with musicians. I guess I'm safe to say he's a frustrated musician himself. And he's got a piano, bass, vibes, drums and all...
How did you get involved with Red Norvo? That came fairly soon after that...

That was even stranger. I've got such a...My life went into all kinds of directions after that was fulfilling, very fulfilling. And so many things happened because of... Well, some people would say they were freak things happening. I don't like that word 'freak'; I like the word fate.

Because I'm a religious person and I think I was put here for a purpose, I think we all were. So these things weren't freak, they were fate. That you were here for a purpose and you did have a job to do, you do have a responsibility, not only to yourself, it's to other. And sometimes when you move a certain place at a certain time, it's for a certain reason. I think that came about with Red Norvo, without question.

I was still going through changes, many changes, even at that late a date in life. I was going through changes, things keep happening in weird ways, but it was always at a certain place, at a certain time, something came up. And I couldn't figure it out myself, but I'm not supposed to deal with it. I'm supposed to go ahead and...I mean, deal with it with my mind. I'm supposed to deal, get involved with it and deal with it.

I was in San Francisco...and what caused me to arrive in San Francisco is because I had broke the group up. It didn't pan out and all those, everything sort of went sour. But in the meantime, my music didn't. My playing didn't. Personally it didn't. These other things went sour. I didn't have all the recipes to make...to do magic. Things that were happening went kind of sour for me, but my music, to me, personally...I was still satisfied. I liked myself, and what I was doing. I liked myself for the outlook I was having in life. So I had to push on with it, in spite of the...I wasn't going to make readjustment to make that particular thing happen. I had to get with the things that would keep me going forward.

The group broke up and some things just went sour, and I said, 'Well, I've got to keep on doing what I'm doing.' I got a horrible write-up in the newspaper from one of the critics, which I don't care to mention. I thought it was unfair and I think...I don't know why I let something like that affect me, but it really, really affected me. It was very bad, because I felt like...not to just rip up a critic for his opinion, but he could have wrote better if he had spoke to me and see where I

was coming from. There was no way in the world he understood enough to express anything about something I've been living with for twenty years, thirty years. I wasn't able to do it myself, but at least...

Anyhow, I ended up in San Francisco. Little things would tear me up, because I had taken them so serious. But somebody turn around and rip me without even knowing where I was coming from, it really tore me up.

I was in San Francisco. I had taken an instrument up, a clavinnet. Clavinets were new on the scene. But I heard something there that I wanted to be involved with. It was electronic, and I guess I was getting into electronics, but getting into them...not freaking out in them. Because I could see my...the sound I was striving for. I felt like that lent itself to it, to accompany what I was doing. Because I didn't want to play the bass like a bass. That's what made me altogether another kind of animal, and I knew that. But I...
...and that's the premise behind the bass method book that you put out?

Could be. Possibly, yeah, sure it is, behind everything I'm doing now. It's because I didn't want to sound like nobody else, not that anybody do. But the approach I was using for the instrument wasn't traditional. It was foreign to whatever...For example, I had two keyboards: the clavinnet and the RMI...
Rocky Mountain Instrument...

Right, because that was the instrument I heard that had the — closer — of the bigger notes in the left hand, rather than an organ to get the bottom, because I knew if I got away from the bottom with my bass, there was no bottom there. I needed something for bottom to give me a chance to go up on top. But I had the clavinnet to mix into the sound, so my group consisted of RMI, clavinnet, drums and bass. Now, that was an odd instrumentation.
Yeah, in — what? — 1969?

Yeah, the year '69, exactly, it was in '69. And I remember I had a gig at Redd Foxx's. Redd Foxx owned a club on La Cienega Blvd, in Los Angeles, called the Redd Foxx Club. And he was having, he did things with jazz things, and also he brought in comedians and everything like that. It was a nice room. But Bill Cosby came in partnership with Redd, and when Bill Cosby came in...I had worked there with Redd, and when Redd's business kind of went down...But Bill said he wanted me to stay there with the group. But he hooked up a partnership with Redd so he could keep the jazz, he wanted the jazz scene to keep happening because that was kind of like a hangout for Bill, too.
And Bill just loves being in that, and he treats it

right. Brought in all the big names and that, but I stayed in. The point I'm trying to make is, when I performed, I knew the people were trying to adjust their ears and also a visual thing. Because I know that they were sitting and looking at me strange.
It wasn't what they expected.

No, it just wasn't conventional. It wasn't the sound...It wasn't like coming and listening to a piano, bass and drums, or whether it was a trio or what it was, or whatever it was. But we had some good arrangements, I thought.
People weren't as used to an electronic sound then?
Right, especially in a...I was using two keyboards. I wasn't pairing off of nobody, I didn't know anybody using two keyboards like that.
But there wasn't enough work to make it last?

It wasn't so cuh of that, I guess. I hadn't, I didn't have enough going for me, a record or a name or...I was experimenting, that's all I was doing. I was going through a phase that I had to get that on. And I...
Who were the keyboard players?

A guy by the name of Lenny Hartley was playing the RMI, and Arthur Zikins(?) was playing the clavinet. And the drummer was Candy Finch. So musically, we knew where we were going. We had accepted it, and we were seriously...with the arrangements, and had us some good charts. And we knew we were kind of turning the people around because we were stretching with the music. We were playing fusion...
But the people weren't stretching with you...
Yeah, they weren't stretching. They hadn't been exposed to Chick Corea and Herbie Hancock.
It was before all that?
It was before all that.
Well, all right, you started to tell me about getting together with Red Norvo.

OK. That broke up. I broke the group up. We made a trip to Vancouver and a trip to so-and-so, but it petered out. I wasn't able to hold the band together. And I was frustrated behind that because I still hadn't reached my thing, that was...I had taken my clavinet, because clavinet wasn't popular at that time and they had one outlet, to have some repair
work done up in Palo Alto. So I had to take my clavinet up to this guy and have him work on it.

And I drove up to Palo Alto and from there over to San Francisco, because the guy say it was going to take a week, I think it was, to get all the parts back in there and to get it right and blah-blah-blah. And this whole chassis or something had gone out and we had to order this part and we'd have to order this part in...Your clavinets was a weird instrument.

I said, 'Well, OK, during that week I'll just go to San Francisco and hang out.' And I was going through a, sort of like, having domestic problems and I needed to get my head cleared up. And the music was sort of like in a real shambles.

And I guess I was still having some kind of fight within myself to get on course of who I was and what I was doing and where my, the direction of my future and all that was happening. I went to San Francisco and I stayed over in Oakland in a really dump hotel. I just wanted to hibernate. I didn't want to hang out in San Francisco, I just wanted to be up there where nobody's know I was around, or be asking about taking a gig or playing and all that. I was just trying to get my head together. And I went to Oakland.

In the meantime, just before I left Los Angeles, I got a call from Herbie Mann. Herbie said he was coming out in a couple of months or something, on his way to Japan and would I join him to go there and work a gig in Japan. I had never been in Japan -- still haven't -- and I was saying, 'Wow, this is great.' But I told Herbie, I said, 'Herbie, call me back a little later. I can't answer that now because I've got some things pending. And if you haven't found anybody in the next few weeks, call me again closer to the date and I'll know about this thing that's pending.' So I made some kind of excuse, because I couldn't just go over there for a week. But it was nothing pending; I was just trying to get my head together.

But I knew right then that I wasn't ready to just start accepting jobs, even going to Japan, which I always wanted to do. And working with Herbie wasn't a drag, but I just couldn't get my head together.

So when I went to San Francisco, to the Bay Area, I didn't want anybody to know I was there because I didn't want to do anything. Had to get my head together, I knew that. I put my instrument in the shop. So I was dealing with a musical problem and a family problem: musical insofar as what I was going to do in the future.
I got a call, because my folks knew where I was at. They said, 'You got a very, very serious call from Red Norvo, and he said it was very urgent.' And I said, 'We don't really
know each other; how could anything be...what's so serious about Red?'

I just met Red in passing; I didn't know Red. I never had the opportunity to sit in and play with him, or hung out with him, or anything. But it's serious. So then I said, 'Well, I'm not going to call him. If he calls me, if he calls and says it's really serious and he's got to reach me, if it's serious enough let him call me.' So maybe that will end it right there. So I wasn't going to pursue it, plus I was in a bad state of mind.

Red called me the next day. He said, 'Yeah, I got your number from your wife and she said you weren't doing anything.' I said, 'No, I'm not working.' I felt like I was doing something, but I wasn't working, I was cooling out.

He said, 'Well, I've got a job, a three-week engagement in Las Vegas.' When he said, 'Las Vegas,' I said, 'What's that got to do with me, man? What's so serious about a three-week job in Las Vegas?' I couldn't imagine Las Vegas; the word Las Vegas just made me angry. I mean literally angry, because...
It was the symbol of things you weren't interested in?

...the symbol of things that were just wrong. Prejudices and...all...I just couldn't...it was just a plastic bubble that had nothing to do with me, nothing that I was trying to think out. To hook me up with Las Vegas was just the wrong thing he could talk about. Forget the money. Money had nothing to do with it. I wasn't thinking money.

He said...Red's a nice man, easy spoken. And he could see that I wasn't happy, I wasn't excited about him calling me. So he proceeded to tell me that this was a good job. The guy that called him was entertainment director of the Tropicana, a friend of his from Los Angeles. He used to own the Peacock, Peacock Lane, I think it was, in North Hollywood, up on Hollywood Blvd. And I remember I had worked at the Peacock Lane myself, I remembered Maynard Sloat.(?)

And Red said, 'Well, he's the entertainment director of the Tropicana now and he wants to put jazz in the lounge. And this is the first time,' and Red said, 'It would be something great for us if we could maybe get some jazz started in Las Vegas.'
The first time there had been any jazz in Las Vegas?

Right...Well, the Tropicana, I guess it was the Tropicana, and it wasn't the first time (in Las Vegas). And I said, 'Red, I just...It isn't any reflection against you, believe me. But the time you called me now, and Las Vegas...' He said,

'Well, Monk the money's good and the job is a good one, the conditions are...' And I said, 'I don't want to go to Las Vegas, it's as simple as that.' I had no intentions of going to Las Vegas and I was wondering why he had called me, with all those musicians in Los Angeles. All the bass players down there was out of work, but still...

He said, 'Well, I wish you would consider it.' And I said, 'Red,' now this was the capper, 'the only reason I would consider going is that if you were stuck.' If that other musician is stuck, I'll go with him. I'll go and help a guy out, that's what I meant. I would help somebody out, no matter what the situation. I can't just turn him away. Knowing what I said wouldn't hold the light, because he wasn't stuck, with all those musicians in Los Angeles, how could he be stuck for a bass player? If he was on an island somewhere, stuck without anything...

Red called me the next day. He said, 'Well, you gave me your word, if I was stuck you'd make it.' He said, 'I'm stuck.' I said, 'Red, that's a dirty trick,' and just somehow we started laughing. We really started laughing, and it felt good, just laughing like that.
So he pried you out of your...

I guess you could say pried, yeah, he pried me. And I said, 'OK. When does the gig start?' I think the job started on a Thursday, something like that, and we had a day or so to get there. And I said that I had my car here with me. I had just picked up my instrument, my clarinet, and that's what the trip took me up there. I had just picked it up and had set it up in that little room, where I was working and playing.

'Well, I got my car. I'll just drive down and meet you in Las Vegas.' He said, 'OK, and we're staying at the Tropicana Motel, across the street, there are rooms there for us. And all you have to do is... I'll see you there. I'll be there on Tuesday,' or Wednesday or whatever it was. And I said, 'Well, what about our rehearsals?' And he said, 'I don't think we need no rehearsals; this is a jazz gig and we can do it without...'
Who was the third person?

He had a kid playing guitar, and I can't think of his name because he only lasted about two or three days, that weekend, whatever, because he was so far out on pills and things... And then Red brought in Lloyd Ellis, he was a guitar player. After just a few days, Lloyd Ellis came in.

And when I met him in Las Vegas, it was almost like meeting a total stranger, meeting Red in terms of here we are and looking over the gig. I always respected him; I had so much respect for Red as a musician. That's the only way I knew of him, his music. And I was happy to be associated with him, and
he gave me the same feeling.

But the first theory jumped in my mind, and it didn't in until after I got there, was 'I'll bet Red thinks I'm playing the upright bass.' I'll bet he thinks...he may not know about the period that I put the upright bass down and went back to the electric bass.' Because how could you have electric bass, vibes and electric guitar? The kind of bottom he was looking for, to make it an acoustical bottom you need, I would...My thing was, you needed an acoustical bottom with that kind of relationship. I played a lot of times, my playing with Buddy with electric bass, but we had drums and all those things.
It's just with that instrumentation, I'm saying, 'God, I should have spoke to Red before I left San Francisco, to let him know...'
What actually did he feel?
He knew I was playing electric bass; it's what he wanted.
And you stayed for two years, didn't you?

The three weeks went into two years. It was a little less than two years, about a year and a half, or nine months, something like that. But it was so strange because when I...it didn't dawn on me what we were doing instrumentation-wise. In fact, I wasn't sure he was...I thought he was going to use a quartet, and have drums. There was no drums. And I said, 'Oh, my God...'

And I told him, 'Hey, did you realize that I'm playing the electric bass?' And he said, 'Yeah, that's what I want.' That relieved me. But what happened when...it was so beautiful vibes. Like I'm saying, these things that can happen in a person's life...And I'd like to take just a minute here and say...maybe I can say something that might be encouraging as to a person accepting what is.

Because some of the things that happen spontaneous, you don't have time to think it out, you can make a very bad choice. You can try and rationalize a thing out, and it's completely out of proportion.

Red said to me, we had a quiet moment of talking after we had kind of settled into the gig, to explain to me what happened, of us coming together. He said, when they called him about that gig, he had gone back to Santa Monica and wasn't going to...just take off a while. He'll do that, you know. It was just he and his wife; his kids were grown and he was doing OK. So he had intended just to take off and don't think about no group. Because Red could just go out and put a group

together and go to work. They called him for this thing with Maynard, called him to do the thing at the Tropicana. And his feelings were kind of similar to mine, that he didn't want to go to Las Vegas. He didn't want to work right then, he was off.

And Maynard talked him into it. So he said to his wife, 'Now, who am I going to get on bass, what bass player am I going to get?' And his wife said to him, 'Well, just get yourself some players and go up and make the job.' So he didn't know who to call. He was kind of...in his mind he didn't have a bass player to call. So he went to the union book and opened the union book, and when he just opened the union book to the bass players and looked, he said my name was right there.

He said he called his wife and said to her, 'Looka here. Why would Monk Montgomery's name come up? I don't know that man.' She said, 'Don't question it. Call him, just call him.' And when he called me, he even said it was urgent. And he talked to me as if he had to have me, and he followed through on that when he called me.
When you stayed here on that job for two years, did you decide that you really like it here; is that why you stayed? How come you stayed?

I decided the whole history of this thing was set up in a sort of way that, once again, I call it fate. The end of that engagement, when I...I guess my feelings about Las Vegas changed in the course of that short period of time that I was here. Because musically it was great, man, it was great.

Playing with Red...Red played just what we wanted to play. He didn't ask for requests; unless somebody hit it right on the head. I never played as much in my life, and I played consistently, for Red. We worked six nights a week. A year-and-a-half-- , never had that. It was a new experience for me. (end of Cassette Master III-A)

...It wasn't great, but I was at the peak of my potential and I knew it. That makes you feel great inside, you know, that's what it's about. It was happening for me. Not only that, but people were just great to me at the hotel where we worked. They treated me like I was...
But jazz in Las Vegas was a rarity then, and it's still a rarity.
Yeah, but what happened to me, I wasn't...My thoughts wasn't didn't hover over Las Vegas. It was just there at the Tropicana.
You didn't consider yourself a Las Vegas resident, really?

Oh, no, not really. And I wasn't really pioneering or anything else. I was pioneering into my music, my playing was number one to me now. My instrument, my playing. And I'm thinking now, 'Wow, look, I'm doing all these thing...' I was beginning to get released inside.

The shackles began to fall off me about my domestic problems and my other kind of problems, because I was working out arrangements so I was going to get with my group later on, and I was playing consistently and making a good income. The pay was good, the people that came, the customers, the place was almost packed every night. People were cheering for you, making you feel good, all the good things were happening that come out of music, you see. Plus that I was developing more and more on my instrument the way I wanted to go. The way I wanted to go. It was just like, we had a thing going, the guitar player and I...
At some point, you made a mental change that made you a Las Vegas resident.

Yeah, that's what I'm saying. All these good things were happening. Las Vegas wasn't a bad image to me. But I didn't extend myself over...I wasn't concerned really as to who was working at the Sahara, who was coming in here and who was coming in there. It was all happening in that room with the jazz, but it made it feel like jazz wasn't a foreign thing in Las Vegas. I thought it was ready for it. And I felt the audience proved it.
But I wasn't on no trip about future jazz in Las Vegas.
When did that happen?
That wasn't no trip about that at all. After the year and a half had passed, and I'd got into feeling home here, really feeling that...I was hanging out with guys and everything like that...
So you decided to stay?

I began to dig the climate, and everything was kind of right for me. Plus that I had saved some money, I bought me some property, and I was...Hey, it was a new life for me. That's what it was really like, a new life. I'm playing every night, what I want to play, and dug the people I was playing with.

And -- snap! -- the job ended like that. The thing happened that they sold the hotel and brought in new owners, so the policies change. New entertainment director, new policy. You get your notice, you know. And I said, 'Wow, this thing is coming to an end too abrupt.' Because Maynard, the entertainment director, had always said, 'As long as I'm here, you got a job.'
But then he wasn't there any more.

But he forgot to mention, to bear in mind...So things were going great, we thought Maynard would be there forever so automatically we'd be there forever. Why would the guy want to sell the hotel? We never thought about that. It was just ridiculous.
But when that ended, then it began to dawn on me, well, it was time for a change. But when you've been on something like that for a year and a half, you get locked into it. Really locked into it.

And I wasn't hurting so far as money or gig was concerned. But now I'm thinking about, I didn't prepare myself for that, as to what my next move would be. But it would be simple. I like it here, it was OK here. Maybe it would be even time for me to move on and get my little thing in another lounge. I'd get me a little job in a lounge and continue playing and keep my thing up. It wasn't like that. All at once it was like, the Red Norvo Trio ended...jazz ended.
Las Vegas was never really very much of a jazz town and that was the exception...
Right, that was really like the exception, at that degree.
Aside from the major acts in the major hotels, there weren't very many black performers there either, were there?

That's true too, very true. You see, that undercurrent is still there. It was there even more, a little stronger then than it is now, but it's still there now to a certain extent. I didn't expect to change that, especially, or anybody else, overnight. I didn't expect no changes there.

But ironically enough, at the Tropicana we worked in the lounge, and the kind of crowd that was coming in, the interest that built up, meant that Maynard Sloat was bringing in things into the Blue Room, which was a room inside of the Tropicana too, the Blue Room. He brought in Count Basie, and he brought in Sarah Vaughan and Joe Williams. Then he brought in some of the Dixieland things, like Pete Fountain and Al Hirt, and there was Anita O'Day. And he brought in a few things into the Blue Room.

We thought it was successful. Louis Armstrong. We thought it was successful but obviously it didn't make it financially because it...those things in the big lounge. But at least there was some involvement with it. And I think it was...if someone in that...if a guy just got ahold of it and
stuck with it and made it happen, it would be no problem.
Is that where the germ of the Las Vegas Jazz Society was born?

Somewhat, because what happened after that, I felt like...I was having a problem getting a job. Not just a job. I could have...and I've had some people talk to me strictly private, even a union official: 'Monk, you know you're really liked here. It will be no problem that you can get a job in one of these showrooms.' And I said, 'Man, that ain't playing. It's not playing. Sorry, but I haven't retired. I want to play.' I want to express myself. That's what playing was for me.
It sounds like...Several good players have gotten stuck in places like that, like Carl Fontana, James Moody, for a number of years.

Right. And I just didn't have any reason to do that. I don't have any babies or anything, that kind of responsibility. Like guys that have got their wife and kids and they got to do this, and they got to work at the post office and got to do these things. I didn't have them kind of commitments, that I had to go do that for them.

So you know I wasn't going to do that for myself or for the dollar. And I just couldn't bring myself to do that. In fact, I wasn't qualified to do that. I wasn't going to go through...I could go and get me a teacher and do what was required in there (reading); and they were trying to convince me to do that. At one point they were saying...I guess there was five or six different hotels that was available that I could have gone into and picked my job. And one of the reasons was because, then I think they needed...That would have been an easy thing to do because there wasn't any black faces there in the first place.
You mean you think it was a conscious effort...
A token.
...to get more...
It was a token thing, you know, I could have been half as good as I am and got it, because, you know...
They wanted black players, to look good...
I think that would have been one of the things. I could have got any room in town.
And you think that's why they, why James Moody worked there?
It had some...Sure.
That's a funny way to choose musicians.
Sure. But you know it's just that James Moody was a name thing, too. 'We got James Moody.'
Are the hotels aware of that, when they hire some-body of that caliber? Are they really aware of the musical value?

The hotel don't hire them. They are hired through whoever the conductor is, or the contractor. The contractor do that. The hotel don't feel nothing one way or the other, you see. But the thing that I'm saying is that, it is a little pathetic and it always has been, and it still is. But I don't need to tamper, to deal with that because it has to change in its own time and its own way.

I'm too concerned about something over here that I can do something about, that I can relate to, that I can relate to. I don't intend to go up and fight my battles with the show rooms, to get black faces in the show rooms, when the whole thing don't mean anything to me.

It's not this show business plastic bubble thing, that's not where my thing is at. My thing is like, I'm kind of dedicated to where I'm at, because that's my life and that's my love, is for the jazz music. And it should be exposed in any and every level and any door that can welcome it and there's an audience to welcome it.
You've always pretty much felt that way, but now, in recent years, you've begun to funnel that, your energies and your direction into that commitment, into music.

Sure. I hope it will stand even beyond that, now. But, like I said, at that particular time and even up till now, that was my prime concern. But I expect that to expand. I wouldn't want to spend all my time and energies just trying to get a little lounge group or getting a club going. We don't have any nightclubs here either, but I don't think that's the place to make it happen.

No, what I'm saying is that a few years back you began looking at it with a broader direction, forming the jazz society and then forming...I'd like you to talk a little bit about the jazz society and the federation (Las Vegas Jazz Society and Western Regional Federation for Jazz).
OK. We can go back and get into the jazz society and that. I got such...
Because that's such a different direction.
Yeah, it is, it was. But it's one of the other things that I say it's funny how some other things that happen to me that had to do with fate. There was a reason for it, I guess.

After things stopped, ended with Red, I wanted to continue living here. I really wanted to continue living here. But I had to have a livelihood, like anybody else. And my thing was, I simply wanted to make my living playing jazz. And that's all I wanted to do, was make a living. I didn't want any more out of it. And I'm sure I spoke for a lot of other people; I didn't stand alone in that field, right?

But then I felt like, now wait a minute! You just proved a thing on that corner, at the Tropicana. What's the big deal? But if it wasn't available for me, it wasn't available for all those others. And I know I only speak just for myself then, but I say...now wait a minute, this is... Well, all I need to do now is find somebody with an open mind and maybe we can make a point here. I wasn't going to say I was going to break the town down but just make it available, somewhere.

It didn't happen. They treated me like I had a tail. I just couldn't make sense to anybody. I made sense to myself, but that's what turned it around. Then I got involved, it sort of like overlapped into not just being a musician and performing, striking the notes. I had to put my energies into hustling up a place that would -- you know what I'm saying -- and that's a whole different thing right there.

Because I wasn't a promoter, and that wasn't what I wanted to come off as necessarily. But somebody had to hear what I was trying to say because there's a need for it. It should be, it's only right, it's only fair, or what are we talking about...the entertainment capital of the world?
And there's no jazz.

...and not a door open for jazz? You got to be kidding. You gotta be kidding. People from all over the world come here, and jazz is all the way around the world, they can wave to, so you insult their intelligence. Not...You don't have to do it for me, because I was turning down jobs with the people calling me other places. But why should I have to leave Las Vegas to get a job playing? I just couldn't bring myself to settle for...

That was frustrating for me, very frustrating. Because I didn't want to leave Las Vegas to get a job, to play, when it had proved successful. So. I began to get involved, and it got heavier and heavier. Without me even realizing, I began to get bitter and angry, really angry about it. I mean really angry until I wasn't even liking myself.

But I couldn't stop, I couldn't give up on it. I really couldn't give up on it. I left town a couple times, went to Los Angeles because I wasn't getting any playing, I wasn't able to play. I couldn't get it out or any kind of way. , and I went down...I took a job in Los Angeles. And while I was there I got a call with Sarah Vaughan. I played with Sarah about a month. It only lasted that long, and I couldn't understand why Sarah would call me, because I know electric bass with Sarah Vaughan just didn't go together.

And I wasn't going to give up the electric bass for the upright, for Sarah or nobody else. I knew what I wanted to do, but because of her husband at that time...We were very tight, and a family thing there and...I guess they just kind of experimented with it. Which is OK with me, because I love Sarah, and musically too. But that period didn't last long.

And of all things, I was in Los Angeles just catching jobs and, whatever it was, and I couldn't get my mind off of, you know, that. I couldn't put my whole mind on seriously anything but coming back to Las Vegas. And here I was, in that short period of time, how do I get back there and do what I want to do? And that was most important in my mind, some way.

I got a call from a local musician to come up and work with The Drifters. And I said, 'This guy has got to be kidding.' And he said, 'Well, Monk, it's for a whole month at the Sahara, in the lounge.' He said, now, he's talking and he's working gigs with them, and he'd worked with them when they came in, and this time he told Ralph when they came in, they needed a bass player, because they usually just pick up somebody, and maybe an organ player.

And when Ralph mentioned that he was going to try to get me, they were familiar with me and they wanted to say, 'Hey, well, try to get him. Try to get Monk.' They didn't know me, but they was familiar. And I know of them, I was familiar but I didn't know them.

But we wasn't nothing in common musically. But I needed a job that bad, plus that I wanted to come back to Las Vegas. I really wanted to come back to Las Vegas. I wasn't through with it. Plus that I had a couple of pieces of property here and I was leasing both houses out. I came up, and worked the job with The Drifters, and it was one of the worst musical experiences I've ever had. No reflection to the Drifters, because they're doing what they do...
It wasn't what you wanted to play.

Yeah, and you know, they'd go through the whole thing of showmanship and stepping and want the guys to do the steps with them and "la-la-la-la" with them, you know. Certain things, and you'd answer back and all that. It wasn't...I was embarrassed, hoping somebody wasn't in there that knew me. But
I came back, I needed the money. And I hate having to prostitute, with a passion, but it got me back in Las Vegas.

I was here, and into it again. Really into it. By this time, now, I'm carrying around a little briefcase, trying to talk to this guy, trying to talk to that entertainment director. Can't see this one, trying to talk to somebody that knew that one...
So you were assaulting the hotels?

Right. I spoke to one guy, and I felt like I had really made a breakthrough. It was at the Hilton. And he had the reputation of being one of the most liberal-minded of them all. It was Dave...David...oh, God, I forgot that man's name... I think I'll mention it in a minute. And he was the entertainment director for the Hilton. And he had been over to the Caesar's for a lot of years, and at one time he had brought in Jimmy Smith. He tried it with...he had Duke Ellington and he had, he brought in Sarah Vaughan. He said he tried it at Caesar's and it never really worked out for him when he brought some of the jazz people up.

And I called him to make an appointment with him, and he said, 'Well, come on in.' And that shocked me, because he was ready, here, he invited me in. I didn't think it would happen at a major hotel, that major hotel, the Hilton. But it was because of the man, you see, the entertainment director.

And I met with him that day and when I...By that time, when I got to him -- and he was a nice man -- and we started talking. I exploded. I was unloading, because I had somebody listening, and I didn't have good tactics. He said, 'Wait, wait a minute, Monk. Don't...Wait, don't get excited.'
You overwhelmed him.

Yeah. He said, 'Don't get excited. You don't have to sell me.' He said, 'I see it in your face. I know about your track record. I'm in agreement with you, but that's not the way it's done.
