It's not the way it's done.' He said, 'Now, what I'd suggest is this. I will give you an attempt, and try and work with you. I can't go to the hotel and convince them that you have this room to bring jazz into, and so-and-so, but I've got a young man that I work with on certain things. We'll have you to four-wall the place, I want you to four-wall it. You can bring in what you want to bring.'

But what did I know? All I knew was like I was a bull in a china closet. Garrett Asif (?), who is a big promoter now in rock and all that sort of thing, that was the one I was going to talk to, to get it on. So I went and met with Garrett Asif. Garry wasn't into jazz but he was into promoting, and making money. And lo and behold, the old man died, heart attack. He

passed away.

That was my first hope and it looked like everything went down with him because he was a nice man, to receive me the way he did. And he understood what I was trying to say. He had a capacity for the music.

And it looked like it was hitting the bottom for me again. I went out again, and I made a couple of breakthroughs, through the entertainment directors, at least to talk to them, a couple of them. But one that really was like the straw that broke the camel's back, I should say...At the M-G-M they were like new, they had just opened, sort of. And the first, at the grand opening, I was fortunate enough to work in the lounge with Mavis Rivers. Mavis Rivers was one of the opening acts in the lounge and she was there three or four weeks. And I was there with her and I had a chance to meet the entertainment director, Bill DeAngeles, at the time.

And after the engagement and everything, I made my way back to Bill DeAngeles and started talking to him about it. Because I felt the M-G-M was the ideal place. Here's a hotel, brand new, coming in with new policies, new concepts. They had jai alai, a whole new concept of gambling, that game, jai alai from Mexico. They had downstairs a theater where nostalgia movies were shown, through the old M-G-M archives, and all of that. And I was saying, 'That's the spot, because I know they're open minded about the subject. Not that jazz is new, but it's a concept that somebody should take advantage of.

And I was talking to Bill DeAngeles because I saw what I visualized was the theater downstairs. Nostalgia. Like the old days, we would see a movie and there was a stage performance. There's be a live...a stage thing. When I used to work with Lionel Hampton, when we traveled, we'd work the Fox Theater...Work the old -- what's the name? -- the Regal Theater. We worked the Apollo Theater, and that's what it was.
The Earle and the Howard...

The Earle and, yeah, all those, we worked those, the Howard Theater in Washington. And when we worked in them, it was like, you run the movie and then you'd run the...The band would come out and play, dancers would be on, and so-and-so. Then run the movie and so-and-so. So I thought that was a great piece for nostalgia.

The room seated about 250-200, whatever. Why didn't they do that down there, against the movies, you know? On a consistent basis. And once a month, we would take the big room upstairs, the show room, and do a spectacular, bring in a concert on Sunday afternoon.
How did they feel about it?

Bill DeAngeles thought it was a great concept, and 'I think so-and-so.' And I sat in his office and talked with him. He said, 'The one thing you have to do is put this on paper. You have to bring me a proposal, so I can submit it to the board. I can't go over there and say, well, Monk's got a great idea, he thinks so-and-so. You got to give me a break-down of the cost and samples of who the artists---- and all this sort of thing.

See, I wasn't into that, but I could see what he was saying and I said, 'Hey, wait, I'll do it.' Because I felt like this was a winner. I came home and it must have taken me, even though I had it all in my head, I put in on paper, to write all of it out and get it down, and get it... I had this friend of mine type it up and put it in a nice beautiful folder. And ready to send it back that I got it all out of my head and on paper. And I went through it over and over, tore up pages and scratching out and... I had a project!

The strange thing is, that weekend I was supposed to submit this back to him, I think I had it ready for him the first of the week. That week, I had to go to Los Angeles, and I was in Los Angeles and I had called Bill Cosby. I gave him a buzz. He said, 'Well, what are you doing in town?' and so-and-so.

I said, 'I just came down for the weekend just to be with my boys.' He said, 'Well, I'm doing a thing at the Lighthouse Sunday night. Why don't you come out and play with me?' And I said, 'Well, I didn't come down here to play. I haven't got my bass or anything.' He said, 'Well, you can get a bass, and come on out. Just come on out and play.' He said, 'Don't worry about it. I'll take care of you, ere you hang up.' Well, we always do that.

So I want to go too. And it was great, to go out to the Lighthouse and a chance to hang out and be with that clown, too, which was a lot of fun. I got a bass and went out. Because it was a gig for me, he always paid. He paid so good you couldn't... He made you an offer you couldn't refuse, when you played with him.

So I went out and made this gig and it was a great... And I was saying, 'You know, Bill, I got something I want you to see.' Because all along, even until today, when something happens for me that I think makes me bubble inside, I find myself talking it over with Bill. He is one of the greatest devil's advocates you can find. And it don't take him a long time to sit and think it out. And I always respect his opinions.
He would go through the challenges with you and...

He would go through it with you and, like, you always feel, if this guy don't find it, can't find the holes in it, there's no holes in it. Because he leans that way with his ideas and thoughts anyhow. And he's a bright man, a very bright man. A funny man, but he's a very bright man.

And I was saying to him, 'You know, I just finished this thing I have;' I finished it out, copied it out and I was so proud of it, I was carrying it around with me. I had it in my little briefcase. And I had gone to Los Angeles and I took it down there with me. Not just for Bill, but just I had it, because I had...You know how you have some special people you like to say, 'Hey, just take a look at this and see what you think.'

And I needed that. I said, 'Bill, perfect, I'm glad I got this thing. Bill, I want you to see this thing.' He said, 'What have you got now, man; what are you into now, what are you doing now?' Because he knew I was banging on the doors and banging on the doors. And he said, 'OK.'

That night after we had played a couple of sets, he came over to me and he said, 'Listen, you guys play the last set. I've had it and I'm going on in because I've got an early rise tomorrow.' See, he played this place for kicks; it wasn't like working a job. The man didn't pay him, he just do that for kicks, to express his thing.

You know, music I mean. Not standing there and telling jokes. Just playing. He gets up there and plays the drums, and he plays vibes and he plays whatever. And he said, 'I had it, I'm going on in. But have Mr. Harris' (that was his number one man) 'call Mr. Harris in the morning, and I'll have Mr. Harris...' No. Mr. Harris was there. He said, 'Have Mr. Harris to pick you up in the morning and bring you out to the set' where they were filming this movie, 'and bring him with you and he can take you straight to the airport.'

Flights were every hour on the hour, and every hour you can get a flight out. Well, I didn't know the exact time he'd be back but I wanted Bill to see this. So he said, 'Have Mr. Harris bring you out,' so I spoke to Mr. Harris and Mr. Harris said, 'I'll pick you up at ten o'clock.' I was staying with Harold then. 'I'll pick you up and take you out to the set, after Bill, you know. Have lunch and see that, and take you to the airport.'

It was perfect. Mr. Harris came right downtown and picked me up at ten o'clock. They were filming this movie, what's the movie that...Harry Belafonte and...Well, anyhow, they were filming on a set way out in the Valley and he drove me on to the scene.
And on the lunch break, the caterer -- they bring the food in in a big truck. The food, the canteens come in and then they all sit on these picnic benches for lunch -- and it
was kind of like a thrill for me to be there on that set, with Sidney Poitier, Harry Belafonte and-all the names.

So at lunch break, you get your lunch and you come back to the picnic table. And he came back to the picnic table with me, and we just had a little soft drink and a roll, and he just sit there and put his foot on the stool and was looking at --reading through it. And he said, 'Did you do this?' I said, 'Yeah.' He said, 'You did it by yourself?' I say, 'Yeah, I thought the whole thing out.' He say, 'I like this one,' and I was pleased.

If he liked it, I can't on wrong, I'm thinking. He said, 'I like it.' He said, 'As a matter of fact, you tell the guy when you go back, if he will accept this project as is, with a spectacular on a Sunday, that you doing it on a Sunday, you're doing it every night down in the theater,' -- and once a month, I had it once a month, every first Sunday of the month we would do a spectacular in the show room and bring in a big concert with Duke Ellington...I had a sample of thing down.

The first one I had was Duke Ellington, Roberta Flack -- she was hot then, she had made this big hit -- Cal Tjader. The second was Quincy Jones, and so-and-so, and so-and-so. Three acts, three names, to

And with the all time good, Just about each one had a big band, then a small combo, and then a singer. They all ran out that way, with combos and singers: Sarah, Carmen. Bill said, 'He'll love that spectacular. You tell him I said if he accepts that as it is, I will speak to my man at NBC and discuss NBC taping it for network TV,' he said. And he would be the master of ceremonies for the spectacular once a month. Because he thought that was fabulous.
So you brought that back?
Oh, I couldn't...I didn't hardly need a plane to get back to Las Vegas. I could have flown back myself.
But how did the Hilton...
I brought it back...No, that was for the M-G-M.
M-G-M.

I took it to the entertainment director, I gave it to him, and I told him what Bill said. He said, 'Oh, wow, are you sure?' I said, 'Yeah,' and (airplane noise ). Knowing Bill that's all---I didn't have to bring no note. Just be sure and tell your people that.' So I have him the thing and he said OK, he'd call me back in a couple of days.
I was so excited. And in a couple of days I called him back. 'I haven't had time to have an answer yet; I'm waiting on an answer.' So I said OK, and I'm really nervous

now. I finally pinned him, and a few days had passed and I'm getting a little shaky, because what's the...what are we talking about here? And he says to me, 'Well, I spoke to Mr. Bernie Rothcall (? Rofcaw?). He said he wasn't interested and didn't want to talk about it. Those were his words.'
Who was he?
Yeah, he was the kingpin, right? Now, I couldn't handle that.

That's a major disappointment. More major than all of them because when the guy said, 'I'm not interested' and didn't even want to talk about it, not even the courtesy of saying that...like, if he can put it another way, even. But after the work I went through, after he's saying that's what they should do...
Why do you think he turned it down?

It's just the same typical thing that's the answer to a whole lot of other things what happen there. Why don't we have jazz? I don't have any answer for that. It just didn't make sense to me any way I looked at it. The answer... to give that kind of answer. Anyhow...
Well, that was kind of a disappointment, but you really regrouped and moved on to other things.
Yeah...
When did you think about the jazz society?

Well, the jazz society came because, that was like, forced you to go somewhere. You either had to give it up or go into something else. I wasn't near about to give it up. It just made me an angry man and I had to pick up arms toward that. I had to fight the system, if that's what it was. There was no question in my mind that that's what it was.

Now, I knew I had posed a threat to someone, when I was just trying to give something. That's a shame, but I had to stand for something and I knew I had to stand for that. And it all came down like this is what I had to do. Then I began to knock on other doors; I made a big issue out of that, and there was a big scene about that.
A public scene, you mean?
No, not a public scene. But I got threats on my phone.
You did?
Yes sir. And threats to the point that...
What kind of threats?

Because I had taken that, what he said to me, and mentioned it to the trade magazines. Billboard printed it as I said it. And I told them, repeated what they had said to me, and they put it in the trades. So naturally, that trade went around the world.

They don't need that kind of...And that's what brought the whole thing about. Because then the threats came on the phone, a couple of threats, and they were saying, 'Don't repeat any names in any more of your articles.' And another call came back making it final, 'No more names.'

In other words, they couldn't tell me not to make any more articles, but don't report any kind of things, don't repeat the names. They didn't want any more names mentioned in my articles. I didn't, at the time, it wasn't because I was trying to cut that particular person down. I was trying to cut down the attitude of the whole town. So I had no objection to that. In fact, I was...I totally agree with that.
My intention wasn't directed at that man, it was directed at the whole system. But the man said it, the system didn't say it.

Now, I'm out there, I knew I had to fight the system. And I'm going on and I made some attempts. I tried another thing and it almost worked, at a downtown hotel where I didn't want to go at all, because what I was trying to get involved with belonged on the Strip. And I kept getting defeated there.
Anyhow, I came to the thing and I knew that one person ...I could not make a dent in anything alone. And I knew I couldn't do it one...single-handedly. That's why I formed the jazz society.
That was in seventy...
...five. '75 I formed the jazz society. And at that time I didn't realize the impact of what the jazz society was going to be. I just knew I had to get...I couldn't do it single-handedly.
How many people are there now involved? I know it's grown enormously.

Yeah, it's grown enormously. We have...we use the figure of 500 as membership, and it's hard to arrive at an exact number because we have different types of membership. On, say, a family membership, you don't know how many is in a family. And it keeps you from arriving at an exact number. We have individual, family and student. But in the neighborhood of 500, so far as how much support we have, it goes way beyond that in terms
of supporters.
You have a pretty strong constituency in Las Vegas...

Oh sure, because we also have...We feel like the associators, that are associated with the jazz society not as membership per se, but we feel we have the press, we have the radio, television, newspapers, which cover so greatly...
An involvement which you couldn't get as an individual...

Right. You can't count that in memberships, but they'll keep you in the eye of the public, to get the support back in return. We feel like we're so strongly supported in the community that it's hard to arrive at any numbers...
The political credibility that you've gained, with things like the state-wide Jazz Month...
All those things came about in good time...
...has given you a lot of strength to use in other areas.

An aful lot. In fact, we are developing to a sort of leadership on a regional level through the efforts of the jazz society. And at early stages of the jazz society, I think the curiosity of it happening sort of attracted a lot of attention.

And the way it came about, like I say, in founding the jazz society I just got on the phone and called...I had a list of about 30 some-odd people and thinking that I knew they could appreciate some jazz action of some sort in town, and asked them to meet at my house. The turnout wasn't near as great as I hoped. They just didn't show up -- it was Sunday afternoon.

I didn't let that discourage me because I asked each one of them to call three people and we would try again the following Sunday. Because some of the people that showed up were the people that would be interested.

The next, following Sunday we had a much better turnout, so we knew what we had. And it turned out to be a little fun thing, discussing it. But it began to dawn on me now, this thing, what we were shaping. That afternoon we come up with the name, which was very simple, there wasn't no big thing about that. And we discussed it thoroughly, to the point that we had to have a board and officers and so-and-so. And I suggested that what we would do was, as many as was there that day was to join, we hadn't arrived at what the membership fee was, but we pulled it together that day. Put the membership at
$15, and $25 a family. And really, that was decided right then and there on the spot for membership. Because we said, 'Let's do something, let's move on it today, just put it in some kind of...'

You have -- I say you, I realize it's a group effort, but everybody knows that you're at the center of it and the core of it -- the society in five years has really been instrumental in bringing some jazz to Las Vegas.
Yeah, this...
...And now you're reaching out to bigger things. Tell me about your federation idea.

Well, the federation (Western Regional Federation for Jazz) grew out of the necessity of a brotherhood, and my particular feeling, my personal feeling. Because I felt like it would go without question that Las Vegas had suffered, badly badly suffered, because of the lack of jazz being available. And I knew the same thing goes for so many other Western major cities. Even the major cities, there's a shortage, so the lesser cities was suffering even more.
Suffering to the degree that it was, had to have been sooner, what we were going through here on another scale, it wasn't available and what else could you make out of that?

That's bad, that's poor, for not being available. And the jazz society, the things that we had experienced and the growth, the life, the years that we had spent on the jazz society, were perfect examples of things that were classics in terms of being a pilot program that would work somewhere else. If it worked here, it would work over there. This was a perfect place to be...if it worked here, it could work anywhere.

So my thinking was, if we'd ever unite, if many unite, it could uncover much more than some of those people, some of those areas could imagine. You take a small area that wasn't doing near as much as...because they felt like a lack of...whatever reasons, the shortage of whatever wasn't there. How encouraging that would be if we had a united effort, where the larger places could help the smaller places.

But even the smaller places would then uncover the resources we have available, they didn't know was there. And I think some of that's been already so true in even this early a stage, because there has been a federation developed and...
Just this year.
Just this year, and in the very early stages now of being legally registered and...
How many states are involved now?

At first there was twelve states involved. And in processing after the original conference in February, we appointed a steering committee, who was appointed to set it up, and in the process of that we come to the...are now of the opinion or agreement, that the boundary lines should have been extended. We use the word 'West' for Western...
So anything West of the Mississippi...
...West of the Mississippi should be welcome within this federation. So now we're talking about 24 states.
And Alaska and Hawaii...Your concept is that these states banded together would have a lot more political influence?
Oh, most certainly. In every aspect of whatever we can say that's good for a small community can be put into a larger hopper and filtered down, a more...sharing...
Helping smaller communities get expert advice?

Right. It would all be there. We'd have all the technical assistance into one headquarters that would be able to service the whole community, rather than the community of Las Vegas or the community of Los Angeles. It would be the community of the West.
In the process of all this, Monk, in the last five years, you've become less and less of a player and more and more of an active politician.

I find that very interesting, because people don't have a tendency to look at me any more as a jazz musician. They don't look at me as a bass player. And that sort of offends me, in a sense, because I think I am still. And I'm sure that I'm going to go back and pick up my instrument because that is my first love.
But you really have not been playing.

No, I haven't done any playing. Well, now...It was in spurts before but then it got to the point where I had to make a choice. I mean a total commitment to one or the other. And being the kind of person I am, I knew that was going to take place, but I had to make a total commitment to either this administrative business or this artistic business of playing. So...
But right now your interest, your total dedication, is more to the administrative...

The priority now is in administrative, because the other way felt to me -- and I really thought it out, I had to give it some serious thought -- to me, playing was...I could always go back and play anything, and perhaps be a better

musician when I got back to it because of the satisfaction I received doing what I'm doing. That's what the music is about anyhow, that's what we are about. That's how you express yourself, you express your experiences. And my experiences now, wasn't a selfish thing.

You see, I thought if I had gone to play my music, which I was entitled to, with anybody else, I couldn't do that and do this. And tolet this go...It's like, of all the efforts I felt like I put into this thing, of the administrative pulling together and that type of thing, if I can just save one person, one kid, if Ijust find it possible for one child to express himself, it's worth it all. It's really worth it all, and I see it that way.

I feel like it's my way of putting something back, because look how much I've gotten out of music. I've been sitting here talking about some things here just a minute, and I can't get it all in, all the wonderful things that's happened, that I received from being a musician, playing.

Now, the greatest thing that happened to me now is to put some of that back, to sort of feed back in, hopefully to pass on, to help make a continuum. Playing for myself is great; it is for any musician. It's the greatest thing in the world to have an outlet to express yourself, especially through something like music. But it's a selfish thing for me to think that way.

Because I wouldn't want to benefit by that, no matter how great a piece I would play, when they would applaud, they would applaud for me, they wouldn't be applauding for...all those other people wouldn't be sharing that, that I'm sharing...
You're building an audience through what you're doing now, in a particular way...
It'll work in its own way. I feel it would, it's better...
But if, as a by-product,after all this effort, you get jazz into places where there has never been jazz before, whether it's the Strip or whether it's some small town in Montana...
Well, if you really analyze what you're saying, this is what I'm counting on to happen to. The thing that I make happen on the Strip is going to make some things happen in Montana.
That's right.
Quiet as it's kept now, believe me, I think by this being what it is, where it is, and what it's about, it's going
to trigger off like you wouldn't believe. We can open another frontier, a whole new frontier. It's going to have some effect around the world. I seriously believe that.
You remember when Dave Brubeck wrote a piece called 'The Real Ambassadors'?
Um-hm. I really believe that.
It's still going on and apparently you're becoming one of the new ambassadors, in ways that you might not have thought about 20 years ago.

Well, I hope now that I can give of myself and I know that I worked very hard to, made a lot of sacrifices, to give of myself. But you know, sometimes one of the hardest things in the world is to give somebody something. Trying to give...It's hard to give sometimes. That period in my life... I feel good about it, because I know things now...It's happening and the motion is going right for it.

There is a future to what we are doing. If something happened to me tomorrow and I pass on, it'll continue. It won't stop. The motion has gotten started, and it won't stop. I don't think they can take it away from us now; I don't think they want to. And I think the ones that I'm trying to reach with an open mind, whether they're there or whoever's there now, that open mind is there.

I think the time is right and it's ready and it's going to prove itself. It's going to be good and it's going to go right along with the trend because jazz now is in its highest resurgence in history. So, our tomorrow is OK. We don't have to worry about the tomorrow. The young people in the colleges and schools, even the high schools, they've gotten more involved with it than ever in the past.
So all these people in the industry and in the system, we don't have to worry about if it's going to last until tomorrow. Tomorrow's OK. Let's get it together today. Tomorrow is being taken care of.

And I'd just like to add to what all I've said. I don't want ever in the rest of my life to fail to say that...Don't look at me for what I've done. I didn't do this by myself. I had assistance. And a person, number one person, is I believe in God, and that filters down through all this other, the friends and everything else. I didn't do it alone. And I don't want it to ever be looked at as 'he did that.' It didn't...It was for a reason I was here and I just think that I happen to be fulfilling that reason, like the rest of them are. They're out there doing, even the bad guys. We're fulfilling it. There's a reason for us all.
And I believe it's starting from number one, not me. It's that man upstairs and it just filtered down. Right through the bad guys and all.

Las Vegas, Nevada
November 2, 1980
